meaning.en: To say, to speak, to utter, to express verbally in a deliberate, meaningful manner. Encompasses all forms of verbal expression — from divine creative command to human conversation, from revealed scripture to inner conviction voiced aloud. The root fundamentally bridges interior thought and exterior articulation.
meaning.ar: النُّطْقُ بِاللِّسَانِ، وَالتَّعْبِيرُ عَمَّا فِي النَّفْسِ بِالْكَلَامِ الْمَفْهُومِ، وَيَشْمَلُ الْأَمْرَ الْإِلٰهِيَّ وَالْحَدِيثَ الْبَشَرِيَّ وَالْوَحْيَ الْمُنَزَّلَ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Intentional, articulated expression — bridging consciousness to communication. The root denotes the act of giving form to thought through sound, ranging from casual speech to divine fiat.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ صَحِيحَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْكَلَامُ — وَهُوَ النُّطْقُ بِاللِّسَانِ، وَالْآخَرُ الْحَاجَةُ وَالطَّلَبُ — أَنْ تَقُولَ لِفُلَانٍ: قُلْ لِي كَذَا، أَيِ اطْلُبْ إِلَيَّ
ibn_faris.en: Two valid roots: (1) speech — utterance with the tongue; (2) need and petition — making a request from someone.

al_raghib.ar: الْقَوْلُ: إِظْهَارُ مَا فِي الضَّمِيرِ بِأَلْفَاظٍ مَنْظُومَةٍ، وَكُلُّ لَفْظٍ قَالَ بِهِ اللِّسَانُ تَامًّا كَانَ أَوْ نَاقِصًا يُسَمَّى قَوْلًا
al_raghib.en: Speech is the expression of what is in the mind through articulated words. Every word the tongue utters, complete or partial, is termed qawl.

quran_examples.ar: قُلْ يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْكَـٰفِرُونَ
quran_examples.en: Say: O disbelievers
quran_examples.context: Prophetic command to declare disavowal of paganism

quran_examples.ar: بَدِيعُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ وَإِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
quran_examples.en: When He decrees a matter, He only says to it: Be, and it is

quran_examples.ar: وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ٱدْعُونِىٓ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ
quran_examples.en: And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you

hadith.ar: مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ
hadith.en: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent.

hadith.ar: إِنَّ الْعَبْدَ لَيَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْكَلِمَةِ مِنْ رِضْوَانِ اللَّهِ لَا يُلْقِي لَهَا بَالًا يَرْفَعُهُ اللَّهُ بِهَا دَرَجَاتٍ، وَإِنَّ الْعَبْدَ لَيَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْكَلِمَةِ مِنْ سَخَطِ اللَّهِ لَا يُلْقِي لَهَا بَالًا يَهْوِي بِهَا فِي جَهَنَّمَ
hadith.en: A servant speaks a word pleasing to Allah, not thinking much of it, and Allah raises him degrees by it. And a servant speaks a word displeasing to Allah, not thinking much of it, and he plummets into Hell by it.

shades.explanation:
This shade represents one of the most profound theological concepts in the Quran: Allah's creative speech that brings existence into being without intermediary, instrument, or temporal delay. When Allah «says» to a thing 'KUN' (Be!), His word is not mere communication — it is the very act of creation. The exegetical tradition distinguishes this as al-qawl al-takwīnī (creative speech) versus al-qawl al-tashrīʿī (legislative speech/revelation).

Al-Ṭabarī notes in his tafsīr of 2:117 that the imperative 'kun' is addressed to the non-existent thing — demonstrating that divine speech transcends the limitations of human language which requires an existing addressee. Al-Rāzī (Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb) elaborates that Allah's qawl here is not a sequence of sounds or letters (which would be created) but rather an eternal attribute — al-kalām al-nafsī — whose effect manifests temporally as creation.

Ibn Taymiyyah (Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā) argues that this Quranic usage refutes the Muʿtazilite claim that the Quran is created, because if every instance of divine qawl were created speech, the creative command 'kun' itself would require a prior 'kun' to come into existence, leading to infinite regress. The Ashʿarī position similarly holds that kalām (speech) is an eternal attribute of Allah's essence (ṣifah nafsiyyah), with the created effects being its temporal manifestations.

The refrain 'innamā yaqūlu lahu KUN fa-yakūn' (He only says to it: BE, and it is) appears eight times in the Quran, always in contexts of affirming divine power over creation — the heavens and earth (2:117, 6:73), Jesus's miraculous birth (3:47, 3:59, 19:35), and the general principle of divine creative power (16:40, 36:82, 40:68). The placement of 'innamā' (only/merely) emphasizes the effortlessness of divine creation — contrasted with human making which requires labor, materials, and time.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَالَ: كُنْ فَيَكُونُ
shades.hadith_en: Indeed Allah said: Be, and it is

shades.name_en: Human Declaration and Testimony of Faith
shades.explanation:
The root distinguishes between outward verbal profession and inward conviction — a distinction central to the Quran's treatment of hypocrisy (nifāq). The hypocrites «yaqūlūna» (they say) with their tongues what is not in their hearts. This shade reveals the Quran's sophisticated moral psychology of speech: qawl is the bridge between the interior and exterior, and its moral value depends entirely on the alignment between what is spoken and what is believed.

The exegetes have extensively analyzed the Quranic formula «qālū āmannā» (they said: we believe) used by the hypocrites in passages like 2:8 and 2:14. Al-Qurṭubī (al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur'ān) notes that the verb «qāla» (he said) is used rather than «iʿtaqada» (he believed) precisely to highlight the gap between verbal claim and internal reality. Ibn Kathīr observes that Allah exposes the munāfiqūn by recording their speech and then immediately refuting their claim («wa-mā hum bi-mu'minīn» — they are not believers).

This shade also encompasses the positive dimension: the shahādah (testimony of faith) — «ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh» — where qawl becomes the verbal expression of genuine īmān. The ḥadīth tradition extensively discusses the salvific power of uttering the kalimah, as in Bukhārī 25: 'I have been commanded to fight people until they say lā ilāha illā Allāh.' The utterance (qawl) of the shahādah is the entry point to Islam, demonstrating that speech, when sincere, carries transformative legal and spiritual weight.
shades.hadith_ar: أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أُقَاتِلَ النَّاسَ حَتَّى يَقُولُوا لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
shades.hadith_en: I have been commanded to fight people until they say: there is no god but Allah

shades.explanation:
The past-tense verb «qāla» (he said) and its variants are among the most frequently occurring words in the Quran — appearing thousands of times. This is not incidental but reflects a deliberate Quranic rhetorical strategy: the entire scripture is structured around divine-human dialogue. The Quran does not merely describe events; it stages them dramatically through quoted speech — prophets addressing their peoples, angels speaking to Mary, Iblīs refusing to prostrate, Pharaoh's court debating Moses.

Al-Shāṭibī (al-Muwāfaqāt) identifies this dialogical structure as central to the Quran's rhetorical method (uslūb al-Qur'ān), designed to engage the listener as if witnessing the events firsthand. Unlike historical narrative that summarizes, the Quran presents direct speech — creating immediacy and moral urgency. Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf) notes that the frequent use of «qāla/qālū» without attribution of tone or expression leaves interpretive space for the reader to infer sarcasm, anger, wonder, or sincerity from context.

The phrase «qāla rasūlu Llāhi» (the Messenger of Allah said) — ubiquitous in ḥadīth literature — extends this narrative function beyond the Quran. The entire ḥadīth corpus is structured around the transmission of qawl (sayings) of the Prophet ﷺ, demonstrating how this root became the epistemological backbone of Islamic tradition: what someone 'said' constitutes knowledge, law, and guidance. The isnād system (chain of transmission) is fundamentally a chain of qawl — person A said that person B said that person C said.
shades.hadith_ar: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ
shades.hadith_en: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Actions are but by intentions

shades.name_en: Qawl as Doctrine, Opinion, and Theological Position
shades.explanation:
In Quranic usage, qawl frequently denotes not just speech but a doctrinal position, an ideological claim, or a theological assertion — especially when the content is grave or blasphemous. The phrase «qālū ttakhadha Llāhu waladan» (they said: Allah has taken a son) is the most prominent example, where «qālū» introduces not casual conversation but a theological claim of the highest gravity.

In 17:40, the Quran confronts the pagan claim that Allah has daughters from among the angels, using the term «la-taqūlūna qawlan ʿaẓīmā» (you are saying a monstrous thing). Al-Rāzī comments that the gravity of the statement is not in its linguistic form but in its theological implication — it attributes to Allah what is beneath His majesty. Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) notes that the indefinite «qawlan» followed by the adjective «ʿaẓīmā» (tremendous/grievous) intensifies the condemnation: not just a statement, but a statement of monstrous proportions.

This shade also explains why Islamic legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh) developed the technical term «qawl» to refer to a scholar's legal opinion or doctrine. The «aqwāl» (plural of qawl) of the ṣaḥābah and the imams of the madhāhib are recorded as authoritative precedents. Al-Shāfiʿī's «al-qawl al-qadīm» and «al-qawl al-jadīd» (the old doctrine and the new doctrine) are the most famous examples of qawl used in this technical sense — demonstrating how the root evolved from 'speech' to 'doctrinal position' in Islamic intellectual history.

The Quran describes itself as 'qawl' — the speech or word of Allah. In 69:40: «innahu la-qawlu rasūlin karīm» (indeed it is the speech of a noble messenger), and in 81:19: «innahu la-qawlu rasūlin karīm» — the Quran is characterized as 'qawl' transmitted through the angel Jibrīl. The root here carries the full weight of divine authority: what is spoken by Allah through His messenger constitutes binding revelation.

The theological implications are profound. If the Quran is «qawl Allāh» (the speech of Allah), then its words are uncreated (according to the orthodox Sunni position), being an eternal attribute of the Divine essence. The Muʿtazilite position — that the Quran is created (makhlūq) — was partly based on a different understanding of the relationship between divine qawl and human language. The miḥnah (inquisition) under the ʿAbbāsid caliph al-Ma'mūn centered precisely on this question: is the Quran the eternal qawl of Allah or created speech?

Al-Ṭaḥāwī's famous creed (al-ʿAqīdah al-Ṭaḥāwiyyah) states: 'The Quran is the speech (kalām) of Allah; it proceeded from Him as articulated speech (qawlan) without us knowing how (bilā kayf).' Al-Māturīdī (Kitāb al-Tawḥīd) argues that the Quran's designation as 'qawl' confirms its divine origin, since no human could produce speech of comparable eloquence and truth.

In 39:23, the Quran describes itself as «aḥsana al-ḥadīthi» (the best of speech/discourse) — linking qawl not only to divine authority but to aesthetic perfection. The Prophet ﷺ himself described the Quran as «aḥsanu al-ḥadīthi kitābu Llāh» (the best speech is the Book of Allah) in his famous khuṭbah recorded in Muslim 867.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ كِتَابُ اللَّهِ، وَأَحْسَنَ الْهَدْيِ هَدْيُ مُحَمَّدٍ
shades.hadith_en: Indeed the best speech is the Book of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad

meaning.en: To be, to exist, to occur, to come into being, to become. The most fundamental ontological verb in Arabic — expressing existence, temporal state, transformation, and the transition from non-existence to existence. Central to Islamic theology as the verb through which Allah's creative power is expressed (KUN fa-yakūn).
meaning.ar: الْوُجُودُ وَالْحُدُوثُ، وَالصَّيْرُورَةُ وَالِاتِّصَافُ بِالْحَالِ. أَصْلُ الْفِعْلِ فِي اللُّغَةِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ الدَّالُّ عَلَى الْكَيْنُونَةِ وَالزَّمَانِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Existence and temporal being — the bridge between nothingness and existence, between past state and present condition, between potential and actuality. The root anchors Arabic's tensed ontology.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حُدُوثِ الشَّيْءِ وَكَوْنِهِ. تَقُولُ: كَانَ الْأَمْرُ يَكُونُ كَوْنًا. وَالْكَيْنُونَةُ: مَصْدَرُ كَانَ
ibn_faris.en: A single root meaning: the occurrence of a thing and its coming into being. You say: kāna l-amru yakūnu kawnan. Kaynūnah is the verbal noun of kāna.

al_raghib.ar: كَانَ تُسْتَعْمَلُ عَلَى أَوْجُهٍ: عِبَارَةٌ عَنِ الْوُجُودِ الْمُطْلَقِ (كَقَوْلِهِ: كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ)، وَعَنِ الزَّمَانِ الْمَاضِي، وَعَنِ الِاتِّصَافِ، وَعَنِ الصَّيْرُورَةِ
al_raghib.en: Kāna is used in multiple ways: to express absolute existence (as in 'Allah existed and nothing was'), past time, attribution of qualities, and becoming/transformation.

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
quran_examples.en: When He decrees a matter, He says: Be, and it is

quran_examples.ar: قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ
quran_examples.en: Say: He is Allah, the One

quran_examples.ar: هُوَ ٱلْأَوَّلُ وَٱلْـَٔاخِرُ وَٱلظَّـٰهِرُ وَٱلْبَاطِنُ ۖ وَهُوَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمٌ
quran_examples.en: He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is Knowing of all things

hadith.ar: كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ قَبْلَهُ، وَكَانَ عَرْشُهُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ، وَكَتَبَ فِي الذِّكْرِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ، وَخَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ
hadith.en: Allah existed and there was nothing before Him. His Throne was upon the water. He wrote in the Remembrance everything, and created the heavens and the earth.

hadith.ar: إِنَّ أَوَّلَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ الْقَلَمَ، فَقَالَ لَهُ: اكْتُبْ. قَالَ: رَبِّ وَمَاذَا أَكْتُبُ؟ قَالَ: اكْتُبْ مَقَادِيرَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
hadith.en: The first thing Allah created was the Pen. He said: Write. It said: My Lord, what shall I write? He said: Write the decrees of everything until the Hour is established.

shades.explanation:
The imperative «KUN» (Be!) is the most theologically dense occurrence of this root — appearing eight times in the Quran as the mechanism of divine creation. When Allah wills something to exist, He says «KUN fa-yakūn» — Be, and it is. The juxtaposition of imperative (kun) and imperfect (fa-yakūn) compresses the entire act of creation into two words, eliminating any notion of process, material, or temporal extension.

Al-Rāzī (Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb) provides a detailed philosophical analysis: the address «kun» is directed to what does not yet exist (al-maʿdūm), proving that divine speech does not require a pre-existing addressee — unlike human speech which presupposes a listener. This, al-Rāzī argues, demonstrates that Allah's kalām is an eternal attribute (ṣifah qadīmah), not created sounds or letters. The thing addressed in «kun» had no prior existence to receive the address, yet it comes into being — proving creation ex nihilo.

Al-Ṭabarī's tafsīr of 2:117 emphasizes that the particle «innamā» (only/merely) in «innamā yaqūlu lahu KUN fa-yakūn» highlights the effortlessness of divine creation: Allah does not need materials, helpers, or instruments — His will alone, expressed as qawl, is sufficient. Al-Qurṭubī adds that this refutes those who claim the world is eternal (qidam al-ʿālam), since the very concept of «kun» implies a beginning and a transition from non-being to being.

The theological debates around this verse are extensive. The Ashāʿirah use «kun fa-yakūn» to prove that Allah's creative act (takwīn) is distinct from the created thing (mukawwan) and is connected to His eternal attribute of Power (qudrah). The Māturīdiyyah emphasize that takwīn is an eternal attribute — Allah was eternally «Khāliq» (Creator) even before creation existed. The Atharī position (represented by Ibn Taymiyyah) sees the verse as affirming that Allah creates by His will and word, without delving into the modality of how the command operates.
shades.hadith_ar: كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ قَبْلَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Allah existed and there was nothing before Him

shades.name_en: Past Existence and Completed State — Kāna (Was)
shades.explanation:
As the primary past-tense copula in Arabic, «kāna» anchors events, states, and descriptions in completed time. Syntactically, kāna and its 'sisters' (kāna wa-akhawātuhā) form the most important class of verbs in Arabic grammar — they enter upon nominal sentences and govern the predicate in the accusative (mansūb), transforming timeless descriptions into time-bound assertions.

The grammarians of Basra and Kufa debated whether kāna carries independent semantic content or functions purely as a temporal marker (zamāniyyah). Sībawayh (al-Kitāb) classifies kāna as a verb that indicates both time and event (ḥadath), while later grammarians like Ibn Mālik (al-Alfiyyah) treat it primarily as indicating time with a weakened event meaning. This grammatical ambiguity reflects a deeper philosophical question: does kāna merely 'locate' a predicate in time, or does it additionally assert the predicate's occurrence?

In Quranic usage, kāna performs critical theological work. In 2:30 «wa-idh qāla rabbuka li-l-malā'ikati innī jāʿilun fī l-arḍi khalīfatan», the surrounding imperfect verbs place the narrative in primordial time — kāna (implicit in the structure) establishes the temporal framework for the pre-creation covenant. In 3:59 «inna mathala ʿĪsā ʿinda Llāhi ka-mathali Ādama khalaqahu min turābin thumma qāla lahu KUN fa-yakūn», the past-tense kāna in the larger discourse anchors the comparison between Jesus and Adam in established theological fact.

The negation «mā kāna» (it was not / it is not befitting) deserves special attention. In 19:35 «mā kāna li-Llāhi an yattakhidha min waladin», the negation of kāna expresses ontological impossibility — it is not merely that Allah did not take a son, but that the very concept is incompatible with divine nature. This usage of kāna to express essential impossibility rather than mere non-occurrence is a distinctively Quranic rhetorical feature noted by al-Zamakhsharī.
shades.hadith_ar: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَجْوَدَ النَّاسِ بِالْخَيْرِ
shades.hadith_en: The Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people in goodness

shades.name_en: Continuous and Habitual Past — Kāna + Imperfect
shades.explanation:
When kāna governs an imperfect verb (fiʿl muḍāriʿ), the combination expresses habitual, continuous, or repeated action in the past — 'he used to do,' 'they would consistently do.' This grammatical pattern is one of the most distinctive features of Quranic narrative style, allowing the text to convey sustained patterns of behavior rather than isolated events.

The grammarians term this usage «kāna li-l-istimrār» (kāna for continuity). Al-Suyūṭī (Hamʿ al-Hawāmiʿ) explains that the imperfect verb after kāna retains its durative aspect while kāna provides the temporal anchoring in the past. The result is a compound meaning: 'the action was ongoing in the past' — whether habitual (ʿādah), continuous (istimrār), or progressive (ḥāl mudāwimah).

This pattern is crucial for Quranic moral characterization. In 2:61 «dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Llāh» (that was because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah) — the kāna + imperfect construction presents disbelief not as a singular event but as a persistent, characteristic behavior that defined the Children of Israel's historical relationship with divine revelation. The use of kāna here carries moral weight: it is not that they disbelieved once, but that disbelief was their habitual state.

In Prophetic biography, this grammatical pattern dominates the sīrah and ḥadīth literature: «kāna rasūlu Llāhi ṣallā Llāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam yuṣallī...» (the Messenger of Allah used to pray...), «kāna yaṣūmu...» (he used to fast...), «kāna yadhkuru Llāha...» (he used to remember Allah...). This grammatical form is the linguistic foundation of the Sunnah — it records not one-time actions but the Prophetic practice (sunnah) as an enduring pattern. The ḥadīth scholars' preference for this formulation reflects their methodological commitment to establishing normative, repeatable precedent rather than isolated incidents.
shades.hadith_ar: كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُحِبُّ التَّيَمُّنَ فِي شَأْنِهِ كُلِّهِ
shades.hadith_en: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to prefer the right side in all his affairs

shades.explanation:
The root can signify transformation or becoming — movement from one state of being to another. In 21:69, when Ibrāhīm is thrown into the fire, Allah commands: «qulnā yā nāru kūnī bardan wa-salāman ʿalā Ibrāhīm» (We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham). The command «kūnī» (Be! — feminine imperative, addressing the fire) transforms the very nature of fire from burning to coolness — a miraculous ontological reversal.

This usage demonstrates that the root's semantic range extends beyond static existence to dynamic transformation. Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf) marvels at this verse: the fire received a command (kūnī) that inverted its essential property (ṭabʿ) — fire by nature burns, yet Allah commanded it to be cold, and it obeyed. This is not merely a temperature change but an ontological transformation — the fire's 'being' was reshaped by divine command.

The shade of ṣayrūrah (becoming) also appears in the repeated Quranic narrative of the angels' prostration to Adam: «idh qāla rabbuka li-l-malā'ikati innī khāliqun basharan min ṭīnin, fa-idhā sawwaituhu wa-nafakhtu fīhi min rūḥī fa-qaʿū lahu sājidīn» — the sequence implies a becoming: from clay to formed body to ensouled being. The implicit kāna/kāna-structures in these creation narratives trace the stages of becoming.

Ibn ʿArabī (al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyyah) develops a sophisticated metaphysical reading: all creation is in constant kawm (becoming) — nothing in the created order is static. Each moment, creation is renewed (tajdīd al-khalq), and the root k-w-n expresses this perpetual ontological flux. This reading connects the Quranic «kun fa-yakūn» to the Ṣūfī concept of perpetual creation — Allah's creative act is not a single past event but an ongoing, instantaneous renewal of existence at every moment.

This shade represents the root's application to Allah's eternal, necessary existence — distinct in kind from all contingent, temporal being. The ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3191 provides the foundational formulation: «kāna Llāhu wa-lam yakun shay'un qablahu» (Allah existed and there was nothing before Him) and «kāna Llāhu wa-lam yakun shay'un ghayruhu» (Allah existed and there was nothing besides Him). Here kāna expresses absolute, unconditioned existence — the wujūd of the Necessary Being (wājib al-wujūd).

The Islamic philosophical tradition, particularly Ibn Sīnā (al-Shifāʾ), developed a rigorous ontology based on the distinction between wājib al-wujūd (the Necessary Existent — whose essence is identical with existence) and mumkin al-wujūd (the contingent existent — whose existence is accidental and dependent). The root k-w-n is central to this discourse: the question «hal yakūnu?» (can it be?) frames all discussions of possibility and actuality.

Al-Ghazālī (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah), while critiquing Ibn Sīnā, preserves the centrality of k-w-n in theological discourse. His famous formulation in Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn — that Allah is «al-Mawjūd al-Ḥaqq» (the Truly Existent) — draws on the root's semantic field. Later kalām theologians (al-Ījī, al-Taftāzānī) structured their discussions of divine attributes around the concept of wujūd (existence) derived from w-j-d, but k-w-n remained the primary verb for predicating existence.

In Ṣūfī thought, particularly Ibn ʿArabī's school, the distinction between kawm (being/becoming) and wujūd (existence/finding) becomes central to the metaphysics of the divine names. «Kāna Llāh» in the ḥadīth is read not merely as 'Allah was' but as a statement about the nature of divine existence: timeless, absolute, prior to all relations and determinations. Al-Qūnawī, Ibn ʿArabī's stepson and commentator, develops a full cosmological theory from this ḥadīth in his Miftāḥ al-Ghayb.
shades.hadith_ar: كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْءٌ غَيْرُهُ
shades.hadith_en: Allah existed and there was nothing besides Him

meaning.en: Lord, master, owner, sustainer, nurturer, sovereign. One who possesses authority, provides care and upbringing, manages affairs, and brings to completion. The most frequent divine title in the Quran — expressing Allah's comprehensive lordship over creation.
meaning.ar: الْمَالِكُ، وَالسَّيِّدُ، وَالْمُدَبِّرُ، وَالْمُرَبِّي، وَالْمُنْعِمُ، وَالْقَيِّمُ، وَالْجَامِعُ. أَشْمَلُ أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ دَلَالَةً عَلَى الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ الْعَامَّةِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Comprehensive lordship — the convergence of ownership (mulk), authority (siyādah), nurturing care (tarbiyah), management (tadbīr), and bringing to completion (tablīgh ilā l-kamāl). The Arabic rabb is a multi-dimensional concept with no exact English equivalent.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا إِصْلَاحُ الشَّيْءِ وَالْقِيَامُ عَلَيْهِ — وَمِنْهُ الرَّبُّ: الْمَالِكُ وَالْخَالِقُ وَالصَّاحِبُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْجَمْعُ وَالشِّدَّةُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) reforming and stewarding something — hence rabb meaning owner, creator, companion; (2) gathering and intensity. The double-bā (gemination) reflects the comprehensive, encompassing nature of lordship.

al_raghib.ar: الرَّبُّ فِي الْأَصْلِ: التَّرْبِيَةُ وَهِيَ إِنْشَاءُ الشَّيْءِ حَالًا فَحَالًا إِلَى حَدِّ التَّمَامِ. فَالرَّبُّ: الْمُبَلِّغُ إِلَى الْكَمَالِ شَيْئًا فَشَيْئًا
al_raghib.en: Rabb originally means tarbiyah: bringing something into being stage by stage to its completion. The rabb is the one who brings to perfection gradually — nurturing from inception to fullness.

quran_examples.ar: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ
quran_examples.en: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds
quran_examples.context: Opening of al-Fātiḥah — the cosmic lordship

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكُمْ وَٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ
quran_examples.en: O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you

quran_examples.ar: ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ
quran_examples.en: Read in the name of your Lord who created
quran_examples.context: First revelation — knowledge in the name of the Rabb

hadith.ar: اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّي لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ، خَلَقْتَنِي وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ، وَأَنَا عَلَى عَهْدِكَ وَوَعْدِكَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ، أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا صَنَعْتُ، أَبُوءُ لَكَ بِنِعْمَتِكَ عَلَيَّ، وَأَبُوءُ بِذَنْبِي، فَاغْفِرْ لِي فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
hadith.en: O Allah, You are my Lord. There is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant. I am upon Your covenant and promise as much as I am able. I seek refuge in You from the evil I have done. I acknowledge Your favor upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.
hadith.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6306 — Sayyid al-Istighfār (Master Supplication for Forgiveness)

hadith.ar: مَنْ رَضِيَ بِاللَّهِ رَبًّا وَبِالْإِسْلَامِ دِينًا وَبِمُحَمَّدٍ رَسُولًا وَجَبَتْ لَهُ الْجَنَّةُ
hadith.en: Whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion, and Muhammad as Messenger — Paradise is guaranteed for him.

shades.explanation:
«Al-ḥamdu li-Llāhi Rabbi l-ʿĀlamīn» — these opening words of al-Fātiḥah establish the foundational Islamic declaration: all praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of all worlds. The term 'ālamīn (worlds) encompasses everything besides Allah — the material universe, the spiritual realms, the human world, the animal kingdom, the angelic domain. By appending «Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn» to «al-ḥamdu li-Llāh», the verse links praise directly to lordship: Allah is praised precisely because He is the Rabb.

The Islamic theological tradition has developed an extensive discourse around rubūbiyyah (lordship) as distinct from ulūhiyyah (divinity). Ibn Taymiyyah, in his detailed analysis in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā and al-Risālah al-Tadmuriyyah, argues that rubūbiyyah encompasses Allah's actions in creation — creating, sustaining, providing, giving life and death, managing affairs — while ulūhiyyah encompasses the rights Allah deserves from His creation — worship, love, fear, hope, obedience. The mushrikūn of Quraysh, Ibn Taymiyyah notes, affirmed rubūbiyyah (they believed Allah was the Creator and Sustainer) but denied ulūhiyyah (they worshipped others alongside Him). Quranic polemics against shirk consistently argue from affirmed rubūbiyyah to demanded ulūhiyyah: if He is your Rabb who created you, why do you worship others? (See 2:21, 10:3, 10:31-32).

Al-Qurṭubī connects the root to the idea of ownership and authority. Rabb derives from the verbal noun tarbiyah, but its scope far exceeds mere 'nurturing' — it includes absolute disposal (taṣarruf), unchallenged command (amr nāfidh), and comprehensive sovereignty. The shaddah (gemination) on the bā' — distinguishing رَبّ from the hypothetical رَب — indicates intensity and completeness of lordship. The definite form «al-Rabb» is reserved exclusively for Allah in Islamic usage; applied to others, it must be in construct (iḍāfah) as in «rabb al-dār» (master of the house).
shades.hadith_ar: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ هِيَ السَّبْعُ الْمَثَانِي وَالْقُرْآنُ الْعَظِيمُ الَّذِي أُوتِيتُهُ
shades.hadith_en: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds — it is the Seven Oft-Repeated (verses) and the Great Quran that I have been given

shades.name_en: Personal Lord and Nurturer — al-Rabb al-Khāṣṣ
shades.explanation:
When the Quran adds possessive pronouns — «rabbuka» (your Lord), «rabbunā» (our Lord), «rabbī» (my Lord) — the impersonal title of cosmic sovereignty becomes intensely personal. «Rabbuka» in the singular address to the Prophet ﷺ («iqra' bi-smi rabbika» — 96:1) personalizes lordship as a direct, caring relationship between the Lord and His Messenger. The Prophet is not merely addressing a distant creator but his personal Rabb who nurtures, guides, and cares for him specifically.

The supplications of the prophets recorded in the Quran are uniformly addressed with «rabbanā» or «rabbi» — never with the abstract «Allāh» or «al-Rabb» alone. Ibrāhīm prays: «rabbi ijʿalnī muqīma l-ṣalāti» (My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer — 14:40). Mūsā pleads: «rabbi innī ẓalamtu nafsī fa-ghfir lī» (My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me — 28:16). Zakariyyā cries: «rabbi lā tadharnī fardan» (My Lord, do not leave me alone — 21:89). The pattern is unmistakable: intimate supplication uses the personal Rabb, not the distant Ilāh.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Madārij al-Sālikīn) develops a profound spiritual psychology from this usage. The soul's journey to Allah progresses through stations (manāzil), and the station of tawḥīd al-rubūbiyyah is foundational — recognizing that every blessing, every moment of guidance, every answered prayer comes from the Rabb who personally tends to His servant. The Prophet's nightly prayer recorded in Bukhārī 1120 — «Allāhumma rabbanā laka l-ḥamdu anta qayyimu l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi» — begins with rabbanā, merging cosmic lordship with personal intimacy. Ibn al-Qayyim comments that the one who truly knows Allah as his personal Rabb cannot despair, because the Rabb does not abandon what He nurtures.

The verse 17:24 «wa-qul rabbi rḥamhumā kamā rabbayānī ṣaghīrā» (and say: My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small) reveals the root's etymological connection to tarbiyah (raising/nurturing). The parents' care for the child — physical, emotional, educational — is described with the same root that describes Allah's care for His creation. This semantic link grounds the Islamic ethic of parental reverence in the very structure of the Arabic language: to be a rabb to one's child is to participate, in a limited human way, in the divine attribute of nurturing lordship.
shades.hadith_ar: رَبِّ أَعِنِّي وَلَا تُعِنْ عَلَيَّ، وَانْصُرْنِي وَلَا تَنْصُرْ عَلَيَّ، وَامْكُرْ لِي وَلَا تَمْكُرْ عَلَيَّ، وَاهْدِنِي وَيَسِّرِ الْهُدَىٰ إِلَيَّ
shades.hadith_en: My Lord, help me and do not help against me; support me and do not support against me; plan for me and do not plan against me; guide me and make guidance easy for me

shades.name_en: Tarbiyah — Gradual Nurturing from Inception to Completion
shades.explanation:
The etymological heart of the root — tarbiyah — is the process of nurturing something from its inception through its developmental stages to its full maturity. This is not instantaneous creation (which is khalq) but gradual, caring cultivation. A rabb is one who tends, raises, educates, provides for, and brings to completion. The metaphor extends from plant cultivation to child-rearing to soul-development.

Al-Rāghib's definition captures this precisely: «inshā'u l-shay'i ḥālan fa-ḥālan ilā ḥaddi l-tamām» — bringing something into being stage by stage to its completion. The rabb is the one who does not merely initiate but accompanies the process, providing what is needed at each developmental stage. This is why «rabb» can be applied to a human master or owner who 'raises' his property, or to a teacher who 'cultivates' his students — the term implies an ongoing, developmental relationship, not a one-time act.

The Quranic usage in 17:24 makes this explicit: «ka-mā rabbayānī ṣaghīrā» (as they raised me when I was small). The verb «rabbā» (Form II) describes the parents' nurturing of the child — feeding, clothing, educating, protecting, loving — the complete process of upbringing. This is the same verb used for Allah's nurturing of creation: the gradual unfolding of a human being from a drop of fluid (nuṭfah) through stages (aṭwār) to a fully formed, reasoning adult (71:13-14).

The concept has profound theological implications. Allah's rubūbiyyah is not static but dynamic — He continually sustains, guides, and brings His creation toward their appointed ends. The mutakallimūn debated whether Allah's attribute of tarbiyah is eternal or originated. The Ashʿarī position: tarbiyah is an originated action (ḥādith) connected to creatures, while the source attribute of Power and Will from which tarbiyah proceeds is eternal. The Māturīdī position: takwīn (bringing into being) is itself an eternal attribute, eternally connected to its objects at their appointed times. Both positions affirm that Allah's nurturing care for creation is continuous and personal, not merely an initial act of creation followed by abandonment.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ رَبَّانِيٌّ يُحِبُّ الرَّبَّانِيِّينَ
shades.hadith_en: Indeed Allah is rabbānī (nurturing Lord), and He loves those who are rabbāniyyūn (devoted to nurturing others in knowledge and character)

shades.explanation:
The semantic overlap between «rabb» and «mālik» (owner/king) in the Quran is deliberate and significant. In 106:3, the Quraysh are commanded to worship «Rabba hādhā l-bayt» (the Lord of this House — the Kaʿbah). The choice of Rabb over Mālik here is instructive: Rabb includes ownership but adds the dimensions of care, protection, and honor. The Kaʿbah is not merely Allah's property — He is its Lord who preserves it, honors those who serve it, and protects those who seek refuge there.

Al-Fātiḥah's progression from «Rabbi l-ʿĀlamīn» (1:2) to «Māliki Yawmi l-Dīn» (1:4) reveals the Quranic distinction between these divine titles. Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn emphasizes Allah's comprehensive lordship in this world — creating, sustaining, guiding, providing. Mālik Yawm al-Dīn emphasizes His exclusive sovereignty on the Day of Judgment — when all pretenders to authority are stripped away and only His ownership remains. The shift from Rabb to Mālik maps onto the shift from dunyā to ākhirah, from the world of means (asbāb) to the world of direct divine judgment.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Badāʾiʿ al-Fawāʾid) notes a linguistic subtlety: «Rabb» is from a doubled root (mudāʿaf — r-b-b) indicating intensity and comprehensiveness, while «Mālik» is from a hollow root (ajwaf — m-l-k). The gemination in Rabb suggests a lordship so complete and intense that no aspect of creation falls outside it. This is why the Quran frequently pairs «lahu mulku l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi» (to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth) with descriptions of His rubūbiyyah — ownership (mulk) is a dimension of lordship (rubūbiyyah), and lordship without ownership would be incomplete.

The ḥadīth literature preserves the Prophet's frequent use of «Rabb» in the possessive: «rabb al-ʿizzati» (Lord of Might), «rabb al-ʿarshi l-ʿaẓīm» (Lord of the Great Throne), «rabb al-mashriqayni wa-rabb al-maghribayn» (Lord of the two Easts and Lord of the two Wests). Each construct pairs Rabb with a domain, asserting comprehensive lordship over that domain while implying lordship over everything within it.
shades.hadith_ar: سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ الْعَظِيمِ — سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ الْأَعْلَىٰ
shades.hadith_en: Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent — Glory be to my Lord, the Most High

shades.name_en: Rabb as Object of Supplication and Refuge
shades.explanation:
The Quran's supplicatory passages are dominated by the vocative «rabbanā» (Our Lord) and «rabbi» (My Lord). This is not merely conventional — it reflects a theological stance. The worshipper approaches Allah not primarily as al-Ilāh (the Deity, which emphasizes His right to be worshipped) but as al-Rabb (the Lord, which emphasizes His care, mercy, and provision). The shift from Ilāh to Rabb in prayer signals a transition from metaphysical affirmation to personal relationship.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn, Book of Invocations) analyzes the structure of prophetic supplications and notes that they universally begin with Rabb, not Allāh or any other name. «Rabbanā ẓalamnā anfusanā» (Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves — 7:23, the prayer of Adam and Eve). «Rabbanā lā tuzigh qulūbanā» (Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate — 3:8, the prayer of the firmly-grounded in knowledge). «Rabbanā innanā samiʿnā munādiyan» (Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller — 3:193, the prayer of the people of understanding). The pattern is consistent across the entire Quran: when humans call upon Allah, they call Him Rabb.

This has profound implications for Islamic spirituality. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh al-Iskandarī (al-Ḥikam) observes that Allah has taught His servants to call Him «Rabb» because the state of being a «marbūb» (one who is lorded over, a dependent) is the truest description of the human condition before Allah. We are not independent beings who choose to worship — we are inherently dependent beings whose very existence is an ongoing gift from the Rabb. Recognizing this dependency (iftiqār) is the essence of ʿubūdiyyah (servitude).

The ḥadīth of the Prophet's night prayer (Bukhārī 1120, Muslim 769) opens with «Allāhumma rabbanā laka l-ḥamdu» — O Allah, our Lord, to You is all praise. The doubling — Allāhumma (O Allah) then rabbanā (our Lord) — combines the two dimensions: the transcendent deity worthy of worship (Allāh) and the immanent Lord who hears and answers (Rabb). This dual address is the linguistic embodiment of tawḥīd: Allah is both the One who deserves worship and the One who cares for His worshippers.
shades.hadith_ar: اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
shades.hadith_en: O Allah, our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter and protect us from the punishment of the Fire

meaning.en: To be secure, safe, at peace, free from fear. To believe, have faith, trust, and be faithful. To entrust something valuable to someone's care. The root bridges the concepts of psychological safety and theological conviction — true faith (īmān) is the ultimate source of security (amn).
meaning.ar: الْأَمَانُ وَالسَّلَامَةُ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةُ — زَوَالُ الْخَوْفِ؛ وَالتَّصْدِيقُ وَالْإِذْعَانُ — الْإِيمَانُ؛ وَالْأَمَانَةُ — حِفْظُ مَا اؤْتُمِنَ عَلَيْهِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: The convergence of security, trust, and belief. The root moves from inward tranquility (amn — absence of fear) to interpersonal trust (amānah — faithfulness) to theological commitment (īmān — belief). The three dimensions are causally linked: only the one who feels secure can trust, and only the trustworthy can truly believe.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ مُتَقَارِبَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْأَمَانَةُ الَّتِي هِيَ ضِدُّ الْخِيَانَةِ — وَمَعْنَاهَا سُكُونُ الْقَلْبِ، وَالْآخَرُ التَّصْدِيقُ
ibn_faris.en: Two closely related roots: (1) amānah — trustworthiness, opposite of betrayal, implying tranquility of heart; (2) taṣdīq — confirmation/belief. The link: security of heart enables trust, and trust enables belief.

al_raghib.ar: أَصْلُ الْأَمْنِ: طُمَأْنِينَةُ النَّفْسِ وَزَوَالُ الْخَوْفِ. وَالْأَمْنُ وَالْأَمَانَةُ وَالْأَمَانُ فِي الْأَصْلِ مَصَادِرُ، وَيُجْعَلُ الْأَمَانُ تَارَةً اسْمًا لِلْحَالَةِ الَّتِي يَكُونُ عَلَيْهَا الْإِنْسَانُ حِينَ يَكُونُ آمِنًا
al_raghib.en: The root of amn is tranquility of the soul and the removal of fear. Amn, amānah, and amān are originally verbal nouns, but amān is sometimes used as a noun for the state of being secure.

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِىٓ أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍۢ وَءَامَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍۭ
quran_examples.en: Who fed them against hunger and gave them security from fear
quran_examples.context: Blessings upon Quraysh — food and security

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ
quran_examples.en: Those who believe in the unseen
quran_examples.context: The defining trait of the muttaqūn — belief in the unseen

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا ٱلْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱلْجِبَالِ فَأَبَيْنَ أَن يَحْمِلْنَهَا
quran_examples.en: We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, but they refused to bear it

hadith.ar: الْمُسْلِمُ مَنْ سَلِمَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ وَيَدِهِ، وَالْمُؤْمِنُ مَنْ أَمِنَهُ النَّاسُ عَلَى دِمَائِهِمْ وَأَمْوَالِهِمْ
hadith.en: The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe. And the believer (mu'min) is one whom the people trust with their blood and wealth.

hadith.ar: لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يُحِبَّ لِأَخِيهِ مَا يُحِبُّ لِنَفْسِهِ
hadith.en: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.

shades.name_en: Īmān — Saving Faith and Theological Conviction
shades.explanation:
The Form IV verb «āmana» (آمَنَ) and its verbal noun «īmān» (إِيمَان) represent one of the most theologically weighty concepts in Islam — translated variously as faith, belief, conviction, and trust. The root's semantic movement from 'security' to 'belief' is not accidental: true īmān is the śource of existential security. The one who has īmān is «mu'min» — one who has entered a state of safety through trust in Allah.

The classical Islamic theological tradition devoted extraordinary attention to defining īmān. The Murji'ah held that īmān is purely a matter of the heart — verbal confession (iqrār bi-l-lisān) and physical action (ʿamal bi-l-arkān) are not constituent parts of īmān but its consequences. The Khawārij held the opposite extreme — that major sins negate īmān entirely. The mainstream Ahl al-Sunnah position, articulated most influentially by Abū Ḥanīfah (al-Fiqh al-Akbar), al-Ashʿarī (al-Ibānah), and al-Ṭaḥāwī (al-ʿAqīdah al-Ṭaḥāwiyyah), holds that īmān is «taṣdīq bi-l-qalb wa-iqrār bi-l-lisān wa-ʿamal bi-l-arkān» — affirmation in the heart, declaration by the tongue, and action by the limbs. Īmān increases with obedience and decreases with disobedience.

The Qur'ānic usage supports this integrative understanding. In 49:14, the Bedouins claim «āmannā» (we have believed), but Allah corrects them: «qul lam tu'minū wa-lākin qūlū aslamnā wa-lammā yadkhuli l-īmānu fī qulūbikum» — you have not yet believed; say rather: we have submitted, for īmān has not yet entered your hearts. This verse establishes a critical distinction between islām (outward submission) and īmān (inward conviction), while not severing them — islām is the gateway to īmān. Al-Qurṭubī comments that the Bedouins' claim was rejected because īmān requires sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and settled conviction (tamakkun fī l-qalb), which they had not yet attained.

The Ḥanbalī tradition, represented by Ibn Taymiyyah (Kitāb al-Īmān), emphasizes that īmān is «qawl wa-ʿamal» — speech and action — and that it increases and decreases. This dynamic understanding of īmān as a living, fluctuating reality in the believer's heart has profound implications for spiritual psychology: the believer is constantly striving to strengthen and renew their īmān, never complacent about its state.
shades.hadith_ar: الْإِيمَانُ بِضْعٌ وَسَبْعُونَ شُعْبَةً، فَأَفْضَلُهَا قَوْلُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَأَدْنَاهَا إِمَاطَةُ الْأَذَى عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ، وَالْحَيَاءُ شُعْبَةٌ مِنَ الْإِيمَانِ
shades.hadith_en: Faith has over seventy branches. The best is saying 'No god but Allah.' The lowest is removing harm from the path. And modesty is a branch of faith.

shades.explanation:
The primary nominal form «amn» (security/safety) designates the state of being free from fear — a fundamental human need elevated in the Quran to a divine blessing and a sign of Allah's favor. Sūrat Quraysh (106:1-4) encapsulates this: the Quraysh are reminded that their commercial security — the winter and summer caravan journeys — is a gift from «Rabbi hādhā l-bayt» (the Lord of this House) who «aṭʿamahum min jūʿin wa-āmanahum min khawf» (fed them against hunger and secured them from fear). Security from hunger and fear are presented as twin foundations of civilized life — without them, no society can flourish.

The concept of the Ḥaram (sanctuary) in Mecca is intimately connected to the root. In 2:125 and 3:97, the Kaʿbah is described as «mathābatan li-l-nāsi wa-amnan» — a place of return for humanity and a sanctuary. Within the Ḥaram's boundaries, even animals and plants are protected from harm — an extraordinary legal-moral zone where the normal rules of survival are suspended in acknowledgment of divine presence. Al-Ṭabarī reports from Mujāhid that in the Jāhiliyyah, a man would encounter his father's murderer in the Ḥaram and not touch him — such was the sanctity of the place.

The political theology of amn is developed in 24:55, where Allah promises the believers that He will «la-yubaddilannahum min baʿdi khawfihim amnan» — surely replace their fear with security — when they establish worship, zakāh, and obedience to the Messenger. Security here is presented not merely as the absence of threat but as a positive state of social and political order grounded in divine law. Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) comments that «amn» in this verse encompasses both internal psychological security (amn nafsī) and external political security (amn siyāsī) — the comprehensive peace that a righteous society enjoys under just governance.

The Prophet's supplication recorded in al-Tirmidhī 2346 — «man aṣbaḥa minkum āminan fī sirbihi muʿāfan fī jasadihi ʿindahu qūtu yawmihi fa-ka-annamā ḥīzat lahu l-dunyā» (whoever among you wakes up secure in his dwelling, healthy in body, with food for the day — it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him) — elevates amn to the highest worldly blessing. The ḥadīth ranks security alongside health and sustenance as the three conditions that, when combined, constitute complete worldly well-being.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ أَصْبَحَ مِنْكُمْ آمِنًا فِي سِرْبِهِ مُعَافًى فِي جَسَدِهِ عِنْدَهُ قُوتُ يَوْمِهِ فَكَأَنَّمَا حِيزَتْ لَهُ الدُّنْيَا
shades.hadith_en: Whoever among you wakes up secure in his home, healthy in body, with food for the day — it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him

shades.name_en: Amānah — The Trust and Moral Responsibility
shades.explanation:
The concept of «amānah» — the Trust — represents one of the most profound theological ideas in the Quran. In 33:72, Allah declares: «Innā ʿaraḍnā l-amānata ʿalā l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi wa-l-jibāli fa-abayna an yaḥmilnahā wa-ashfaqna minhā wa-ḥamalahā l-insānu innahu kāna ẓalūman jahūlā» (We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains — they refused to bear it and were afraid of it — but man bore it. Indeed he was unjust and ignorant). The cosmic drama of this verse has generated centuries of exegetical reflection.

Al-Ṭabarī collects numerous interpretations from the early exegetes: the amānah is the obligation of religious duties (farā'iḍ), the faculty of reason (ʿaql), the capacity for free choice (ikhtiyār), the witnessing that there is no god but Allah, or the comprehensive moral-legal responsibility (taklīf) that defines human existence. Ibn Kathīr synthesizes these: the amānah is the capacity to choose between obedience and disobedience — the very thing that distinguishes humanity from the rest of creation, which obeys Allah by natural compulsion (ṭabʿ). The heavens, earth, and mountains refused the amānah not out of disobedience but out of recognition of its terrifying weight — they preferred the safety of compulsory obedience to the risk of free choice.

The verse's conclusion — «innahu kāna ẓalūman jahūlā» — is not a condemnation but a description of the human condition. Man is ẓalūm (prone to injustice — against himself) and jahūl (prone to ignorance — of the consequences of his choices) precisely because he accepted a Trust whose demands exceed his natural capacity. This is the tragic dignity of humanity: we accepted a responsibility we could barely understand and can only fulfill through divine guidance and grace.

In interpersonal ethics, amānah extends to every trust placed in a person: financial deposits (2:283), positions of authority (4:58), secrets confided, promises made. The ḥadīth «lā īmāna li-man lā amānata lahu» (there is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness — Musnad Aḥmad 12383) establishes amānah as a necessary condition of īmān, not an optional virtue. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Trustworthiness) analyzes the psychology of khiyānah (betrayal of trust) as rooted in prioritizing transient worldly gain over eternal divine covenant — the same choice that the heavens, earth, and mountains wisely refused but humanity foolishly accepted.
shades.hadith_ar: لَا إِيمَانَ لِمَنْ لَا أَمَانَةَ لَهُ، وَلَا دِينَ لِمَنْ لَا عَهْدَ لَهُ
shades.hadith_en: There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness, and no religion for one who has no covenant

shades.name_en: Mu'min — The Believer as Trustworthy Agent
shades.explanation:
The active participle «mu'min» (believer) synthesizes the root's twin dimensions: one who believes (āmana) and one who is trustworthy (amīn). The Prophet's ﷺ definition in al-Tirmidhī 2627 makes this synthesis explicit: «al-mu'minu man aminahu l-nāsu ʿalā dimā'ihim wa-amwālihim» — the believer is one whom people trust with their blood and wealth. Īmān without amānah is hollow; trustworthiness without belief is merely social convention.

The Quran characterizes the Prophet ﷺ himself with this root's superlative form: in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, multiple prophets are addressed by their peoples with the recognition «innī lakum rasūlun amīn» (I am a trustworthy messenger to you — 26:107, 26:125, 26:143, 26:162, 26:178). The title «amīn» (trustworthy) was the Prophet's ﷺ recognized epithet among the Quraysh long before his prophethood — he was known as «al-Amīn» (the Trustworthy One). When he asked the Quraysh after the first revelation whether they would believe him if he told them of an army behind the mountain, they replied: «naʿam, anta ʿindanā ghayru muttaham, mā jarrabnā ʿalayka kadhiban» — Yes, you are above suspicion among us; we have never known you to lie. This pre-prophetic trustworthiness was the moral foundation upon which the prophetic mission rested.

The Quran's portrayal of hypocrites (munāfiqūn) contrasts sharply with mu'minūn precisely on the axis of the root's meaning. The hypocrite «yaqūlu āmannā» (they say: we believe — 2:8) but their claim is contradicted by their actions. They lack amānah — they cannot be trusted with the community's secrets, resources, or security. In 9:61, when the hypocrites claim the Prophet is «udhun» (one who listens and believes everyone), Allah corrects them: «huwa udhnu khayrin lakum, yu'minu bi-Llāh wa-yu'minu li-l-mu'minīn» — he is one who listens to good for you; he believes in Allah and trusts the believers. Here the verb «yu'minu» in relation to the believers means 'he believes them/trusts them' — the root's interpersonal dimension is applied to the Prophet's relationship with his community.
shades.hadith_ar: آيَةُ الْمُنَافِقِ ثَلَاثٌ: إِذَا حَدَّثَ كَذَبَ، وَإِذَا وَعَدَ أَخْلَفَ، وَإِذَا اؤْتُمِنَ خَانَ
shades.hadith_en: The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; when he is entrusted, he betrays

shades.name_en: Tasdiq — Confirmation and Affirmation of Truth
shades.explanation:
At its most elemental, the root means 'to affirm as true' — taṣdīq. To believe (āmana) in the Quran, the Prophet, the angels, the Last Day is to affirm that these realities are true — not merely to hope they are, or to accept them provisionally, but to stake one's existence on their truth. This epistemological dimension of īmān — belief as knowledge-claim — has been central to Islamic theological debates about the relationship between faith and reason.

The Muʿtazilite school, represented by figures like ʿAbd al-Jabbār (Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsah), emphasized that īmān is fundamentally maʿrifah (knowledge) — rational cognition of divine truths. For the Muʿtazilah, taṣdīq requires prior knowledge (ʿilm) of what is being affirmed; one cannot truly believe in something without understanding it. This rationalist approach made the acquisition of īmān a cognitive process grounded in evidence and argument, not mere acceptance of authority.

The Ashʿarī tradition, while affirming the cognitive dimension of īmān, emphasized that mere intellectual assent (taṣdīq ʿaqlī) is insufficient without the heart's submission (idhʿān qalbī). Al-Ashʿarī (al-Lumaʿ) argues that Iblīs knew the truth — he had taṣdīq — but his refusal to prostrate to Adam was an act of the will, not a failure of cognition. True īmān requires the alignment of intellect, heart, and will — knowing the truth, loving it, and acting upon it.

The Quran's polemic against the People of the Book frequently turns on the root's tasdīq dimension. In 2:41, the Jews are commanded: «wa-āminū bi-mā anzaltu muṣaddiqan li-mā maʿakum» — and believe in what I have revealed confirming what is with you. The Quran's self-description as «muṣaddiq» (that which confirms/affirms) previous scriptures is a recurring refrain: it does not abrogate the Torah and Gospel entirely but affirms the truth within them while correcting distortions. The interplay between taṣdīq (confirmation) and taḥrīf (distortion) frames the Quran's relationship to prior revelation — it is simultaneously affirming and corrective.

meaning.en: To know, to have knowledge, to be aware, to perceive, to recognize; to teach, to inform, to instruct; to mark, to distinguish by a sign. The root encompasses the full spectrum of cognition — from divine omniscience to human learning, from instinctive recognition to scholarly expertise, from sensory perception to rational understanding.
meaning.ar: الْإِدْرَاكُ وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْفَهْمُ وَالتَّبَيُّنُ؛ وَالتَّعْلِيمُ وَالْإِعْلَامُ وَالْإِرْشَادُ؛ وَالْعَلَامَةُ وَالتَّمْيِيزُ وَالتَّحْدِيدُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Cognition and its marks — the root links the act of knowing with the signs (ʿalāmāt) by which things are known. To know (ʿalima) is to recognize the marks (aʿlām) that distinguish truth from falsehood, reality from illusion. Knowledge is not passive reception but active discernment.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَثَرٍ بِالشَّيْءِ يَتَمَيَّزُ بِهِ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ. فَالْعِلْمُ: الْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْفَهْمُ
ibn_faris.en: A single root indicating a distinguishing mark by which something is differentiated from others. Hence ʿilm: cognition and understanding — knowing something by its distinguishing features.

al_raghib.ar: الْعِلْمُ: إِدْرَاكُ الشَّيْءِ بِحَقِيقَتِهِ. وَهُوَ ضَرْبَانِ: إِدْرَاكُ ذَاتِ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْحُكْمُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ بِوُجُودِ شَيْءٍ أَوْ نَفْيِهِ
al_raghib.en: Knowledge: perception of a thing in its reality. Two types: perception of essence, and judgment — affirming or negating attributes.

quran_examples.ar: عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ
quran_examples.en: He taught man what he did not know
quran_examples.context: First revelation — knowledge as divine gift

quran_examples.ar: قَالُوا۟ سُبْحَـٰنَكَ لَا عِلْمَ لَنَآ إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمْتَنَآ
quran_examples.en: They said: Glory to You, we have no knowledge except what You taught us

quran_examples.ar: يَرْفَعِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ مِنكُمْ وَٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْعِلْمَ دَرَجَـٰتٍ
quran_examples.en: Allah raises those who believe and those given knowledge by degrees
quran_examples.context: Knowledge as basis for spiritual elevation

hadith.ar: طَلَبُ الْعِلْمِ فَرِيضَةٌ عَلَى كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ
hadith.en: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.

hadith.ar: مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ، وَإِنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ لَتَضَعُ أَجْنِحَتَهَا رِضًا لِطَالِبِ الْعِلْمِ، وَإِنَّ الْعَالِمَ لَيَسْتَغْفِرُ لَهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ حَتَّى الْحِيتَانُ فِي الْمَاءِ
hadith.en: Whoever follows a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. The angels lower their wings in pleasure for the seeker of knowledge. Everything in the heavens and earth — even the fish in the water — seeks forgiveness for the scholar.
hadith.source: Sunan Abī Dāwūd 3641 | Sunan al-Tirmidhī 2682 | Sunan Ibn Mājah 223

shades.name_en: ʿIlm al-Ilāhī — Divine Knowledge, Absolute and All-Encompassing
shades.explanation:
Allah's ʿilm is the most frequently affirmed divine attribute in the Quran — al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing) appears over 150 times, often paired with al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise) or al-Samīʿ (the All-Hearing). Divine knowledge is presented as absolute, all-encompassing, and immediate — not acquired, not limited, not mediated. «Wa-huwa bi-kulli shay'in ʿalīm» (He knows everything) is the Quran's characteristic refrain.

The Āyat al-Kursī (2:255) presents the most comprehensive statement of divine ʿilm: «yaʿlamu mā bayna aydīhim wa-mā khalfahum wa-lā yuḥīṭūna bi-shay'in min ʿilmihi illā bi-mā shā'a» — He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Al-Rāzī's extensive commentary on this verse in Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb analyzes each epistemic category — past and future, manifest and hidden — that falls within divine ʿilm, concluding that nothing in the temporal or spatial universe escapes it.

The Quran repeatedly challenges false deities with the argument from knowledge: «qul hal yastawī lladhīna yaʿlamūna wa-lladhīna lā yaʿlamūn» (say: are those who know equal to those who do not know? — 39:9). The polemic against idolatry in 13:16 and elsewhere uses the argument from ʿilm: the idols «lā yaʿlamūna shay'an» (they know nothing), while Allah knows all. The connection between exclusive divinity and exclusive knowledge is a recurring Quranic argument: only the One who knows all is worthy of worship. Ibn Taymiyyah (al-Risālah al-Tadmuriyyah) develops this into a formal proof: the perfection of divinity requires the perfection of knowledge; any being lacking knowledge is necessarily imperfect and unworthy of worship.

In Islamic kalām, divine ʿilm was the subject of intense philosophical debate. The Muʿtazilah argued that Allah's knowledge of particulars (juz'iyyāt) is identical with His essence and eternal — but they struggled to explain how eternal knowledge relates to temporally occurring events. Ibn Sīnā proposed that Allah knows particulars «ʿalā nahwin kulliyyin» (in a universal manner) — knowing the universal causes from which particulars flow, without direct cognition of individual events. Al-Ghazālī's famous critique in Tahāfut al-Falāsifah accused Ibn Sīnā of effectively limiting divine knowledge, and mainstream Sunni kalām (Ashāʿirah and Māturīdiyyah) affirmed that Allah knows each particular — every leaf that falls (6:59), every thought in every heart (67:13) — with a knowledge that is one, eternal, and identical with His essence.
shades.hadith_ar: وَعِنْدَهُ مَفَاتِحُ الْغَيْبِ لَا يَعْلَمُهَا إِلَّا هُوَ، وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِي الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ
shades.hadith_en: With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows what is on land and sea.

shades.name_en: Taʿlīm — Divine Teaching and the Gift of Knowledge
shades.explanation:
Knowledge in the Quran is fundamentally a divine gift — «ʿallama l-insāna mā lam yaʿlam» (He taught man what he did not know — 96:5). The verb ʿallama (Form II — to teach) appears with Allah as subject throughout the Quran, initially in the primordial scene of 2:31: «wa-ʿallama Ādama l-asmā'a kullahā» (He taught Adam all the names). Adam's knowledge — the capacity for language, for naming, for categorizing reality — is presented not as a human achievement but as divine instruction. The angels, who initially questioned Adam's creation, are proven wrong precisely through this divinely-taught knowledge: they do not know the names (2:32), while Adam does.

The pedagogical relationship between Allah and humanity structures the entire Quranic revelation: «al-Raḥmān, ʿallama l-Qur'ān, khalaqa l-insān, ʿallamahu l-bayān» (The Most Merciful — taught the Quran, created man, taught him clear expression — 55:1-4). The sequence is significant: creation is paired with teaching, and the teaching of the Quran is placed before the teaching of speech itself. Taʿlīm is co-original with creation — to be human is to be taught.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Knowledge) develops a comprehensive theory of taʿlīm as the noblest human activity because it is participation in the divine attribute of teaching. The scholar (ʿālim) who teaches others is fulfilling the role of warāthat al-anbiyāʾ (inheritance of the prophets), since «inna l-ʿulamā'a warathatu l-anbiyā'i» (the scholars are the heirs of the prophets). The prophetic inheritance is not wealth but knowledge — and the one who transmits it participates in the prophetic mission. Al-Ghazālī distinguishes between ʿilm muʿāmalah (knowledge of practical religion — how to live) and ʿilm mukāshafah (knowledge of spiritual realities — what to know of God), arguing that taʿlīm of the former is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah) while the latter is the path of the spiritual elite.

The Quran's own pedagogy — its use of repetition, parable, oath, story, and argument — is a manifestation of divine taʿlīm. In 75:19, Allah promises the Prophet: «thumma inna ʿalaynā bayānah» (then it is upon Us to explain it). The revelation is not merely text but accompanied by divine instruction in its interpretation. This verse is foundational for the Islamic theory of bayān (elucidation) — that the Quran's meanings are not hidden but made clear through divine teaching operating through the Prophet's sunnah and the scholarly tradition.
shades.hadith_ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
shades.hadith_en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

shades.name_en: al-ʿĀlim — The Scholar as Inheritor of Prophetic Knowledge
shades.explanation:
The active participle «ʿālim» (scholar/knower) and its plural «ʿulamāʾ» designate those who possess deep, rooted knowledge — «al-rāsikhūna fī l-ʿilm» (those firmly grounded in knowledge — 3:7). The Quranic concept of the ʿālim is not merely the possessor of information but the one whose knowledge has transformed their being: «innamā yakhshā Llāha min ʿibādihi l-ʿulamāʾu» (only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah — 35:28). This verse establishes the organic link between authentic ʿilm and khashyah (awe-filled fear of Allah) — knowledge that does not produce humility before Allah is incomplete or counterfeit.

Al-Qurṭubī's commentary on 35:28 collects the early interpretations: the ʿulamāʾ are those who know Allah's power, majesty, and attributes — and this knowledge produces reverential fear. Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly said: «al-ʿālimu bi-l-Raḥmāni man lam yushrik bihi shay'an, wa-aḥalla ḥalālahu wa-ḥarrama ḥarāmahu, wa-ḥafiẓa waṣiyyatahu, wa-ayqana annahu mulāqīhi» — the one who truly knows the Most Merciful is he who associates nothing with Him, permits what He permits, forbids what He forbids, keeps His command, and is certain of meeting Him. Knowledge is measured by its fruits in character and conduct, not by the quantity of information stored.

The ḥadīth tradition establishes the ʿulamāʾ as the legitimate heirs and successors of the prophets. The famous ḥadīth in Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī: «inna l-ʿulamāʾa warathatu l-anbiyāʾi, inna l-anbiyāʾa lam yūrithū dīnāran wa-lā dirhaman, wa-innamā warithū l-ʿilma» (the scholars are the heirs of the prophets; the prophets left neither dinar nor dirham — they only left knowledge). This ḥadīth fundamentally shaped Islamic civilization's respect for scholarship and the institutional autonomy of the ʿulamāʾ. Unlike political authority which is contested and temporal, scholarly authority derives from prophetic inheritance and is validated by the Quranic text itself.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn) develops a detailed typology of the ʿālim: the true scholar is one who combines ʿilm (knowledge), fiqh (understanding), ḥikmah (wisdom), and khashyah (fear of Allah). He warns against three types of pseudo-scholars: the one who has memorized texts without understanding (ḥāfiẓ ghayr faqīh), the one who has rational understanding without spiritual grounding (ʿāqil ghayr mutadayyin), and the one who has spiritual pretensions without textual knowledge (mutaʿabbid ghayr ʿālim). The authentic ʿālim integrates all dimensions — text, reason, and spirituality.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ الْعُلَمَاءَ وَرَثَةُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ، إِنَّ الْأَنْبِيَاءَ لَمْ يُوَرِّثُوا دِينَارًا وَلَا دِرْهَمًا، وَإِنَّمَا وَرَّثُوا الْعِلْمَ
shades.hadith_en: The scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets did not leave behind dinar or dirham — they only left behind knowledge.

shades.name_en: ʿAlam and ʿAlāmah — Signs, Marks, and Distinguishing Features
shades.explanation:
The root's connection to marking and signifying is crucial: an ʿalam is a signpost, a banner, a distinguishing mark. In the Quranic worldview, the cosmos itself is filled with āyāt (signs — from a different root) and aʿlām (markers) that point to the Creator if one has the ʿilm to read them. The progression is: Allah places marks (aʿlām) in creation and revelation → the knower (ʿālim) perceives these marks through knowledge (ʿilm) → this knowledge leads to recognition (maʿrifah) of Allah.

The word ʿālam (world, universe) itself derives from this root — the cosmos is that which serves as a mark (ʿalāmah) pointing to its Creator. Ibn Fāris explicitly connects ʿālam to the root ʿ-l-m: the world is so named because it is a sign indicating its Maker. Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly said: «al-ʿālamūna: al-samāwātu wa-l-arḍu wa-mā fīhinna wa-mā baynahunna» — the worlds: the heavens, the earth, what is in them, and what is between them. The plural ʿālamīn encompasses all categories of created beings — each a sign, each a mark pointing beyond itself.

In eschatological context, aʿlām serve as distinguishing markers. In 55:17, «rabbu l-mashriqayni wa-rabbu l-maghribayn» (Lord of the two Easts and Lord of the two Wests) — the two Easts and two Wests are aʿlām (markers) of Allah's cosmic sovereignty. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:128) criticizes ʿĀd for building «bi-kulli rīʿin āyatan» (on every high place a sign/monument) — the āyah here is a visible marker, an ʿalam of human arrogance rather than divine guidance.

shades.name_en: Human Knowledge — Maʿrifah, Fiqh, and Epistemic Humility
shades.name_ar: الْعِلْمُ الْبَشَرِيُّ — الْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْفِقْهُ وَالتَّوَاضُعُ الْمَعْرِفِيُّ
shades.explanation:
The Quran consistently distinguishes between divine ʿilm (absolute, all-encompassing) and human ʿilm (partial, acquired, fallible). In 17:85: «wa-mā ūtītum mina l-ʿilmi illā qalīlā» (you have been given only a little knowledge) — this verse is read by the exegetical tradition as a statement about the inherent limits of human cognition, not merely about the specific question of the soul (rūḥ) being discussed. Ibn Kathīr notes that the verse was revealed when the Jews of Medina asked the Prophet about the nature of the soul, but its principle is universal: human knowledge is infinitesimal compared to divine knowledge.

This epistemic humility is foundational to the Islamic intellectual tradition. Al-Ghazālī's celebrated spiritual autobiography (al-Munqidh min al-Ḍalāl) is structured around the crisis of epistemology — how can a finite mind attain certainty about ultimate reality? His resolution — that certainty comes through divine illumination (nūr) cast into the heart, not through rational demonstration alone — draws on the Quranic insistence that ʿilm is ultimately a gift from Allah, not a human conquest. The ʿālim is not the one who has mastered knowledge but the one whom knowledge has mastered — transformed into a state of intellectual humility before the All-Knowing.

Yet the Quran is not anti-intellectual. The repeated refrain «afalā taʿqilūn» (will you not reason?), «laʿallakum tatafakkarūn» (that you may reflect), «laʿallakum yaʿlamūn» (that they may know) invites human cognition, not its suppression. The Islamic epistemological tradition distinguishes between modes of knowing: ʿilm al-yaqīn (knowledge of certainty — rational-deductive), ʿayn al-yaqīn (eye of certainty — empirical-observational), and ḥaqq al-yaqīn (truth of certainty — experiential-intuitive). The Quran itself models this progression: from hearing about Paradise (ʿilm al-yaqīn) to seeing it (ʿayn al-yaqīn) to entering it (ḥaqq al-yaqīn). Knowledge is a spectrum, not a binary — and the highest knowledge is tasting (dhawq), direct experience that transcends discursive reason.
shades.hadith_ar: وَمَا أُوتِيتُمْ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
shades.hadith_en: You have been given only a little knowledge

meaning.en: To stand, rise, establish, maintain; a people, nation, community. The root's core physical sense of 'standing upright' extends metaphorically to moral uprightness (istiqāmah), social organization (qawm), custodianship (qayyim), and eschatological resurrection (qiyāmah).
meaning.ar: الْقِيَامُ وَالِانْتِصَابُ وَالثَّبَاتُ؛ وَالْجَمَاعَةُ وَالْأُمَّةُ؛ وَالِاسْتِقَامَةُ وَالْعَدْلُ؛ وَالْقِيَمُ وَالْحِفَاظُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Uprightness in all dimensions — physical (standing), moral (rectitude), social (community organization), and cosmic (divine maintenance of creation). The root provides the language for Islam's most central ethical concept: al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm (the straight/upright path).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا جَمَاعَةُ النَّاسِ — وَمِنْهُ الْقَوْمُ، وَالْآخَرُ الِانْتِصَابُ وَالْعَزْمُ — وَمِنْهُ قَامَ يَقُومُ قِيَامًا
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) a group of people — hence qawm; (2) standing upright with resolve — hence qāma yaqūmu qiyāman.

al_raghib.ar: الْقِيَامُ: ضِدُّ الْقُعُودِ، ثُمَّ يُعَبَّرُ بِهِ عَنِ الثَّبَاتِ وَالْمُحَافَظَةِ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ وَتَعَهُّدِهِ
al_raghib.en: Qiyām: opposite of sitting. Then by extension: constancy, preserving/minding something, and attending to it.

quran_examples.ar: ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ
quran_examples.en: Guide us to the straight path

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ وَيُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ
quran_examples.en: Those who believe in the unseen and establish prayer
quran_examples.context: Iqāmah of ṣalāh as a defining trait of believers

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْإِنسَـٰنُ مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ ٱلْكَرِيمِ
quran_examples.en: O man, what has deceived you about your Lord, the Generous?
quran_examples.context: Eschatological awakening — the Day of Standing

hadith.ar: اسْتَقِيمُوا وَلَنْ تُحْصُوا، وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ خَيْرَ أَعْمَالِكُمُ الصَّلَاةُ، وَلَا يُحَافِظُ عَلَى الْوُضُوءِ إِلَّا مُؤْمِنٌ
hadith.en: Remain upright (istaqīmū), though you will not be able to do so perfectly. Know that the best of your deeds is prayer, and none maintains ablution except a believer.

hadith.ar: قُلْ آمَنْتُ بِاللَّهِ ثُمَّ اسْتَقِمْ
hadith.en: Say: I believe in Allah, then remain upright (istaqim).

shades.explanation:
The concept of al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm — the straight, upright path — is the most important ethical-religious term derived from this root. Muslims petition for guidance to this path seventeen times daily in their obligatory prayers, in every unit (rakʿah). The term mustaqīm is the Form X active participle from qāma (to stand): istaqāma means 'to stand straight,' 'to be upright,' 'to follow the right course without deviation.' The ṣirāṭ that is mustaqīm is the path that does not bend, waver, or lead astray.

Ibn Kathīr, opening his tafsīr of al-Fātiḥah, collects the authoritative early interpretations: al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm is the Book of Allah (according to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib via al-Ḥākim), Islam (according to Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās), the path of the Prophet and his Companions (according to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī), and the path that leads to Allah's pleasure (according to Abū l-ʿĀliyah). These are not contradictory but concentric: the Quran is the guide, Islam is the religion, the Sunnah is the method, and Allah's pleasure is the destination.

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī provides a linguistic analysis: istaqāma istaqāmata l-ʿūd (like a branch that has been straightened) — the Form X verb (istafʿala) here means 'to seek/attain uprightness.' The ṣirāṭ mustaqīm is 'the path that has been made straight' — it does not acquire its straightness from the traveler but from the One who established it. This passive sense of mustaqīm is theologically significant: rectitude is not a human construction but a divine gift to those who follow the revealed path.

The Quran's contrast between al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm and sabīl al-ghayy (the path of error — 7:16) frames human life as a moral journey where the fundamental choice is between uprightness and deviation. Ibn al-Qayyim (Madārij al-Sālikīn) develops this journey metaphor extensively: the ṣirāṭ is the path, istiqāmah is staying on it, and the various spiritual stations (manāzil) are milestones along the way. The ultimate ṣirāṭ is the bridge over Hell in the eschaton — where only those who walked the straight path in this life will cross safely (Bukhārī 7437, Muslim 183).
shades.hadith_ar: اسْتَقِيمُوا وَلَنْ تُحْصُوا
shades.hadith_en: Remain upright (istaqīmū), though you will not be able to do so perfectly

shades.name_en: Iqāmah — Establishing Prayer and Religious Practice
shades.explanation:
The phrase «aqāma l-ṣalāh» (Form IV — to establish prayer) appears over 40 times in the Quran, always paired with «ātā l-zakāh» (to give zakāh — obligatory charity). The verb aqāma does not mean merely 'to perform' prayer — for that, Arabic has ṣallā — but rather 'to make it stand,' 'to establish it firmly and continuously.' The distinction is crucial: anyone can pray occasionally; the mu'min establishes prayer as a standing pillar of their existence.

Al-Rāzī analyzes the semantic difference between ṣallā (simply performing prayer) and aqāma al-ṣalāh (establishing it): aqāma implies perseverance (dawām), proper execution (ḥusn al-adāʾ), outward form and inward presence (al-ẓāhir wa-l-bāṭin), and public, communal performance (al-iẓhār wa-l-jamāʿah). Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that aqāma suggests making the prayer 'stand upright' — meaning performed with its full conditions, pillars, and sunnahs, not hastily or carelessly. The iqāmah (call immediately before prayer — also from this root) signals the community standing for worship.

This shade connects the root's physical sense of 'standing' with its spiritual sense of 'establishing.' The worshipper literally stands (qiyām) before Allah in prayer — and this standing is the most intimate form of divine address, as in the ḥadīth qudsī: «qasamtu l-ṣalāta baynī wa-bayna ʿabdī niṣfayn» (I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves — Muslim 395). The standing posture (qiyām) in ṣalāh is the physical embodiment of the spiritual state of istiqāmah — the body stands straight before Allah as the soul should stand straight in devotion.

The pairing of aqāma al-ṣalāh with ātā al-zakāh throughout the Quran has profound social-economic implications: uprightness before Allah (prayer) must be accompanied by uprightness toward creation (charity). One cannot be mustaqīm with Allah while neglecting the rights of His servants. Ibn Taymiyyah (al-Siyāsah al-Sharʿiyyah) develops this into a principle of Islamic governance: the state's primary function is to facilitate iqāmat al-ṣalāh (religious practice) and ītāʾ al-zakāh (economic justice).
shades.hadith_ar: بُنِيَ الْإِسْلَامُ عَلَى خَمْسٍ: شَهَادَةِ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وَإِقَامِ الصَّلَاةِ، وَإِيتَاءِ الزَّكَاةِ، وَصَوْمِ رَمَضَانَ، وَحَجِّ الْبَيْتِ
shades.hadith_en: Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His Messenger, establishing prayer, giving zakah, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House.

shades.explanation:
The noun «qawm» is the most common word in the Quran for a people, nation, or community — appearing over 380 times, almost always in the context of prophetic missions. A qawm is a group united by kinship, language, geography, or shared historical destiny — the natural unit of social organization to which prophets are sent. The Quranic formula «ilā qawmihim» (to their people) frames every prophetic mission as directed to a specific qawm, not to an abstract 'humanity.' This particularity is essential: divine guidance takes concrete historical form, addressing actual communities in their own languages and contexts.

The relationship between the nabi (prophet) and his qawm is one of the Quran's central dramatic tensions. Prophets are consistently rejected by their qawm: «qawmu Nūḥin kadhdhabati l-mursalīn» (the people of Noah denied the messengers — 26:105), «kadhdhabat qawmu Lūṭini l-mursalīn» (the people of Lot denied — 26:160). The qawm is both the object of prophetic care («la-qad arsalnā Mūsā bi-āyātinā an akhrij qawmaka min al-ẓulumāti ilā l-nūr» — We sent Moses with Our signs: bring your people out of darkness into light — 14:5) and the agent of prophetic rejection. This tension between prophetic love for the qawm and the qawm's rejection of the prophet structures the entire Quranic narrative cycle.

The concept of qawm also carries ethical weight: Allah does not change the condition of a qawm until they change what is in themselves («inna Llāha lā yughayyiru mā bi-qawmin ḥattā yughayyirū mā bi-anfusihim» — 13:11). This verse is the Quranic charter of collective moral responsibility — the rise and fall of communities (aqwām) is not arbitrary but follows moral laws. Al-Qurṭubī comments that this verse refutes both pure determinism (which would make collective fate independent of collective action) and pure voluntarism (which would deny divine sovereignty over history). The middle path: Allah's sunnah (normative law) in history operates through, not despite, human agency.
