In Islamic legal and political thought, the concept of qawm was further developed into aqalliyyāt (minority communities), qawmiyyah (nationalism/ethnic identity), and the relationship between the Muslim ummah and other aqwām. The Quran's recognition of the diversity of aqwām (49:13: «jaʿalnākum shuʿūban wa-qabā'ila li-taʿārafū» — We made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another) provides the foundation for an Islamic ethic of inter-community relations based on mutual recognition rather than erasure of difference.
shades.hadith_ar: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ، إِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ وَاحِدٌ، وَإِنَّ أَبَاكُمْ وَاحِدٌ. أَلَا لَا فَضْلَ لِعَرَبِيٍّ عَلَى أَعْجَمِيٍّ، وَلَا لِأَعْجَمِيٍّ عَلَى عَرَبِيٍّ، إِلَّا بِالتَّقْوَى
shades.hadith_en: O people, your Lord is One and your father is one. There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except through piety.

shades.explanation:
The intensive participial form «qayyim» (one who stands over, maintains, guards) appears in critically important Quranic contexts. In Āyat al-Kursī (2:255): «Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa l-ḥayyu l-qayyūm» — Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer. Al-Qayyūm is the superlative form: the One who stands eternally by Himself (qā'im bi-nafsihi) and upon whom all creation depends for its standing (muqīm li-ghayrihi). This divine name encapsulates the root's metaphysical dimension: Allah is the ultimate ground of all existence — everything else 'stands' only through His sustaining power.

Al-Ṭabarī collects the early interpretations of al-Qayyūm: the One who never sleeps nor dies (Ibn ʿAbbās), the One who manages all affairs (Mujāhid), the One who stands over every soul with what it has earned (Qatādah), the Ever-Existing who has no end (al-Ḍaḥḥāk). Ibn Kathīr synthesizes: al-Qayyūm is the One who is independently established (al-qā'im bi-nafsihi) and upon whom all things are established — the Necessary Being whose existence is self-sufficient and upon whom all contingent beings depend.

In 30:30, «fa-aqim wajhaka li-l-dīni ḥanīfā, fiṭrata Llāhi llatī faṭara l-nāsa ʿalayhā... dhālika l-dīnu l-qayyimu» — direct your face to the upright religion, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created humanity. That is the upright (qayyim) religion. The religion is described as qayyim — upright, standing firm, self-consistent, and the standard by which other ways are judged. Al-Rāzī explains that dīn qayyim means 'the religion that is straight in itself and that straightens those who follow it' — it is both descriptive (the religion is upright) and transformative (the religion makes upright).

The legal concept of qayyim (guardian/custodian) in Islamic law extends this meaning: a qayyim is appointed to stand over (yaqūmu ʿalā) the affairs of an orphan, a waqf (endowment), or a public institution — managing, preserving, and protecting. The qayyim does not own what he guards but stands responsible for it before Allah and the community.
shades.hadith_ar: اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ، لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
shades.hadith_en: O Allah, You are the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer. There is no god but You.

shades.name_en: Yawm al-Qiyāmah — The Day of Standing/Resurrection
shades.explanation:
The Arabic name for the Day of Judgment — «yawm al-qiyāmah» — is literally 'the Day of Standing.' The name derives from the root's core physical meaning: all humanity will 'stand' (yaqūmu) before the Lord of the Worlds for judgment. This standing is not metaphorical but literal, physical, and inescapable: «yawma yaqūmu l-nāsu li-rabbi l-ʿālamīn» (the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the Worlds — 83:6). The choice of 'standing' rather than 'sitting' or 'lying' is deliberate: standing is the posture of accountability, of being called to answer, of bearing the weight of one's deeds.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of the Remembrance of Death) describes the eschatological standing with terrifying vividness: the sun brought near, sweat rising to various levels according to one's sins, people standing for fifty thousand years (70:4) awaiting judgment. The physical qiyām mirrors the moral qiyām: those who 'stood straight' in this world through istiqāmah will find the standing of the Hereafter bearable, while those who were crooked in their dealings will find it unbearable.

The Quran uses several names for the Last Day, each highlighting a different aspect: yawm al-qiyāmah (the Day of Standing — accountability), yawm al-dīn (the Day of Judgment — recompense), yawm al-ākhir (the Last Day — finality), al-sāʿah (the Hour — suddenness), yawm al-baʿth (the Day of Resurrection — emergence). The preference for qiyāmah in many contexts emphasizes the moral dimension: the Last Day is fundamentally about standing to account, about deeds being weighed, about the truth of one's life being made manifest.

The theological debates about bodily resurrection (baʿth al-ajsād) in Islamic kalām are connected to the root's physicality: the Quran insists on bodily resurrection because standing (qiyām) requires a body. The Muʿtazilah and Ashāʿirah both affirmed bodily resurrection, against the philosophers who argued for purely spiritual afterlife. The Quran's vivid descriptions of the physical qiyāmah — bones reassembled, fingertips restored (75:3-4) — emphasize that the moral standing requires the physical body through which deeds were performed.
shades.hadith_ar: يَوْمَ يَقُومُ النَّاسُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
shades.hadith_en: The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the Worlds

meaning.en: To come, to arrive, to bring, to approach. Expresses motion toward a destination — physical, temporal, or metaphysical. Includes the coming of divine command, death, the Hour, revelation, and sustenance.
meaning.ar: الْمَجِيءُ وَالْإِتْيَانُ وَالْوُصُولُ، وَالْإِحْضَارُ وَالتَّقْدِيمُ. يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَرَكَةِ نَحْوَ غَايَةٍ مَكَانِيَّةٍ أَوْ زَمَانِيَّةٍ أَوْ مَعْنَوِيَّةٍ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Motion toward — the root captures the directed movement of an agent or object toward a terminus, whether literal (arriving at a place), temporal (the coming of an appointed time), or metaphysical (the coming of divine decree).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا مَجِيءُ الشَّيْءِ وَإِتْيَانُهُ، وَالْآخَرُ قِيَاسٌ — وَهُوَ الْمَوَاعِيدُ وَالْآجَالُ الَّتِي تَأْتِي
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) the coming/arrival of something; (2) appointed times and terms that come due.

al_raghib.ar: الْإِتْيَانُ: مَجِيءٌ بِسُهُولَةٍ، وَيُسْتَعْمَلُ لِلْمَجِيءِ بِالشَّيْءِ وَالذَّهَابِ بِهِ
al_raghib.en: Ityān: coming with ease. Used for bringing something and going with it.

quran_examples.ar: إِذَا جَآءَ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْفَتْحُ
quran_examples.en: When the help of Allah comes and the victory

quran_examples.ar: وَدَّ كَثِيرٌۭ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَـٰبِ لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكُم مِّنۢ بَعْدِ إِيمَـٰنِكُمْ كُفَّارًا
quran_examples.en: Many of the People of the Book wish to turn you back to disbelief after your faith
quran_examples.context: Testing and trials that come to believers

quran_examples.ar: هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَّآ أَن تَأْتِيَهُمُ ٱلْمَلَـٰٓئِكَةُ أَوْ يَأْتِىَ رَبُّكَ أَوْ يَأْتِىَ بَعْضُ ءَايَـٰتِ رَبِّكَ
quran_examples.en: Do they await but that the angels should come, or your Lord should come, or some signs of your Lord should come?

hadith.ar: إِذَا جَاءَ رَمَضَانُ فُتِّحَتْ أَبْوَابُ الْجَنَّةِ وَغُلِّقَتْ أَبْوَابُ النَّارِ وَصُفِّدَتِ الشَّيَاطِينُ
hadith.en: When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained.

hadith.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُمْلِي لِلظَّالِمِ حَتَّى إِذَا أَخَذَهُ لَمْ يُفْلِتْهُ
hadith.en: Allah grants respite to the wrongdoer until, when He seizes him, He does not let him escape.

shades.name_en: Coming of Divine Help and Victory (Nasr Allāh)
shades.explanation:
Sūrat al-Naṣr (110) opens with «idhā jā'a naṣru Llāhi wa-l-fatḥ» — when the help of Allah comes and the opening/victory. The verb «jā'a» (came) — a near-synonym of atā — captures the decisive, transformative moment of divine intervention in history. Al-Ṭabarī records that this sūrah was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, signaling the completion of the Prophet's mission. Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly understood it as an announcement of the Prophet's impending death — the 'coming' of help meant the 'completion' of the mission, and completion meant departure.

The Quranic theology of divine help consistently presents it as «coming» (ityān/majīʾ) — not as something the believers manufacture or deserve, but as a gift that arrives from Allah at His appointed time. In 2:214, the believers are reminded that help has not yet «come» to them as it came to those before them — the language of arrival (atā) frames divine help as an eschatological promise whose timing is entirely in Allah's hands. Al-Qurṭubī comments that the delay of help is a test (fitnah), and the coming of help is a mercy (raḥmah) — both are aspects of divine wisdom, not reflections of human merit or demerit.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Zād al-Maʿād) connects the «coming» of divine help to the stations of spiritual wayfaring: the sālik (traveler) must not demand immediate results but must trust that when help «comes,» it comes at the perfect moment, neither early nor late. The impatience of the believers at Badr and Uḥud — «matā naṣru Llāh?» (when is the help of Allah? — 2:214) — is answered with the promise that Allah's help is near (qarīb), but its 'coming' is governed by divine wisdom, not human urgency.
shades.hadith_ar: إِذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ وَالْفَتْحُ
shades.hadith_en: When the help of Allah comes and the victory

shades.name_en: Eschatological Coming — Death, the Hour, and Divine Arrival
shades.name_ar: الْإِتْيَانُ الْأُخْرَوِيُّ — الْمَوْتُ وَالسَّاعَةُ وَمَجِيءُ الرَّبِّ
shades.explanation:
The root is the primary verb for the eschatological arrival — death «comes» (atā/jā'a), the Hour «comes,» and in the most theologically charged usage, Allah «comes» (6:158: «aw ya'tiya rabbuka» — or your Lord should come). This last verse has generated extensive exegetical and theological discussion about the ṣifāt (divine attributes) and the modality of divine 'coming.'

The early Salaf, represented by Mālik ibn Anas and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, affirmed «ya'tī rabbuka» without asking kayf (how) — accepting the text as revealed while rejecting any corporeal or temporal understanding of divine coming. Al-Ṭabarī's tafsīr of 6:158 reports from the early exegetes that «ya'tī rabbuka» means 'the command of your Lord comes' (amr rabbika) or 'the punishment of your Lord comes' — interpreting the coming metaphorically to avoid anthropomorphism. The Khalaf (later theologians), particularly the Ashāʿirah, interpreted «ityān» (coming) as the coming of Allah's command, decree, or signs, not His essence — since movement (ḥarakah) and arrival (intiqāl) are attributes of bodies and impossibilities for the Eternal.

Ibn Taymiyyah (Sharḥ Ḥadīth al-Nuzūl) takes a middle position: affirming the text as it has come while rejecting both taʿṭīl (denial of the attribute's meaning) and tashbīh (likening Allah to creation). He argues that the coming (ityān/majīʾ) of Allah is a ṣifah fiʿliyyah (attribute of action) — real in a manner befitting His majesty, not like the coming of creatures. This debate reflects the centrality of carefully navigating the root's implications in theological discourse.

Beyond the divine coming, the root frames the entire eschatological drama as a sequence of arrivals: death comes to each soul (2:109 in context), the angels come to take the soul (6:93), the trumpet comes, the reckoning comes. The Quran's repeated use of «atā» and «jā'a» in eschatological contexts creates a sense of inevitable, unstoppable movement toward a divinely appointed terminus. Nothing can prevent what is «coming» (ātin) — this certainty is the ground of Quranic moral urgency.
shades.hadith_ar: يَأْتِي الشَّيْطَانُ أَحَدَكُمْ فَيَقُولُ: مَنْ خَلَقَ كَذَا؟ مَنْ خَلَقَ كَذَا؟ حَتَّى يَقُولَ: مَنْ خَلَقَ رَبَّكَ؟
shades.hadith_en: Satan comes to one of you and says: Who created this? Who created that? Until he says: Who created your Lord?

shades.explanation:
The Form IV verb «ātā» (آتَى) — to give, to grant, to bring — is one of the most theologically significant derivatives of the root, appearing predominantly in the context of divine giving. Allah «ātā» knowledge, wisdom, scripture, prophethood, kingdom, mercy, sustenance — the verb marks the transfer of something precious from the Divine Giver to the human recipient. Unlike the simple Form I «atā» (to come), Form IV is transitive: it is not merely that something comes, but that Allah actively brings it to His servants.

The phrase «ātā l-zakāh» (to give the zakāh — obligatory charity) appears over 30 times, paired with «aqāma l-ṣalāh» (establish prayer). The verb ātā rather than aʿṭā (another verb for giving) carries the connotation of bringing the due right to its recipient — zakāh is not a gift but an obligation that one 'brings' to those entitled to it. Al-Rāzī notes that ātā implies fulfillment of a duty (adāʾ al-wājib), while aʿṭā is more general. The choice of ātā for zakāh underscores that charity is not voluntary benevolence but a right that the poor possess and that the wealthy must deliver.

In 2:251, «wa-ātāhu Llāhu l-mulka wa-l-ḥikmata» (Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom) — referring to David (Dāwūd). The verb ātā here conveys the gratuitous nature of divine gifts: David did not earn kingship through hereditary succession or military conquest; it was «brought» to him by Allah's choice. This usage reinforces the Quranic theology of divine sovereignty (mulk): all authority, knowledge, and provision ultimately «come» from Allah, not from human effort alone.

In 3:79, the Quran clarifies that no prophet would command people to worship him rather than Allah after Allah had «ātāhu l-kitāba wa-l-ḥukma wa-l-nubuwwah» (given him the Book, the Judgment, and the Prophethood). The sequence — Book, then Judgment, then Prophethood — reflects the theological ordering: revelation is the foundation, understanding (ḥukm) is its fruit, and prophethood is the office that delivers both. All are «brought» (ūtiya) by Allah as pure gifts.
shades.hadith_ar: وَآتَى الْمَالَ عَلَى حُبِّهِ ذَوِي الْقُرْبَىٰ وَالْيَتَامَىٰ وَالْمَسَاكِينَ وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ
shades.hadith_en: And gives wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler

shades.name_en: Coming of Command, Decree, and Appointed Term (Ajal)
shades.explanation:
The root frames the execution of divine decree as an arrival — «idhā jā'a amrunā» (when Our command comes — 11:40, 23:27, referring to the Flood). The command (amr) is personified as an agent that «comes» at its appointed time — neither early nor late, neither resistible nor escapable. This personification is rhetorically powerful: divine decree is not an abstraction but a living force that moves toward its target with certainty.

In the narratives of destroyed nations, the recurring pattern is: the people reject the messenger, the messenger warns them of an impending punishment, they mock and demand its hastening, and then — «jā'ahum amrunā» (Our command came to them) or «atāhum ba'sunā» (Our punishment came to them). The 'coming' of punishment is sudden and irreversible: «fa-mā kāna lahum min maḥīṣ» (there was no escape for them). Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf) notes the dramatic irony: the people who demanded that punishment come quickly (istiʿjāl) are the same people who, when it actually comes, find it unbearable. The root's temporal dimension — the coming of an appointed time (ajal) — teaches that divine decree operates on a divine timetable, not a human one.

The Quran's use of «atā amru Llāh» (the command of Allah has come — 16:1) in the perfect (past) tense, even for future events, expresses the certainty of divine decree: what Allah has decreed is as certain as if it has already happened. Arabic grammarians call this «al-māḍī li-taḥqīq al-wuqūʿ» (using the past tense to affirm certainty of occurrence). The coming is so certain that it is spoken of in the past — a linguistic embodiment of the theological principle that Allah's decree cannot fail.

Revelation and knowledge «come» — they arrive from a source beyond human reach. The prophets are sent with «al-bayyināt» (clear proofs) that «came» (jā'at) to people through them. This framing is epistemologically significant: revealed knowledge is not discovered or constructed by human reason — it comes from outside the human cognitive system, from the transcendent source. The human role is recognition and response, not origination.

In 2:87, «wa-la-qad ātaynā Mūsā l-kitāba» (We gave Moses the Book) — again the Form IV «ātaynā» frames revelation as divine giving. The Torah did not 'arise' from Moses's reflection or emerge from Israelite tradition; it was «brought» to him by Allah. This theology of revelation as «coming» from outside contrasts with the modern view of religious texts as products of their historical contexts — the Quran presents scripture as an arrival from transcendence, breaking into history from beyond it.

The Quran's self-description in 10:57 reinforces this: «yā ayyuhā l-nāsu qad jā'atkum mawʿiẓatun min rabbikum» (O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord). The Quran «came» — jā'at — it was sent, delivered, brought. The passive framing eliminates human agency in the production of revelation: the Prophet is the recipient (upon whom it came), not the author (who produced it). This grammatical choice is theologically motivated — it supports the doctrine of waḥy (revelation) as divine dictation (tanzīl) rather than prophetic inspiration.
shades.hadith_ar: وَمَا أَتَاكُمْ عَنِّي مِنْ خَبَرٍ فَاعْرِضُوهُ عَلَى كِتَابِ اللَّهِ
shades.hadith_en: Whatever comes to you from me, compare it with the Book of Allah

meaning.en: Between, among; to be clear, distinct, evident; to make manifest, explain, elucidate. The root bridges spatial separation (bayn — betweenness) and cognitive clarity (bayān — clear expression, elucidation).
meaning.ar: الْبَيْنُ: الْفَصْلُ وَالْوَصْلُ — بَيْنَ الشَّيْئَيْنِ؛ وَالْبَيَانُ: الْوُضُوحُ وَالْإِيضَاحُ وَالْإِفْصَاحُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Separation and clarity — the root links the physical concept of 'betweenness' (distance/distinction between two things) with the cognitive concept of 'clear distinction' (making something evident and unambiguous). What is 'between' is distinct; what is 'clear' is distinguished.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا بُعْدُ الشَّيْءِ وَانْكِشَافُهُ — تَقُولُ: بَانَ يَبِينُ بَيْنًا وَبَيْنُونَةً، وَالْآخَرُ جِنْسٌ مِنَ الْإِظْهَارِ وَالْإِيضَاحِ — تَقُولُ: بَيَّنْتُ الشَّيْءَ تَبْيِينًا
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) distance and disclosure — bāna yabīnu baynan (it became distant/clear); (2) manifestation and elucidation — bayyantu l-shay'a tabyīnan.

al_raghib.ar: الْبَيْنُ: الْفُرْقَةُ وَالْبُعْدُ. وَالْبَيَانُ: الْكَشْفُ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ وَإِيضَاحُهُ. وَسُمِّيَ الْكَلَامُ بَيَانًا لِكَشْفِهِ عَنِ الْمَعَانِي
al_raghib.en: Bayn: separation and distance. Bayān: uncovering something and clarifying it. Speech is called bayān because it reveals meanings.

quran_examples.ar: بَيْنَهُمَا بَرْزَخٌۭ لَّا يَبْغِيَانِ
quran_examples.en: Between them is a barrier they do not transgress
quran_examples.context: The two seas separated by divine decree

quran_examples.ar: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَـٰتٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ وَٱلْفُرْقَانِ
quran_examples.en: Ramadan — the Quran was revealed as guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion

quran_examples.ar: ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُۥ
quran_examples.en: Then upon Us is its clarification

hadith.ar: الْحَلَالُ بَيِّنٌ وَالْحَرَامُ بَيِّنٌ، وَبَيْنَهُمَا أُمُورٌ مُشْتَبِهَاتٌ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ كَثِيرٌۭ مِّنَ النَّاسِ
hadith.en: The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters unknown to many.

hadith.ar: إِنَّ مِنَ الْبَيَانِ لَسِحْرًا
hadith.en: Indeed some eloquence (bayān) is like magic.

shades.name_en: Bayn — Spatial Separation and Intermediate Position
shades.explanation:
The spatial sense of 'between' (bayna) is the root's most basic meaning — the space or relationship that both separates and connects two things. The Quran's cosmic imagery repeatedly invokes «bayna»: between the two seas is a barzakh (barrier — 25:53, 55:20), between the heavens and earth is divine command descending (57:4), between the believer and the disbeliever on the Last Day is a wall with a gate (57:13). 

Al-Rāzī's commentary on 55:20 — «baynahumā barzakhun» — marvels at the natural phenomenon of two bodies of water meeting yet not mixing, each maintaining its distinct salinity and temperature. The «barzakh» is the bayn — the intermediate reality that is neither one sea nor the other but the space of their encounter. This physical «betweenness» becomes a metaphor for eschatological states: between death and resurrection is the barzakh (23:100), an intermediate realm of the grave. The root thus provides the language for liminality — states of being that are neither fully this nor fully that.

In Islamic philosophical cosmology, Ibn Sīnā and the falāsifah developed the concept of al-barzakh as an intermediate ontological realm between the purely spiritual (mujarradāt) and the purely material (māddiyyāt). Al-Suhrawardī (Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq) expanded this into a full ishrāqī cosmology of intermediate worlds (ʿawālim barzakhiyyah) populated by imaginal forms. The root's capacity to denote 'betweenness' made it the natural vehicle for philosophical speculation about the structure of reality.
shades.hadith_ar: بَيْنَ النَّفْخَتَيْنِ أَرْبَعُونَ
shades.hadith_en: Between the two trumpet blasts is forty

shades.name_en: Bayān — Clarity, Eloquence, and Divine Elucidation
shades.explanation:
The Quran describes itself as «bayān» — clear elucidation — and Allah as the teacher of bayān: «al-Raḥmān, ʿallama l-Qur'ān, khalaqa l-insān, ʿallamahu l-bayān» (The Most Merciful — taught the Quran, created man, taught him clear expression — 55:1-4). The sequence is extraordinary: the teaching of the Quran precedes the creation of man, and the teaching of speech (bayān) is paired with human creation itself. Bayān — the capacity for clear, articulate expression — is presented as a defining human faculty, a divine gift that distinguishes humanity from the rest of creation.

Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf) glosses «ʿallamahu l-bayān» as 'He taught him speech by which he makes clear what is in his heart and distinguishes between truth and falsehood.' Ibn ʿĀshūr expands: bayān is the human capacity for linguistic articulation (al-naṭq al-mubīn) that enables conceptual thought, social communication, and moral reasoning. Without bayān, humanity would be indistinguishable from animals — it is the faculty that makes civilization, law, science, and religion possible.

The Quranic challenge (taḥaddī) to produce something like the Quran is grounded in the concept of bayān. The Quran is «bayānun li-l-nās» (a clear statement to mankind — 3:138) — its clarity is part of its miraculous nature. The Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah, who prided themselves on bayān (eloquence), were challenged to match the Quran's bayān — and they could not. Al-Bāqillānī (Iʿjāz al-Qur'ān) argues that the Quran's bayān — its unique combination of clarity, beauty, and profundity — is the primary evidence of its divine origin. The root y-n thus provides the conceptual framework for Islamic theories of rhetoric, eloquence, and the miraculous nature of the Quran.

In 75:19, Allah promises the Prophet: «thumma inna ʿalaynā bayānahu» — then it is upon Us to clarify it (the Quran). This verse guarantees that the Quran's meanings are not hidden or esoteric but made clear by divine elucidation. The science of tafsīr (Quranic exegesis) is essentially the human attempt to participate in this divine bayān — to make clear what Allah has made clear, to the extent of human capacity.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ مِنَ الْبَيَانِ لَسِحْرًا
shades.hadith_en: Indeed some eloquence (bayān) is like magic

shades.name_en: Bayyinah — Clear Proof, Evidence, Manifest Sign
shades.explanation:
The noun «bayyinah» (plural: bayyināt) — clear proof, manifest evidence, decisive sign — is the Quran's primary term for prophetic evidence. A bayyinah is not merely an argument (dalīl) or a miracle (muʿjizah); it is a proof that makes the truth «clear» (bayyin) — self-evident, requiring no further interpretation. Sūrat al-Bayyinah (98) is named after this concept: the People of the Book did not differ «ḥattā ta'tiyahumu l-bayyinah» (until the clear proof came to them — 98:1).

Al-Ṭabarī identifies the bayyinah in 98:1 as the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ himself — he is the living proof, the embodied clarity. Other exegetes identify it as the Quran, or the combination of the Prophet and the Quran. Al-Rāzī synthesizes: the bayyinah is the comprehensive divine address (al-khiṭāb al-ilāhī al-kāmil) that includes the Prophet, the Book, the miracles, and the rational arguments — everything that makes the truth unmistakably clear.

The legal-epistemological dimension of bayyinah is developed in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh): the bayyinah is the standard of proof in judicial proceedings — clear, convincing evidence that removes doubt and establishes legal fact. The famous legal maxim «al-bayyinatu ʿalā l-muddaʿī wa-l-yamīnu ʿalā man ankar» (the burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the denier) places bayyinah at the center of Islamic procedural law. A claim without bayyinah is legally weightless; a claim supported by bayyinah becomes judicially binding.

In the Quran's polemical structure, the rejection of bayyināt is the hallmark of kufr. Pharaoh is offered bayyināt by Moses and rejects them (7:105). The Quraysh are offered bayyināt and turn away (6:157, 47:14). The Quran itself is «bayyinātun min al-hudā» (clear proofs of guidance — 2:185). The tragic arc of disbelief in the Quran is not ignorance of the truth but rejection of what has been made clear — a willful turning away from bayyināt.
shades.hadith_ar: لَوْ يَعْلَمُ النَّاسُ مَا فِي النِّدَاءِ وَالصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَجِدُوا إِلَّا أَنْ يَسْتَهِمُوا عَلَيْهِ لَاسْتَهَمُوا
shades.hadith_en: If people knew what is in the call to prayer and the first row, they would draw lots for it

shades.explanation:
The Form V verb «tabayyana» (to become clear, to be verified) and the command «tabayyanū» (verify! make sure!) appear in contexts of critical moral instruction. In 49:6: «yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū in jā'akum fāsiqun bi-naba'in fa-tabayyanū an tuṣībū qawman bi-jahālatin fa-tuṣbiḥū ʿalā mā faʿaltum nādimīn» — O believers, if a sinful person brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and become regretful. This verse is the Quranic charter of epistemic responsibility — the obligation to verify information before acting on it.

Al-Qurṭubī comments that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah, who was sent by the Prophet to collect zakāh from the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq but returned claiming they had apostatized and threatened him. Allah revealed this verse commanding verification — preventing military action based on unverified report. The principle established is universal: no serious action may be taken on the basis of unverified information, especially when human lives, reputations, or community peace are at stake.

Ibn Kathīr extends the application: tabayyun is not merely a legal command but a moral and intellectual virtue. The mu'min is characterized by caution in judgment, reluctance to accept unverified claims, and commitment to evidence-based action. This Quranic principle anticipates modern concerns about misinformation and the ethics of information — but grounds them in taqwā (God-consciousness) rather than merely pragmatic concerns.

The closely related Form X «istabāna» and Form V «tabayyana» both express the intransitive 'becoming clear' — the truth making itself known. In 2:260, Abraham asks Allah to show him how He resurrects the dead, «qāla a-wa-lam tu'min? qāla balā wa-lākin li-yaṭma'inna qalbī» (He said: Do you not believe? He said: Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be at peace). The request is not from doubt but for tabayyun — for the certainty that comes from witnessing rather than merely accepting. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Certainty) uses this verse to distinguish ʿilm al-yaqīn (knowledge of certainty) from ʿayn al-yaqīn (the eye of certainty) — tabayyun transforms abstract knowledge into lived certainty.
shades.hadith_ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالظَّنَّ، فَإِنَّ الظَّنَّ أَكْذَبُ الْحَدِيثِ
shades.hadith_en: Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech

meaning.en: To cover, conceal, hide; to disbelieve, deny, reject, be ungrateful. The root's physical sense (covering — as a farmer covers seed with soil) extends metaphorically to the covering of truth with denial, and the covering of divine favors with ingratitude.
meaning.ar: السَّتْرُ وَالتَّغْطِيَةُ — وَمِنْهُ كَفَرَ الزَّارِعُ الْبَذْرَ: غَطَّاهُ بِالتُّرَابِ؛ وَالْجُحُودُ وَالْإِنْكَارُ وَعَدَمُ الْإِيمَانِ؛ وَكُفْرَانُ النِّعْمَةِ: جُحُودُهَا وَسَتْرُهَا

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Covering — the root's physical meaning (covering seed with soil) provides the metaphor for its theological meanings: kufr is the covering of truth with denial, of divine signs with rejection, of favors with ingratitude. The kāfir is one who 'covers' what should be manifest.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى السَّتْرِ وَالتَّغْطِيَةِ — وَمِنْهُ الْكُفْرُ: ضِدُّ الْإِيمَانِ لِأَنَّهُ تَغْطِيَةُ الْحَقِّ، وَالْآخَرُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْجُحُودِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) covering and concealing — hence kufr, opposite of īmān, because it covers the truth; (2) denial and rejection.

al_raghib.ar: الْكُفْرُ فِي اللُّغَةِ: سَتْرُ الشَّيْءِ. وَوُصِفَ بِهِ مَنْ جَحَدَ النِّعَمَ لِأَنَّهُ يَسْتُرُهَا. وَأَعْظَمُ الْكُفْرِ: جُحُودُ وَحْدَانِيَّةِ اللَّهِ أَوْ شَرِيعَتِهِ أَوْ نُبُوَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ
al_raghib.en: Kufr linguistically: covering something. Applied to one who denies favors because he covers them. The greatest kufr: denying Allah's oneness, His law, or the prophethood of Muhammad.

quran_examples.ar: قُلْ يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْكَـٰفِرُونَ
quran_examples.en: Say: O disbelievers
quran_examples.context: Direct address to those who reject faith

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ أَمْ لَمْ تُنذِرْهُمْ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ
quran_examples.en: Indeed those who disbelieve — it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe
quran_examples.context: The sealed hearts of committed disbelievers

quran_examples.ar: ٱعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّمَا ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَا لَعِبٌۭ وَلَهْوٌۭ وَزِينَةٌۭ وَتَفَاخُرٌۢ بَيْنَكُمْ وَتَكَاثُرٌۭ فِى ٱلْأَمْوَٰلِ وَٱلْأَوْلَـٰدِ ۖ كَمَثَلِ غَيْثٍ أَعْجَبَ ٱلْكُفَّارَ نَبَاتُهُۥ
quran_examples.en: Know that the life of this world is play and diversion... like rain whose plant growth pleases the tillers (kuffār)
quran_examples.context: Kuffār as farmers — the root's original meaning

hadith.ar: سِبَابُ الْمُسْلِمِ فُسُوقٌ وَقِتَالُهُ كُفْرٌ
hadith.en: Abusing a Muslim is disobedience and fighting him is disbelief (kufr).

hadith.ar: لَا تَرْجِعُوا بَعْدِي كُفَّارًا يَضْرِبُ بَعْضُكُمْ رِقَابَ بَعْضٍ
hadith.en: Do not return after me to disbelief (kufr), striking one another's necks.

shades.name_en: Kufr as Denial of Truth — Rejection of Faith
shades.name_ar: كُفْرُ الْجُحُودِ — إِنْكَارُ الْحَقِّ وَرَفْضُ الْإِيمَانِ
shades.explanation:
Kufr as theological disbelief is the root's most frequent and weighty Quranic usage. The kāfir (disbeliever) is defined not primarily by ignorance but by rejection — having received the truth through revelation, reason, and prophetic mission, they «cover» it with denial. This understanding distinguishes Quranic kufr from mere unbelief (absence of faith): the kāfir actively refuses what has been made clear (bayyināt), while the jāhil (ignorant one) has not yet encountered the truth. The Quran itself makes this distinction: those who have not received a messenger are not judged as kuffār until a messenger has been sent to them (17:15).

The Islamic theological tradition developed elaborate taxonomies of kufr. Al-Ghazālī (Fayṣal al-Tafriqah) distinguishes kufr al-juhūd (denial after recognition), kufr al-ʿinād (stubborn rejection despite knowing the truth), and kufr al-takdhīb (disbelief based on considering the Prophet a liar) — each with different moral and eschatological consequences. Ibn Taymiyyah (al-Īmān) emphasizes that kufr can be by the heart (iʿtiqād), by the tongue (qawl), or by action (ʿamal) — it is not merely a cognitive state but a volitional stance that manifests in speech and conduct. The Khawārij erred, in the Sunni analysis, by applying the label of kufr to major sins — confusing kufr dūna kufr (lesser kufr — acts that resemble disbelief but do not exit one from Islam) with al-kufr al-akbar (major kufr — that which negates īmān entirely).

The Quran's portrayal of the psychology of kufr is nuanced. In 2:6-7, Allah has «sealed» the hearts of certain disbelievers — their kufr has become so entrenched that further warning is futile. But in 4:137, those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve — the oscillation between īmān and kufr is presented as a spiritual pathology leading to increasingly severe divine response. The kāfir is not a static category but a moral trajectory — one can move toward or away from kufr through choices, actions, and divine guidance or its withdrawal.
shades.hadith_ar: بَيْنَ الرَّجُلِ وَبَيْنَ الشِّرْكِ وَالْكُفْرِ تَرْكُ الصَّلَاةِ
shades.hadith_en: Between a man and shirk and kufr is abandoning the prayer

shades.name_en: Kufrān al-Niʿmah — Ingratitude, Denial of Favors
shades.explanation:
The Quran explicitly links kufr (disbelief) with kufrān (ingratitude) — to reject Allah's signs is, at root, to be ungrateful for His favors. In 14:7, Allah declares through Moses: «la'in shakartum la-azīdannakum wa-la'in kafartum inna ʿadhābī la-shadīd» — if you are grateful, I will increase you; but if you are ungrateful (kafartum), My punishment is severe. The verb «kafartum» here primarily means 'you are ungrateful,' but the Quranic context layers the theological meaning — ingratitude for divine favors leads to rejection of the Divine Giver.

The surah of the Bee (al-Naḥl) develops this theme extensively. In 16:112, Allah presents the parable of a town that was secure and well-provided, «fa-kafarat bi-anʿumi Llāh» (but it was ungrateful for the favors of Allah) — so Allah made it taste hunger and fear. The verb kafara here is directly linked to its object: anʿum (favors). Ingratitude is not merely bad manners — it is a spiritual condition that severs the recipient from the Giver. Al-Rāzī comments that shukr (gratitude) is the acknowledgment that blessings come from Allah and using them in His obedience, while kufrān is either denying their divine source or using them in disobedience.

Ibn al-Qayyim (ʿUddat al-Ṣābirīn) develops a spiritual psychology of shukr and kufrān: the grateful heart sees every blessing as a gift and every trial as a test, while the ungrateful heart sees blessings as entitlements and trials as injustices. Kufrān is ultimately a failure of perception — the inability or refusal to see the Giver behind the gift. This connects the root's two meanings: the kāfir «covers» (satara) the truth, and the ungrateful «covers» (satara) the divine source of blessings. In both cases, something manifest is rendered hidden by an act of will.
shades.hadith_ar: انْظُرُوا إِلَى مَنْ هُوَ أَسْفَلَ مِنْكُمْ وَلَا تَنْظُرُوا إِلَى مَنْ هُوَ فَوْقَكُمْ، فَهُوَ أَجْدَرُ أَنْ لَا تَزْدَرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ
shades.hadith_en: Look at those below you and do not look at those above you, lest you belittle the favors of Allah upon you

shades.explanation:
From the root's sense of 'covering' derives the concept of kaffārah (expiation) — an act that «covers» sins, concealing them from divine punishment. The Form II verb «kaffara» (to expiate) is used primarily with Allah as subject: «yukaffiru ʿanhum sayyi'ātihim» (He expiates their evil deeds — 3:193, 39:35, 47:2). The grammatical construction with «ʿan» (from/away) suggests sins being removed or covered over — Allah «covers» the sins so they no longer stand against the servant.

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī explains the semantic logic: just as the farmer covers the seed with soil (kafara l-zāriʿu l-badhra), protecting it and preparing it for growth, so kaffārah covers sins, protecting the sinner from their consequences and preparing the soul for spiritual growth. The expiation does not eliminate the ontological reality of the sin but «covers» its legal and eschatological effects — a divine act of merciful concealment.

In Islamic jurisprudence, kaffārāt (plural) are specific acts of expiation prescribed for certain violations: feeding the poor, fasting, freeing a slave, or offering a sacrifice. These acts do not automatically erase the sin but are conditions for divine forgiveness — the sinner demonstrates repentance through prescribed action, and Allah, in His mercy, covers the sin. The theology of kaffārah thus balances divine justice (sin has consequences) with divine mercy (consequences can be averted through divinely prescribed means). The Ashʿarī emphasis on divine will means that kaffārah is effective only when Allah wills to accept it; the Māturīdī emphasis on divine wisdom means that kaffārah is intrinsically connected to forgiveness as cause to effect.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ
shades.hadith_en: Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith and seeking reward — his previous sins are forgiven

shades.explanation:
The root's original Arabic meaning — preserved in one Quranic verse — is agricultural: the kāfir is the farmer who «covers» (yakfuru) the seed with soil after planting. In 57:20, the parable of worldly life is compared to rain that produces plants «aʿjaba l-kuffāra nabātuhu» (whose growth pleases the tillers/farmers). The word «kuffār» here is the plural of kāfir in its original, non-theological sense — the farmers who cover seeds with earth.

This single verse is exegetically significant because it preserves the linguistic root from which the theological meaning developed. Al-Ṭabarī notes that some early exegetes interpreted «al-kuffār» in this verse as «al-zurrāʿ» (the farmers/cultivators), drawing on the pre-Islamic Bedouin usage. The semantic development is instructive: the farmer covers seed → covering becomes the root's core idea → theological kufr is the covering of truth, of divine signs, of favors. The apparently disparate meanings — farming and disbelief — are unified by the concept of 'covering.'

Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) observes that the Quran's retention of the original agricultural meaning alongside the developed theological meaning demonstrates the richness of Arabic semantics: a root can carry multiple, seemingly unrelated meanings that are in fact connected by an underlying conceptual metaphor. The farmer who covers seed to bring forth life is also, in a sense, the opposite of the disbeliever who covers truth to suppress it — both «cover,» but one for growth and one for suppression.

meaning.en: To send, dispatch, release; a messenger, envoy, apostle. The root encompasses the act of sending (irsāl), the one sent (rasūl), the message carried (risālah), and the gradual, unhurried manner of sending (rasal — gentleness, deliberation).
meaning.ar: الْإِرْسَالُ وَالْبَعْثُ وَالتَّوْجِيهُ؛ وَالرَّسُولُ: الْمَبْعُوثُ بِرِسَالَةٍ؛ وَالرِّسَالَةُ: مَا أُرْسِلَ بِهِ؛ وَالرَّسَلُ: التُّؤَدَةُ وَالرِّفْقُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Directed sending — the dispatch of a message or messenger from a sender to a recipient. The root carries connotations of authority (the sender commissions the messenger), representation (the messenger speaks for the sender), and purpose (the sending has an intended outcome).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْإِرْسَالُ وَالْإِطْلَاقُ، وَالْآخَرُ التُّؤَدَةُ وَالرِّفْقُ. تَقُولُ: جَاءُوا رَسَلًا — أَيْ مُتَرَسِّلِينَ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) sending and releasing; (2) gentleness and deliberation. You say: they came rasalan — meaning unhurriedly, gently.

al_raghib.ar: الرَّسُولُ: كُلُّ مَنْ أُرْسِلَ بِأَمْرٍ يَتَحَمَّلُهُ. وَأَصْلُهُ فِي اللُّغَةِ: الْإِرْسَالُ — وَهُوَ التَّوْجِيهُ وَالتَّسْيِيرُ. وَالرَّسُولُ يَكُونُ مِنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ وَمِنَ الْبَشَرِ
al_raghib.en: Rasūl: anyone sent with a command he bears. Its linguistic origin: irsāl — directing and dispatching. A rasūl can be from the angels or from humanity.

quran_examples.ar: تِلْكَ ءَايَـٰتُ ٱللَّهِ نَتْلُوهَا عَلَيْكَ بِٱلْحَقِّ ۚ وَإِنَّكَ لَمِنَ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ
quran_examples.en: These are the signs of Allah — We recite them to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers

quran_examples.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱبْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًۭا مِّنْهُمْ
quran_examples.en: Our Lord, raise among them a messenger from themselves
quran_examples.context: Abraham and Ishmael's prayer for a messenger

quran_examples.ar: تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى نَزَّلَ ٱلْفُرْقَانَ عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِۦ لِيَكُونَ لِلْعَـٰلَمِينَ نَذِيرًا
quran_examples.en: Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds
quran_examples.context: The universal mission of the Messenger

hadith.ar: إِنَّ لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ دَعْوَةً مُسْتَجَابَةً، وَإِنِّي اخْتَبَأْتُ دَعْوَتِي شَفَاعَةً لِأُمَّتِي يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
hadith.en: Every prophet has an answered supplication, and I have reserved my supplication as intercession for my ummah on the Day of Judgment.

hadith.ar: كَانَتْ بَنُو إِسْرَائِيلَ تَسُوسُهُمُ الْأَنْبِيَاءُ، كُلَّمَا هَلَكَ نَبِيٌّ خَلَفَهُ نَبِيٌّ، وَإِنَّهُ لَا نَبِيَّ بَعْدِي
hadith.en: The Children of Israel were led by prophets; whenever a prophet died, another succeeded him. But there is no prophet after me.

shades.name_en: Rasūl — The Messenger as Divine Envoy
shades.name_ar: الرَّسُولُ — الْمَبْعُوثُ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ بِرِسَالَةٍ
shades.explanation:
The rasūl is the divinely commissioned messenger — a human being chosen by Allah to convey His message (risālah) to a specific people or to all humanity. The Quran distinguishes between nabī (prophet — one who receives divine inspiration) and rasūl (messenger — one additionally commissioned to deliver a message and establish a community). Every rasūl is a nabī, but not every nabī is a rasūl. The distinction, while not always explicit in the Quranic text, is developed in Islamic theology based on verses like 22:52 which mention both categories.

The Quran's theology of risālah (messengership) is built on several principles: (1) Allah sends messengers from among the people themselves, speaking their language (14:4), so the message is accessible; (2) messengers come with clear proofs (bayyināt) so that rejection is culpable, not excusable (4:165); (3) messengers are human beings who eat, walk in markets, and are subject to human limitations — their miracle is the message, not superhuman nature (25:7, 25:20); (4) messengers are witnesses over their communities on the Day of Judgment (2:143, 4:41) — the sending of messengers establishes the moral accountability of communities.

The finality of Muhammad's ﷺ messengership — «khātam al-nabiyyīn» (Seal of the Prophets — 33:40) — is the theological foundation of Islam's self-understanding as the completed and universal divine message. Ibn Kathīr, in his tafsīr of 33:40, collects the ḥadīth evidence for the finality of prophethood and states that this is a matter of consensus (ijmāʿ) among the Muslim ummah. Anyone claiming prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ is, by definition, a false claimant (kadhdhāb).
shades.hadith_ar: مَثَلِي وَمَثَلُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ كَمَثَلِ رَجُلٍ بَنَى دَارًا فَأَكْمَلَهَا وَأَحْسَنَهَا إِلَّا مَوْضِعَ لَبِنَةٍ، فَجَعَلَ النَّاسُ يَطُوفُونَ بِهَا وَيَتَعَجَّبُونَ وَيَقُولُونَ: هَلَّا وُضِعَتْ هَٰذِهِ اللَّبِنَةُ؟ فَأَنَا تِلْكَ اللَّبِنَةُ، وَأَنَا خَاتَمُ النَّبِيِّينَ
shades.hadith_en: My example and the example of the prophets is like a man who built a house — he completed it and made it beautiful except for the place of one brick. People would go around admiring it and say: If only this brick were placed! I am that brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets.

shades.name_en: Risālah — The Message, The Divine Communication
shades.explanation:
The risālah is the content entrusted to the rasūl for delivery (tablīgh). The Quran emphasizes that the messenger's sole obligation is «al-balāgh al-mubīn» (clear conveyance — 5:92, 16:35, 24:54, 29:18, 64:12) — to deliver the message completely and clearly, not to compel acceptance. This principle has profound implications for Islamic theology of free will and religious pluralism: the messenger delivers; Allah guides whom He wills. The messenger is not responsible for the response of his audience — only for the faithful transmission of what he has received.

The verse «yā ayyuhā l-rasūlu balligh mā unzila ilayka min rabbika» (O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord — 5:67) is the charter of prophetic responsibility. Al-Ṭabarī reports that this verse was revealed after the Prophet hesitated to convey certain revelations, fearing rejection or harm, and Allah commanded him to deliver the message without fear of people. The verse «wa-llāhu yaʿṣimuka min al-nās» (Allah will protect you from the people) guarantees divine protection for the messenger in the execution of his mission.

Ibn Taymiyyah (al-Risālah al-Tadmuriyyah) develops the concept of risālah as the middle path between two extremes: the extreme of those who elevate the Prophet to divine status (ghulāt), and the extreme of those who reduce him to a mere postman delivering a letter he did not compose (ḥashwiyyah). The correct position: the Prophet is a human being chosen by Allah, entrusted with a divine message, protected from error in conveying it (ʿiṣmah fī l-tablīgh), and owed obedience as the authoritative interpreter of the revelation (4:59). The risālah is divine in origin, human in delivery, and binding in authority.
shades.hadith_ar: بَلِّغُوا عَنِّي وَلَوْ آيَةً
shades.hadith_en: Convey from me, even if it is a single verse

shades.explanation:
The Form IV verb «arsala» (to send) frames prophethood as a divine act of commissioning. Allah «sends» (yursilu) messengers — the active voice emphasizes divine initiative. Messengers do not volunteer or earn prophethood; they are chosen and dispatched. This grammar of sending reinforces the absolute sovereignty of Allah over the institution of prophethood: «Allāhu aʿlamu ḥaythu yajʿalu risālatahu» (Allah knows best where to place His messengership — 6:124).

The Quran presents the sending of messengers as a universal divine practice (sunnah): «wa-la-qad baʿathnā fī kulli ummatin rasūlan» (We have raised in every nation a messenger — 16:36). This verse is fundamental to the Islamic theology of religious pluralism: every human community has received divine guidance through a messenger, making the human race universally addressed by Allah. The differences between religions are not due to Allah's failure to send guidance but to human distortion of the received messages. The Quran's role is to confirm the truth in previous scriptures and correct the distortions (5:48).

The sending of messengers is also tied to the principle of divine justice: «wa-mā kunnā muʿadhdhibīna ḥattā nabʿatha rasūlan» (We would never punish until We have sent a messenger — 17:15). Divine punishment — whether in this world or the next — is morally conditioned on the prior delivery of warning through a messenger. No community is punished for disbelief unless a messenger has come to them with clear proofs and they have rejected him. This principle reconciles divine justice with the reality of religious diversity: those who never received the message are not held accountable for rejecting it.
shades.hadith_ar: وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِنْ قَبْلِكَ مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا نُوحِي إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنَا فَاعْبُدُونِ
shades.hadith_en: We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him: There is no god but Me, so worship Me

shades.explanation:
The root's secondary meaning — rasal (gentleness, deliberation) — reveals an essential quality of the divine method: Allah sends His messages and decrees with taraffuq (gentleness) and tawaddud (deliberation), without haste. The Quran was revealed «ʿalā mukthin» (gradually, over time — 25:32) so that the Prophet's heart might be strengthened — the gradual sending (tarsīl) of revelation is itself a mercy. The Prophet's recitation of the Quran with tartīl (measured, unhurried recitation — from a different root but semantically related to tarsīl in this sense) reflects this quality of deliberate, gentle delivery.

The early linguists noted the connection: a camel that walks gently, unhurriedly, at a comfortable pace is described as walking «rasalan.» The same quality is attributed to the divine method: Allah does not overwhelm His servants with revelation all at once but sends it gradually, gently, at a pace they can absorb. This pedagogical wisdom — divine rasal — reflects the divine names al-Rafīq (the Gentle) and al-Ḥalīm (the Forbearing). Al-Ghazālī (al-Maqṣad al-Asnā) explains that Allah's taraffuq with His servants is among the manifestations of His mercy — He knows human weakness and accommodates it in the method of revelation.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ رَفِيقٌ يُحِبُّ الرِّفْقَ فِي الْأَمْرِ كُلِّهِ
shades.hadith_en: Indeed Allah is Gentle and loves gentleness in all matters

meaning.en: Slave, servant; to worship, to serve with humility and submission. The root encompasses the relationship of total devotion and obedience to Allah — ʿubūdiyyah is the highest human station, combining love, fear, hope, and absolute submission.
meaning.ar: الْعُبُودِيَّةُ وَالْخُضُوعُ وَالذُّلُّ — وَالْعِبَادَةُ: غَايَةُ التَّذَلُّلِ وَالْخُشُوعِ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Servitude — complete subordination of will to the Master. The ʿabd is one who has no independent will before his Lord; ʿibādah is the comprehensive expression of this servitude through worship, obedience, and devotion.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ مُتَقَارِبَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا اللِّينُ وَالذُّلُّ، وَالْآخَرُ الشِّدَّةُ وَالْغِلَظُ. فَالْعَبْدُ: الْمَمْلُوكُ — سُمِّيَ بِذَٰلِكَ لِذُلِّهِ لِمَوْلَاهُ
ibn_faris.en: Two related roots: (1) softness and humility; (2) severity and harshness. The ʿabd (slave) is so named for his humility before his master.

al_raghib.ar: الْعُبُودِيَّةُ: إِظْهَارُ التَّذَلُّلِ. وَالْعِبَادَةُ أَبْلَغُ مِنْهَا لِأَنَّهَا غَايَةُ التَّذَلُّلِ. وَلَا يَسْتَحِقُّهَا إِلَّا مَنْ لَهُ غَايَةُ الْإِفْضَالِ — وَهُوَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَىٰ
al_raghib.en: ʿUbūdiyyah: showing humility. ʿIbādah is more intense — it is the ultimate humility, and none deserves it except the One who has ultimate beneficence — Allah the Exalted.

quran_examples.ar: إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ
quran_examples.en: You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help

quran_examples.ar: وَمَا خَلَقْتُ ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ
quran_examples.en: I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ رَبَّكُمُ
quran_examples.en: O mankind, worship your Lord

hadith.ar: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ
hadith.en: To worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He indeed sees you.

hadith.ar: أَحَبُّ الْأَعْمَالِ إِلَى اللَّهِ أَدْوَمُهَا وَإِنْ قَلَّ
hadith.en: The most beloved of deeds to Allah are those most consistent, even if few.

shades.explanation:
ʿIbādah is the most comprehensive term for worship in the Quran — encompassing all acts of devotion, obedience, love, fear, hope, and submission directed to Allah alone. Ibn Taymiyyah's famous definition in al-ʿUbūdiyyah states: «al-ʿibādah ism jāmiʿ li-kulli mā yuḥibbuhu Llāhu wa-yarḍāhu min al-aqwāl wa-l-aʿmāl al-ẓāhirah wa-l-bāṭinah» — ʿibādah is a comprehensive name for everything Allah loves and is pleased with, from statements and actions, outward and inward. This definition expands ʿibādah beyond ritual acts (prayer, fasting, pilgrimage) to encompass every aspect of life lived in obedience to Allah — including honesty in business, kindness to parents, justice in governance, and even permissible enjoyments when accompanied by the intention of drawing near to Allah.

The exclusivity of ʿibādah is the Quran's central demand: «iyyāka naʿbudu» (You alone we worship — 1:5). The fronting of the object (iyyāka — You alone) before the verb creates the rhetorical emphasis of exclusivity in Arabic grammar (qasr/ḥaṣr). Al-Zamakhsharī comments that this word order establishes tawḥīd al-ʿibādah (the oneness of worship) as the foundation of the relationship between Creator and creation: no act of ultimate devotion, no prostration of the heart or body, may be directed to anyone or anything other than Allah.

The Quran's polemic against shirk (associating partners with Allah) is fundamentally about ʿibādah. The mushrikūn of Quraysh did not deny Allah's existence or His role as Creator (rubūbiyyah) — as evidenced in 10:31, 23:84-89, 29:61-63, 31:25, 39:38, 43:9, 43:87. Their error was directing ʿibādah to other beings — idols, angels, saints, jinn — as intermediaries. The Quran's response is uncompromising: ʿibādah belongs to Allah alone because He alone is the Creator, Sustainer, and ultimate Benefactor. The argument from rubūbiyyah to ulūhiyyah — from exclusive lordship to exclusive worship — is the Quran's central theological proof.
shades.hadith_ar: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ
shades.hadith_en: To worship Allah as if you see Him

shades.name_en: ʿAbd — The Human as Slave of Allah
shades.explanation:
The term «ʿabd» (slave/servant) is the Quran's primary designation for the human being in relation to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ is described as «ʿabduhu wa-rasūluhu» (His servant and His messenger) — servant before messenger, ʿubūdiyyah before risālah. In the Isra and Miʿrāj narrative, the journey begins with «subḥāna lladhī asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan» (Glorified is He who took His servant by night — 17:1). The Prophet's most exalted station — being transported to the divine presence — is predicated on his being «ʿabd» — slave. The highest honor is servitude.

The Quran's anthropology is built on the ʿabd concept: every human being, believer or disbeliever, is ontologically an ʿabd of Allah — created, owned, sustained, and ultimately returned to their Master. The difference is existential, not ontological: the believer recognizes their ʿubūdiyyah and lives accordingly; the disbeliever denies or ignores it and lives in rebellion. In 19:93, «in kullu man fī l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi illā ātī l-Raḥmāni ʿabdā» — everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Most Merciful as a slave. The Day of Judgment is the universal revelation of ʿubūdiyyah — all pretensions to independence, all claims to lordship, are stripped away and every being stands as ʿabd before the true Rabb.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Madārij al-Sālikīn) develops a spiritual typology of ʿubūdiyyah: there is ʿubūdiyyah ʿāmmah (general servitude — the ontological dependence of all creation on Allah) and ʿubūdiyyah khāṣṣah (specific servitude — the voluntary devotion of the believers). The latter has stations (manāzil): ʿubūdiyyat al-ḥubb (servitude of love), ʿubūdiyyat al-khawf (servitude of fear), ʿubūdiyyat al-rajāʾ (servitude of hope), ʿubūdiyyat al-tafwīḍ (servitude of entrustment). The perfect ʿabd combines all stations in balance, like the Prophet ﷺ who was the most loving, most fearing, most hopeful, and most entrusting of all creation to his Lord.
shades.hadith_ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي عَبْدُكَ، وَابْنُ عَبْدِكَ، وَابْنُ أَمَتِكَ، نَاصِيَتِي بِيَدِكَ
shades.hadith_en: O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your maidservant. My forelock is in Your hand.

shades.name_en: Taʿabbud — Devotional Practice and Cultivation of Servitude
shades.explanation:
The Form V verb «taʿabbada» (to devote oneself to worship, to cultivate servitude) and its derivatives describe the process of making oneself a servant (mutaʿabbid) through consistent devotional practice. The taʿabbud (devotional life) of the believer includes ritual acts (ṣalāh, ṣawm, ḥajj) and extends to the cultivation of interior states: khushūʿ (reverent humility), ikhlāṣ (sincerity), murāqabah (vigilant awareness of Allah), and maḥabbah (love).

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Worship) structures his magnum opus around the taʿabbud concept: the outer acts of worship (ʿibādāt ẓāhirah) are the scaffold for the inner states (aḥwāl bāṭinah). The purpose of ritual is not the ritual itself but the spiritual transformation it cultivates. Ṣalāh is not merely physical movement but the training of the heart in presence (ḥuḍūr) before Allah; ṣawm is not merely abstention from food but the training of the soul in self-mastery (taḥakkum); ḥajj is not merely pilgrimage but the rehearsal of death and resurrection.

The Quran's depiction of the ideal worshippers in passages like 25:63-76 — «wa-ʿibādu l-Raḥmāni lladhīna yamshūna ʿalā l-arḍi hawnan» (the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly) — describes taʿabbud as a comprehensive character transformation. The ʿibād al-Raḥmān are characterized by humility, peacefulness, night prayer, charitable spending, chastity, honesty, attentiveness to revelation, and prayer for righteous families — their worship is not compartmentalized but infuses every aspect of their being.
shades.hadith_ar: اعْبُدِ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، وَاعْدُدْ نَفْسَكَ فِي الْمَوْتَى
shades.hadith_en: Worship Allah as if you see Him, and count yourself among the dead

meaning.en: To help, aid, support, grant victory. Expresses active assistance — divine or human — that turns the tide in favor of the oppressed or the righteous against overwhelming odds.
meaning.ar: الْإِعَانَةُ وَالْإِغَاثَةُ وَالتَّأْيِيدُ — وَالنَّصْرُ: إِتْيَانُ الْخَيْرِ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ لِعِبَادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Decisive assistance — help that changes the balance, support that enables the weak to overcome the strong, divine intervention that grants victory to the righteous against all odds.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْإِتْيَانُ بِالْخَيْرِ وَالْإِعَانَةُ، وَالْآخَرُ خِلَافُ الْخِذْلَانِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) bringing good and providing aid; (2) the opposite of abandonment/forsaking.

al_raghib.ar: النَّصْرُ: الْإِعَانَةُ عَلَى الْعَدُوِّ. وَالنَّصِيرُ: الْمُبَالِغُ فِي النَّصْرِ. وَاللَّهُ تَعَالَىٰ هُوَ نَصِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
al_raghib.en: Naṣr: aid against the enemy. Al-Naṣīr: the one who abundantly helps. Allah is the Naṣīr of the believers.

quran_examples.ar: إِذَا جَآءَ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْفَتْحُ
quran_examples.en: When the help of Allah comes and the victory

quran_examples.ar: وَمَا جَعَلَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَّا بُشْرَىٰ لَكُمْ وَلِتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُكُم بِهِۦ ۗ وَمَا ٱلنَّصْرُ إِلَّا مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ
quran_examples.en: Allah made it only as good news for you and to reassure your hearts. Victory comes only from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
quran_examples.context: The source of all victory is Allah alone

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن تَنصُرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ يَنصُرْكُمْ وَيُثَبِّتْ أَقْدَامَكُمْ
quran_examples.en: O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you and plant your feet firmly.
quran_examples.context: Mutual help — human support for Allah's cause brings divine support

hadith.ar: انْصُرْ أَخَاكَ ظَالِمًا أَوْ مَظْلُومًا
hadith.en: Help your brother, whether he is the oppressor or the oppressed.

hadith.ar: مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ
hadith.en: Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress on the Day of Resurrection.

shades.explanation:
«Naṣr Allāh» — the help/victory of Allah — is one of the Quran's most powerful theological concepts. It expresses the divine intervention in history on behalf of the believers against overwhelming odds. The paradigm is the Battle of Badr, where 313 ill-equipped Muslims defeated ~1,000 well-armed Quraysh — a victory the Quran repeatedly attributes solely to Allah: «wa-mā l-naṣru illā min ʿindi Llāh» (victory is only from Allah — 3:126, 8:10). The preposition «min ʿindi» (from the presence of) emphasizes the direct, unmediated nature of divine help — it comes from Allah's immediate power, not through secondary causes.

Al-Ṭabarī, in his extensive commentary on the Badr verses, documents the early community's understanding: the Companions did not attribute their victory to their own courage, numbers, or strategy — they knew it was naṣr from Allah, and this knowledge shaped their subsequent humility and trust (tawakkul). The danger of attributing victory to oneself — the sin of self-reliance (iʿjāb) — is a recurring Quranic theme. Victory is a test as much as defeat: will the victorious become arrogant or grateful?

Sūrat al-Naṣr (110) — the final complete surah revealed — announces «idhā jā'a naṣru Llāhi wa-l-fatḥ» (when the help of Allah comes and the opening/victory). Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly understood this surah as an announcement of the Prophet's ﷺ approaching death: when the mission is complete and victory has come, the Messenger's work on earth is done. The pairing of naṣr (divine help) with fatḥ (opening/conquest) reveals the Quranic vision of history: Allah's help does not merely defeat enemies but «opens» new possibilities — the conquest of Mecca led not to revenge but to mass conversion and the establishment of justice.

In 47:7, the Quran establishes a reciprocal relationship: «in tanṣurū Llāha yanṣurkum» — if you help Allah (by supporting His cause), He will help you. The human role is to provide naṣr to Allah's dīn — through faith, obedience, sacrifice, and struggle — and Allah responds with naṣr from His presence. This reciprocity is not a bargain (as if Allah needed human help) but a moral law (sunnah) embedded in the fabric of existence: divine help flows to those who align themselves with divine purpose. Ibn al-Qayyim (Zād al-Maʿād) develops this into a spiritual principle: the believer's naṣr of Allah is through taqwā and ṭāʿah; Allah's naṣr of the believer is through ta'yīd and tamkīn.
shades.hadith_ar: إِذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ وَالْفَتْحُ
shades.hadith_en: When the help of Allah comes and the victory

shades.name_ar: الِانْتِصَارُ — الدِّفَاعُ عَنِ النَّفْسِ وَطَلَبُ النُّصْرَةِ
shades.explanation:
The Form VIII verb «intaṣara» (to seek help, to defend oneself, to be vindicated) appears in contexts of legitimate self-defense and the prophetic plea for divine assistance against oppressors. In 42:39, the believers are described as those who «wa-lladhīna idhā aṣābahumu l-baghyu hum yantaṣirūn» — when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves (yantaṣirūn). This verse establishes the Quranic ethics of resistance: self-defense against oppression (baghy) is not only permitted but is a characteristic of the righteous community.

Al-Qurṭubī comments that this verse was revealed in Mecca, before the permission for armed struggle (jihād), and establishes the principle that the Muslim community is not to be passive in the face of injustice. The verb «yantaṣirūn» — they seek help/defense — carries the reflexive sense of Form VIII: the believers actively seek naṣr, not passively waiting for it. However, 42:40 adds the moral calculus: «wa-jazā'u sayyi'atin sayyi'atun mithluhā, fa-man ʿafā wa-aṣlaḥa fa-ajruhu ʿalā Llāh» — the recompense of an evil is an evil like it, but whoever forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. The Quran balances the right to intiṣār with the virtue of ʿafw (forgiveness), establishing a spectrum of morally legitimate responses to injustice.

The prophetic supplications for intiṣār form some of the most poignant passages in the Quran. Noah cries: «rabbi innī maghlūbun fa-ntaṣir» (My Lord, I am overcome, so help me! — 54:10). Lot pleads: «rabbi nṣurnī ʿalā l-qawmi l-mufsidīn» (My Lord, help me against the corrupt people — 29:30). Moses is commanded: «fa-ntaṣir» (seek help/vindication — 26:10). These prophetic cries for intiṣār are not expressions of weakness but acknowledgments of dependence — the messenger, despite his prophetic status, is helpless without divine naṣr.
shades.hadith_ar: انْصُرْ أَخَاكَ ظَالِمًا أَوْ مَظْلُومًا
shades.hadith_en: Help your brother, whether oppressor or oppressed

shades.name_en: Naṣīr and Anṣār — The Helpers, Divine and Human
shades.name_ar: النَّصِيرُ وَالْأَنْصَارُ — الْمُعِينُونَ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمِنَ النَّاسِ
shades.explanation:
«Al-Naṣīr» (the Helper) is a divine name — Allah is the ultimate Helper, the one whose aid is sufficient and decisive. In 22:78, «wa-niʿma l-mawlā wa-niʿma l-naṣīr» (How excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper!) — the pairing of mawlā (protector/patron) with naṣīr (helper) expresses the completeness of divine support. The intensive form (faʿīl) indicates abundance and perfection: Allah's help is not occasional or partial but constant and comprehensive.

The human counterpart — «anṣār» (helpers) — is most famously applied to the Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet ﷺ and the Meccan emigrants (muhājirūn). The term «al-Anṣār» became their permanent honorific, recorded in the Quran itself in 9:100 and 9:117. The anṣār of Medina provided not merely political asylum but comprehensive support — housing, food, protection, and brotherhood. Their naṣr of the Prophet ﷺ and his mission became the paradigmatic act of human support for divine cause, rewarded with divine praise and the promise of Paradise.

The Quran also records the prophetic seeking of anṣār: in 3:52 and 61:14, Jesus asks his disciples «man anṣārī ilā Llāh?» (Who are my helpers toward Allah?), and the ḥawāriyyūn (disciples) respond «naḥnu anṣāru Llāh» (We are the helpers of Allah). This scene — a prophet seeking human helpers for the divine mission — establishes the principle that divine naṣr often operates through human anṣār. Allah's help descends through human instruments who volunteer their lives, wealth, and efforts in support of the prophetic mission. The relationship between divine Naṣīr and human anṣār is not competitive but complementary: human help is the visible manifestation of divine help in history.
shades.hadith_ar: الْأَنْصَارُ لَا يُحِبُّهُمْ إِلَّا مُؤْمِنٌ وَلَا يُبْغِضُهُمْ إِلَّا مُنَافِقٌ
shades.hadith_en: None loves the Ansar except a believer, and none hates them except a hypocrite

meaning.en: To make, create, place, appoint, establish, render. A versatile verb of causation — expressing divine creative action, human manufacturing, and the transformation of one thing into another. Less primordial than khalaqa (to create ex nihilo); implies making from existing material or appointing to a role.
meaning.ar: الصُّنْعُ وَالْإِيجَادُ وَالتَّصْيِيرُ — جَعَلَ الشَّيْءَ: صَنَعَهُ أَوْ وَضَعَهُ أَوْ صَيَّرَهُ إِلَى حَالٍ أُخْرَى

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Making and appointing — the root covers the spectrum from physical fabrication to metaphysical establishment. Jaʿala can mean to create from existing materials (as opposed to khalqa from nothing), to transform one thing into another, or to designate someone to a role or status.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الصُّنْعُ وَالشَّيْءُ يُصْنَعُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْوَضْعُ وَالتَّعْيِينُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) making/fabricating something; (2) placing and appointing/designating.

al_raghib.ar: جَعَلَ: لَفْظٌ عَامٌّ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ — يُقَالُ جَعَلَ يَفْعَلُ كَذَا، وَجَعَلَ الشَّيْءَ: صَنَعَهُ، وَجَعَلَهُ كَذَا: صَيَّرَهُ. وَهُوَ أَخَصُّ مِنْ فَعَلَ وَأَعَمُّ مِنْ خَلَقَ
al_raghib.en: Jaʿala: a general term for actions — 'he began doing such,' 'he made something,' 'he transformed it into such.' More specific than faʿala (to do), more general than khalaqa (to create).

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلْأَرْضَ فِرَٰشًۭا وَٱلسَّمَآءَ بِنَآءًۭ
quran_examples.en: Who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky a canopy
quran_examples.context: Divine making of the cosmos for human benefit

quran_examples.ar: تَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ بُرُوجًۭا وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا سِرَٰجًۭا وَقَمَرًۭا مُّنِيرًۭا
quran_examples.en: Blessed is He who placed constellations in the sky and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلَـٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّى جَاعِلٌۭ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةًۭ
quran_examples.en: When your Lord said to the angels: I am placing a vicegerent on earth

hadith.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ جَعَلَ الرَّحْمَةَ مِائَةَ جُزْءٍ، فَأَمْسَكَ عِنْدَهُ تِسْعَةً وَتِسْعِينَ جُزْءًا، وَأَنْزَلَ فِي الْأَرْضِ جُزْءًا وَاحِدًا
hadith.en: Allah created mercy as one hundred parts; He retained ninety-nine parts and sent down one part to earth.

hadith.ar: جَعَلَ اللَّهُ الْحَسَنَةَ بِعَشْرِ أَمْثَالِهَا
hadith.en: Allah has made a good deed worth ten times its like.

shades.name_en: Divine Creative Making — Jaʿl as Cosmological Act
shades.explanation:
The verb «jaʿala» appears throughout the Quran's cosmological passages describing Allah's making of the world for human habitation and benefit. «Alladhī jaʿala lakumu l-arḍa firāshan» (Who made the earth a resting place for you — 2:22) — the verb jaʿala here means 'to make something serve as something else for a purpose.' The earth is made firāsh (spread/cradle) — not merely created as a physical object but given a specific function and orientation toward human benefit.

The theological significance of jaʿala in cosmological contexts lies in its purposive character. Unlike khalaqa (to create — which emphasizes bringing into existence from nothing), jaʿala emphasizes the ordering and functional arrangement of creation. Al-Rāzī distinguishes: khalaqa refers to the origination of substance (ījād al-dhāt), while jaʿala refers to the bestowal of form, function, and arrangement (al-tashkīl wa-l-tadbīr). The heavens are not merely created; they are «made» into a protected ceiling (saqfan maḥfūẓan — 21:32). The night is not merely created; it is «made» into a covering (libāsan — 78:10). These jaʿls express divine intentionality — creation is not random but purposefully configured for life, guidance, and worship.

In 2:30, the most theologically charged usage: «innī jāʿilun fī l-arḍi khalīfatan» (I am placing/making a vicegerent on earth). The active participle «jāʿilun» (maker/placer) is used rather than «khāliqun» (creator) — emphasizing that Adam's appointment as khalīfah is not merely his creation as a biological being but his installation into a role, a status, a function within the cosmic order. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that jaʿl here encompasses both the creation of Adam's physical form and his designation as Allah's representative — the making of both body and office.
shades.hadith_ar: جَعَلَ اللَّهُ الرَّحْمَةَ مِائَةَ جُزْءٍ
shades.hadith_en: Allah created mercy as one hundred parts

shades.name_ar: التَّصْيِيرُ — تَحْوِيلُ الشَّيْءِ إِلَى حَالَةٍ أُخْرَى
shades.explanation:
One of the root's distinctive usages in Arabic grammar is «jaʿala» as a verb of transformation (taṣyīr) — to render something into a different state. The Quran uses this grammatically to describe divine transformative acts: «fa-jaʿalnāhum aḥādītha» (We made them into tales/stories — 23:44, i.e., We destroyed them so thoroughly that only their stories remained). «Fa-jaʿalnāhu habā'an manthūrā» (We will make their deeds like scattered dust — 25:23). «Wa-jaʿalnā mina l-mā'i kulla shay'in ḥayy» (We made every living thing from water — 21:30).

The grammatical structure of jaʿala + first object + second object (both in the accusative) expresses the transformation: jaʿala X Y = 'He made X into Y.' This syntactic pattern is rich in theological implication. In 2:65, the Sabbath-breakers are told «kūnū qiradatan khāsi'īn» (Be apes, despised) — they are transformed into apes as divine punishment. The transformation is expressed through kāna (to be), but the underlying concept is jaʿl: Allah «made» them into apes through His transformative power.

Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Kashshāf) analyzes the rhetoric of jaʿala as taṣyīr in eschatological passages: when Allah «makes» mountains like carded wool (101:5), the verb jaʿala emphasizes divine agency over cosmic destruction — the mountains do not merely dissolve; they are actively «made» into dust by the One who originally «made» them stable. The symmetry between creative jaʿl and destructive jaʿl reinforces the theological message: the One who «made» the cosmos can just as easily «unmake» it.

shades.name_en: Jaʿl as Appointment — Designation to Role and Status
shades.name_ar: جَعْلُ التَّعْيِينِ — النَّصْبُ فِي الْمَنْصِبِ وَالْوَظِيفَةِ
shades.explanation:
The root is the primary Quranic term for divine appointment — designating individuals or communities to specific roles in the divine plan. Abraham is «jaʿala» as an imām for humanity (2:124). David is «jaʿala» as khalīfah on earth (38:26). The Children of Israel are «jaʿala» as successors (khalā'if) after the destruction of Pharaoh's people (10:14). The Muslim ummah is «jaʿala» as a middle/balanced community (ummatan wasaṭan — 2:143). In each case, jaʿl involves both honor (divine choice) and responsibility (divine accountability).

Ibn Taymiyyah (Minhāj al-Sunnah) develops a political theology from this usage: legitimate authority (imāmah, khilāfah, wilāyah) is fundamentally a divine jaʿl — an appointment that originates in Allah's will and is actualized through historical processes. The appointment of Abraham as imām (2:124) establishes that religious-political leadership is a divine gift (mawhibah), not a hereditary right or a democratic election — though divine jaʿl may operate through human recognition and bayʿah (pledge of allegiance).

The Quran's emphasis on divine jaʿl of leadership serves to relativize all human claims to authority. No dynasty, no elected government, no self-appointed leader can claim intrinsic legitimacy — all authority is contingent on divine appointment and conditional on justice. When David is appointed khalīfah, he is immediately commanded to «rule between people with justice» (38:26) — the jaʿl of authority is inseparable from the obligation of ʿadl (justice). Al-Māwardī (al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyyah) builds his theory of Islamic governance on this principle: the imām is appointed (jāʿala) by divine law, actualized through human selection (ikhtiyār), and accountable to divine standards of justice.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ جَعَلَنِي عَبْدًا كَرِيمًا وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْنِي جَبَّارًا عَنِيدًا
shades.hadith_en: Allah made me a noble servant and did not make me a stubborn tyrant

meaning.en: To find, discover, encounter, experience; to possess, to be able; existence, being. The root moves from the act of finding (discovering something sought) to the state of possession (having found, one now owns) to the metaphysical concept of existence (wujūd — that which is 'found' to be).
meaning.ar: الظَّفَرُ بِالشَّيْءِ وَالْإِصَابَةُ — وَالْوُجُودُ: ضِدُّ الْعَدَمِ، وَالْوِجْدَانُ: الْغِنَى وَالْمِلْكُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Finding and being found — the root links the subjective act of discovery with the objective fact of existence. What is 'found' (mawjūd) is what exists; what exists is what can be found. The philosophical concept of wujūd (existence) derives from this root but far exceeds its Quranic usage.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْوُجُودُ — ضِدُّ الْعَدَمِ، وَالْآخَرُ الْغِنَى — وَمِنْهُ الْوِجْدَانُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) existence — opposite of nonexistence; (2) wealth/possession — hence wijdān (finding/possessing).

al_raghib.ar: الْوُجُودُ: ضِدُّ الْعَدَمِ، وَهُوَ يَكُونُ بِالْإِدْرَاكِ. وَيُقَالُ: وَجَدْتُ الشَّيْءَ إِذَا أَدْرَكْتَهُ بِحَاسَّةٍ أَوْ عَقْلٍ
al_raghib.en: Wujūd: opposite of nonexistence — it involves perception. You say 'I found something' when you perceived it by sense or intellect.

quran_examples.ar: أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًۭا فَـَٔاوَىٰ
quran_examples.en: Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?
quran_examples.context: Divine finding and caring for the Prophet

quran_examples.ar: كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًۭا
quran_examples.en: Whenever Zechariah entered the sanctuary, he found with her provision

quran_examples.ar: أَفَلَا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ ۚ وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِندِ غَيْرِ ٱللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا۟ فِيهِ ٱخْتِلَـٰفًۭا كَثِيرًۭا
quran_examples.en: Do they not reflect on the Quran? If it were from other than Allah, they would find in it much contradiction

hadith.ar: مَنْ وَجَدَ سَعَةً فَلَمْ يُضَحِّ فَلَا يَقْرَبَنَّ مُصَلَّانَا
hadith.en: Whoever has the means (wajada saʿah) but does not offer a sacrifice, let him not approach our place of prayer.

hadith.ar: لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يُحِبَّ لِأَخِيهِ مَا يُحِبُّ لِنَفْسِهِ
hadith.en: None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves (yajidu) for himself.

shades.name_en: Divine Finding — Allah's Knowledge and Care
shades.explanation:
The verb «wajada» (He found) applied to Allah in Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā (93) carries extraordinary theological weight: «a-lam yajidka yatīman fa-āwā» (Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? — 93:6). Allah's 'finding' of the Prophet ﷺ as an orphan is not a discovery in ignorance (as human finding implies) but a knowledge accompanied by care — He 'found' him in the sense of knowing his state and responding with provision. Al-Rāzī explains that divine «wujūd» here means comprehensive knowledge (ʿilm muḥīṭ) accompanied by mercy and care — Allah's finding is always also His providing.

The Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā triad — found you an orphan, found you lost/unguided, found you poor — establishes the pattern of divine care: Allah's 'finding' of human need is the prelude to His meeting of that need. The orphan is sheltered, the lost is guided, the poor is enriched. This pattern becomes a moral imperative for the Prophet: «fa-ammā l-yatīma fa-lā taqhar, wa-ammā l-sā'ila fa-lā tanhar, wa-ammā bi-niʿmati rabbika fa-ḥaddith» (So as for the orphan, do not oppress; as for the asker, do not repel; as for the favor of your Lord, speak of it — 93:9-11). The one who was 'found' in need must respond to others 'found' in need — divine finding generates human compassion.

The Quran's use of «wajada» for Allah is rare and carefully placed — it appears in contexts of intimate divine care rather than abstract divine knowledge (for which ʿalima is used). This lexical choice humanizes the divine-human relationship while maintaining absolute transcendence: Allah 'finds' His servants not because He was previously unaware (as human finding implies) but because His knowledge encompasses every state and His mercy responds to every need.
shades.hadith_ar: أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَى
shades.hadith_en: Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?

shades.explanation:
The root's most basic meaning — to find, to come upon, to encounter — generates the concept of wujūd (existence/presence). What «exists» (mawjūd) is what is «found» — the passive participle (mawjūd) literally means 'that which has been found' or 'that which is findable.'
