This semantic link between being-found and being-real is philosophically significant: in the pre-modern Islamic worldview, existence is not a brute fact but a relational concept — to exist is to be present to a finder, whether divine or human.

The Islamic philosophical tradition developed elaborate theories of wujūd from this root — far beyond its Quranic usage. Ibn Sīnā's distinction between wājib al-wujūd (the Necessary Existent — whose essence is identical with existence) and mumkin al-wujūd (the contingent existent — whose existence depends on another) became the foundation of Islamic metaphysics. Mullā Ṣadrā's theory of aṣālat al-wujūd (the fundamentality of existence) — that existence is real and essences are derived — revolutionized later Islamic philosophy. These developments far exceed the Quran's own usage of the root but are linguistically anchored in it: the Quranic «wajada» (to find) provides the lexical seed from which the philosophical «wujūd» (existence) grows.

In the Quran itself, «wajada» most often describes human encounter with reality: Zechariah «finds» Mary with provision (3:37), Moses «finds» two men fighting (28:15), the believers «find» no deviation in the Quran (4:82). These usages ground the root in concrete human experience — finding is a fundamental epistemic act: one knows what one finds, and what one finds shapes what one believes.

meaning.en: To call, summon, invite; to supplicate, pray, invoke. The root encompasses the full spectrum of calling — from the divine call to faith (daʿwah), to prophetic invitation of people to Allah, to the believer's intimate supplication (duʿāʾ), to the naming of things.
meaning.ar: النِّدَاءُ وَالطَّلَبُ وَالِاسْتِدْعَاءُ — الدَّعْوَةُ إِلَى اللَّهِ، وَالدُّعَاءُ: طَلَبُ الْعَبْدِ مِنْ رَبِّهِ، وَدَعَوْتُهُ: سَمَّيْتُهُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Calling — the root covers every form of directed address: Allah calling humanity to faith, the Prophet calling people to Islam, the believer calling upon Allah in prayer, and even the act of naming (calling someone by a name).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا النِّدَاءُ وَالطَّلَبُ، وَالْآخَرُ التَّسْمِيَةُ. تَقُولُ: دَعَوْتُ فُلَانًا — أَيْ نَادَيْتُهُ أَوْ طَلَبْتُهُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) calling and requesting; (2) naming. You say: daʿawtu fulānan — I called him or requested him.

al_raghib.ar: الدُّعَاءُ: طَلَبُ الْأَدْنَى لِلْأَعْلَى فِعْلًا عَلَى جِهَةِ الْخُضُوعِ وَالِاسْتِكَانَةِ. وَقَدْ يَكُونُ بِمَعْنَى النِّدَاءِ وَالتَّسْمِيَةِ
al_raghib.en: Duʿāʾ: the lower requesting from the higher an action, in a manner of humility and submission. Sometimes means calling or naming.

quran_examples.ar: وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ٱدْعُونِىٓ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ
quran_examples.en: Your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ
quran_examples.en: When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me.

quran_examples.ar: ٱدْعُ إِلَىٰ سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِٱلْحِكْمَةِ
quran_examples.en: Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom

hadith.ar: الدُّعَاءُ هُوَ الْعِبَادَةُ
hadith.en: Supplication (duʿāʾ) is worship itself.
hadith.source: Sunan al-Tirmidhī 3371 | Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1479 | Sunan Ibn Mājah 3828

hadith.ar: مَنْ دَعَا إِلَى هُدًى كَانَ لَهُ مِنَ الْأَجْرِ مِثْلُ أُجُورِ مَنْ تَبِعَهُ لَا يَنْقُصُ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ أُجُورِهِمْ شَيْئًا
hadith.en: Whoever calls to guidance receives the reward of all who follow him, without diminishing their rewards at all.

shades.name_en: Duʿāʾ — Supplication as the Essence of Worship
shades.name_ar: الدُّعَاءُ — مُخُّ الْعِبَادَةِ وَصِلَةُ الْعَبْدِ بِرَبِّهِ
shades.explanation:
The ḥadīth «al-duʿāʾu huwa l-ʿibādah» (supplication is worship — Tirmidhī 3371) encapsulates the Quranic theology of duʿāʾ. Duʿāʾ is not merely one act of worship among many — it is the «essence» (mukhkh) of worship because it expresses the fundamental human posture before Allah: need, dependency, humility, hope, and trust. When the believer raises their hands and calls «yā Rabb» (O Lord), they actualize the ontological truth of ʿubūdiyyah — that the human being is inherently needy (faqīr) and Allah is inherently self-sufficient (ghanī).

The Quran records the supplications of every prophet as models of duʿāʾ. Noah: «rabbi innī maghlūbun fa-ntaṣir» (My Lord, I am overcome, so help me — 54:10). Abraham: «rabbi ijʿalnī muqīma l-ṣalāti wa-min dhurriyyatī» (My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [many] from my descendants — 14:40). Job: «annī massaniya l-ḍurru wa-anta arḥamu l-rāḥimīn» (Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful — 21:83). Jonah in the belly of the whale: «lā ilāha illā anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min al-ẓālimīn» (No god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers — 21:87). The variety of circumstances and supplications reveals duʿāʾ as the universal prophetic language — every situation, every need, every emotion has its duʿāʾ.

The Quran establishes the conditions for answered duʿāʾ: sincerity (ikhlāṣ — 40:14), humility and fear (40:60), hope (7:56), lawful provision (2:172), and response to Allah's call before expecting Allah to respond to one's own (2:186). The verse 2:186 — nestled between the verses on fasting — teaches that Allah's nearness and responsiveness are particularly manifest in the context of worship and obedience: the one who draws near to Allah through ṣawm (fasting) finds Allah near in duʿāʾ.
shades.hadith_ar: يَنْزِلُ رَبُّنَا تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا حِينَ يَبْقَى ثُلُثُ اللَّيْلِ الْآخِرُ فَيَقُولُ: مَنْ يَدْعُونِي فَأَسْتَجِيبَ لَهُ، مَنْ يَسْأَلُنِي فَأُعْطِيَهُ، مَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُنِي فَأَغْفِرَ لَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night, saying: Who is calling upon Me that I may answer him? Who is asking Me that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness that I may forgive him?

shades.name_en: Daʿwah — The Call to Allah, Missionary Invitation
shades.name_ar: الدَّعْوَةُ — النِّدَاءُ إِلَى دِينِ اللَّهِ وَالْإِسْلَامِ
shades.explanation:
Daʿwah — the call to Islam — is the prophetic mission in its active, outward-facing dimension. The command «udʿu ilā sabīli rabbika bi-l-ḥikmati wa-l-mawʿiẓati l-ḥasanah» (Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition — 16:125) establishes the methodology of Islamic outreach: wisdom (ḥikmah) — addressing each audience according to their intellectual and cultural context; good admonition (mawʿiẓah ḥasanah) — persuasive ethical appeal; and gentle debate (jādilhum bi-llatī hiya aḥsan) — respectful engagement with objections. The verse prohibits compulsion in religion (2:256) while commanding invitation to it — daʿwah is persuasion, not coercion.

The Quran describes the daʿwah as a response to Allah's prior call: «yā qawmanā ajībū dāʿiya Llāh» (O our people, respond to the caller of Allah — 46:31). The jinn who heard the Quran described it as a «dāʿī» (caller) inviting to guidance. The human daʿwah (missionary invitation) is the echo of the divine daʿwah (the primordial call imprinted on the fiṭrah of every human being). The Prophet ﷺ is described as «dāʿiyan ilā Llāh bi-idhnihi» (one who calls to Allah by His permission — 33:46) — the daʿwah is authorized, empowered, and bounded by divine permission.

In 41:33, the Quran asks rhetorically: «wa-man aḥsanu qawlan mimman daʿā ilā Llāh» (Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah?). This verse elevates daʿwah to the highest form of qawl (speech) — the best use of the human capacity for language is to invite others to their Creator. The daʿwah is the continuation of the prophetic mission through the ummah — the community of believers inherits the responsibility of calling humanity to Allah after the Prophet's ﷺ death.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ دَعَا إِلَى هُدًى كَانَ لَهُ مِنَ الْأَجْرِ مِثْلُ أُجُورِ مَنْ تَبِعَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Whoever calls to guidance receives the reward of all who follow him

meaning.en: To recompense, reward, punish, requite. The root expresses the principle of moral reciprocity — every deed receives its due recompense, whether good or evil. Central to Quranic eschatology as the foundation of divine justice.
meaning.ar: الْمُكَافَأَةُ وَالْعِوَضُ — الْجَزَاءُ عَلَى الْعَمَلِ، خَيْرًا كَانَ أَوْ شَرًّا. وَأَصْلُهُ: الْقَضَاءُ وَالْوَفَاءُ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Moral requital — the necessary connection between act and consequence, established by divine justice and operative in both this world and the Hereafter.

al_raghib.ar: الْجَزَاءُ: الْغِنَى وَالْكِفَايَةُ. وَيُقَالُ: جَزَيْتُ فُلَانًا كَذَا — أَيْ كَافَأْتُهُ. ثُمَّ اُسْتُعْمِلَ فِي كُلِّ مُكَافَأَةٍ عَلَى فِعْلٍ — خَيْرًا أَوْ شَرًّا
al_raghib.en: Jazāʾ: sufficiency and requital. One says: I recompensed so-and-so — meaning I rewarded him. Then applied to every requital for an action, good or evil.

quran_examples.ar: فَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًۭا يَرَهُۥ
quran_examples.en: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it

quran_examples.ar: وَٱتَّقُوا۟ يَوْمًۭا لَّا تَجْزِى نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍۢ شَيْـًٔا
quran_examples.en: Fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all

hadith.ar: إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُمْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ
hadith.en: The patient will be given their reward without measure.

shades.name_en: Eschatological Recompense — Divine Justice in the Hereafter
shades.explanation:
The Quran's eschatology is fundamentally a theology of jazāʾ — every soul receives exactly what it has earned, «lā tuẓlamūna fatīlā» (you will not be wronged even by a thread — 4:77, 17:71). The Day of Judgment is «yawm al-jazāʾ» (the Day of Recompense) in multiple passages. The absolute justice of divine recompense is a non-negotiable Quranic principle: the scales of justice (mawāzīn al-qisṭ) are set, and no soul is wronged (21:47). The precision of recompense — to the weight of a mustard seed (21:47), to the weight of an atom (99:7-8) — emphasizes the completeness of divine justice.

Al-Rāzī (Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb) in his commentary on the eschatological verses develops a philosophical argument from jazāʾ for bodily resurrection: if recompense is to be just, it must be experienced by the same entity that performed the deed — the body-soul composite, not merely a disembodied soul. The Quran's graphic descriptions of physical reward and punishment serve to emphasize that the person being recompensed is the same person who acted — not a ghostly remnant but the full human being restored to embodied life.

The Quran's doctrine of jazāʾ balances divine mercy and divine justice. While «wa-mā khalaqtu l-jinna wa-l-insa illā li-yaʿbudūn» (I created jinn and humans only to worship Me — 51:56) establishes worship as the purpose of creation, the principle of jazāʾ ensures that worship is not meaningless but leads to eternal consequences — Paradise for the obedient, Hell for the defiant. The threat of punishment and the promise of reward are not extrinsic to the moral order but intrinsic to the structure of a universe created by a Just Judge. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Fear and Hope) argues that fear of jazāʾ (khawf) and hope for jazāʾ (rajāʾ) are twin spiritual states that motivate the believer toward righteousness — neither should overwhelm the other, and both should lead to loving obedience rather than mere calculation.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُمْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ
shades.hadith_en: The patient will be given their reward without measure

meaning.en: Self, soul, spirit, person. The root designates the individual human being in their totality — as a living consciousness, a moral agent, and a unique irreplaceable entity. Also: to breathe, to relieve, to bring comfort.
meaning.ar: الذَّاتُ وَالرُّوحُ وَالشَّخْصُ — النَّفْسُ: حَقِيقَةُ الْإِنْسَانِ الْجَامِعَةُ لِلْجَسَدِ وَالرُّوحِ، وَمِنْهُ التَّنْفِيسُ: إِزَالَةُ الْكُرْبَةِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: The living self — the root's physical sense (breath, breathing) anchors its psychological and spiritual meaning (self, soul, person). The nafs is the breathing, living core of human identity.

al_raghib.ar: النَّفْسُ: الرُّوحُ وَالْحَيَاةُ. وَقَدْ تُسْتَعْمَلُ بِمَعْنَى الذَّاتِ وَالْحَقِيقَةِ. وَالنَّفَسُ: الْخُرُوجُ مِنَ الْجَوْفِ وَالدُّخُولُ فِيهِ
al_raghib.en: Nafs: spirit and life. Sometimes used to mean the essence and reality. Nafas: the exhalation and inhalation of breath.

quran_examples.ar: وَنَفْسٍۢ وَمَا سَوَّىٰهَا
quran_examples.en: By the soul and He who proportioned it

quran_examples.ar: مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًۢا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًۭا
quran_examples.en: Whoever kills a soul for other than a soul or corruption in the land — it is as if he killed all humanity

quran_examples.ar: وَٱتَّقُوا۟ يَوْمًۭا لَّا تَجْزِى نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍۢ شَيْـًٔا
quran_examples.en: Fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all

hadith.ar: مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ
hadith.en: Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the Day of Resurrection.

shades.name_en: al-Nafs — The Human Self in its Moral Struggles
shades.name_ar: النَّفْسُ — الذَّاتُ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةُ فِي صِرَاعِهَا الْأَخْلَاقِيِّ
shades.explanation:
The nafs in the Quran is the arena of moral struggle — the self that can be purified (tazkiyah) or corrupted, elevated or debased. Sūrat al-Shams (91:7-10) presents the most concentrated anthropology of the nafs: «wa-nafsin wa-mā sawwāhā, fa-alhamahā fujūrahā wa-taqwāhā, qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā, wa-qad khāba man dassāhā» — By the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness; he has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it. The nafs is created with the dual capacity for fujūr (transgression) and taqwā (God-consciousness) — moral orientation is not predetermined but chosen through the exercise of free will guided by divine inspiration.

The Islamic tradition developed a threefold typology of the nafs based on Quranic usage: al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ (the soul that commands to evil — 12:53, as Joseph confesses about his own soul), al-nafs al-lawwāmah (the self-reproaching soul — 75:2, which feels guilt and strives for reform), and al-nafs al-muṭma'innah (the soul at peace — 89:27, called to return to its Lord in contentment). This typology, elaborated by al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī (Bayān al-Farq) and systematized by later Ṣūfī masters, maps the spiritual journey from the lower self dominated by desire, through the struggling self that holds itself to account, to the purified self that has attained tranquility through remembrance of Allah.

The Quran's moral psychology of the nafs is fundamentally optimistic: the nafs is not inherently sinful (as in the Christian doctrine of original sin) but is created in a state of fiṭrah (primordial purity — 30:30) with the capacity for both good and evil. The purpose of religion is to support the nafs in its struggle toward purification — through prayer (29:45), charity (9:103), fasting (2:183), remembrance (13:28), and righteous company (18:28). The nafs that succeeds in this struggle (tazkiyah) attains falāḥ (ultimate success — 91:9), while the nafs that fails (tadsiyah — burying it in sin) faces khaybah (ultimate failure — 91:10).
shades.hadith_ar: أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ نَفْسِي وَمِنْ شَرِّ الشَّيْطَانِ وَشِرْكِهِ
shades.hadith_en: I seek refuge in You from the evil of my own soul and from the evil of Satan and his polytheism

meaning.en: To go astray, to err, to be lost, to deviate from the right path. The root's core image is that of a traveler losing their way in the desert — extended metaphorically to moral, intellectual, and spiritual deviation from divine guidance.
meaning.ar: الذَّهَابُ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ وَالْحَيْرَةُ — وَالضَّلَالُ: ضِدُّ الْهُدَى، وَهُوَ الْعُدُولُ عَنِ الصِّرَاطِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Losing the way — the root encapsulates the condition of being without guidance, whether literally (lost in a physical space), intellectually (holding false beliefs), or spiritually (disconnected from Allah).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَيَاعِ الشَّيْءِ وَذَهَابِهِ فِي غَيْرِ حَقِّهِ. تَقُولُ: ضَلَّ الْمَاءُ فِي اللَّبَنِ: إِذَا ذَهَبَ فِيهِ
ibn_faris.en: A single root indicating the loss of something and its departure from its proper place. You say: the water disappeared (ḍalla) in the milk — when it vanished into it.

al_raghib.ar: الضَّلَالُ: الْعُدُولُ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ. وَيُقَالُ: ضَلَّ فُلَانٌ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ — إِذَا جَاوَزَهُ وَلَمْ يَهْتَدِ إِلَيْهِ
al_raghib.en: Ḍalāl: deviation from the straight path. It is said: so-and-so went astray from the road — when he missed it and could not find guidance.

quran_examples.ar: صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ
quran_examples.en: The path of those You have blessed — not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray

quran_examples.ar: وَوَجَدَكَ ضَآلًّۭا فَهَدَىٰ
quran_examples.en: He found you lost and guided you
quran_examples.context: Allah's guidance of the Prophet from misguidance

quran_examples.ar: قَالَ فَعَلْتُهَآ إِذًۭا وَأَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ
quran_examples.en: Moses said: I did it then, when I was among those astray

hadith.ar: كُلُّكُمْ ضَالٌّ إِلَّا مَنْ هَدَيْتُهُ، فَاسْتَهْدُونِي أَهْدِكُمْ
hadith.en: All of you are astray except those I guide; so seek guidance from Me and I will guide you.

shades.name_en: Ḍalāl as Moral and Theological Deviance
shades.explanation:
Ḍalāl in the Quran is the comprehensive term for deviation from divine guidance — encompassing false belief, wrong action, and spiritual disconnection. Al-Fātiḥah's final verse distinguishes two categories of the misguided: «al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim» (those who have incurred divine anger — identified by the exegetes as the Jews who knew the truth but acted against it) and «al-ḍāllīn» (those who are astray — identified as the Christians who deviated from the truth out of ignorance or excess in devotion). The distinction is crucial: one can be misguided through willful rebellion against known truth (ghaḍab) or through sincere but mistaken belief (ḍalāl). The daily petition for guidance away from both paths reflects the comprehensive Islamic concern with both moral and intellectual deviation.

The Quran's theology of ḍalāl is predicated on divine sovereignty over guidance. «Man yahdi Llāhu fa-huwa l-muhtadī, wa-man yuḍlil fa-lan tajida lahu waliyyan murshidā» (Whomever Allah guides is rightly guided, and whomever He leads astray — you will never find for him a guiding protector — 18:17). This verse, and its numerous parallels, has been the site of intense theological debate. The Qadariyyah and later Muʿtazilah argued that aḍalla (He led astray) means 'He judged them to be astray' or 'He abandoned them to their misguidance' — not that Allah actively creates misguidance. The Ashāʿirah and Ahl al-Ḥadīth maintained that Allah is the Creator of all actions, including misguidance, but that His act of 'leading astray' is a just punishment for the servant's prior choice of misguidance. The Māturīdiyyah took a middle position: Allah creates misguidance as a consequence of the servant's free choice, not arbitrarily.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl) devotes extensive analysis to the Quranic treatment of ḍalāl, arguing that Allah never leads astray anyone who sincerely seeks guidance — «wa-lladhīna jāhadū fīnā la-nahdiyannahum subulanā» (those who strive for Us, We will guide them to Our paths — 29:69). The divine act of iḍlāl (leading astray) is always consequent upon the servant's prior turning away from guidance. Ḍalāl, in this analysis, has a human cause and a divine consequence — the servant chooses misguidance, and Allah confirms them in it as a punishment and a manifestation of His justice.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلَا هَادِيَ لَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him

meaning.en: To guide, to direct to the right path, to lead aright. The root encompasses divine guidance through revelation and inspiration, prophetic guidance through teaching and example, and the human response of being guided (ihtidāʾ).
meaning.ar: الْإِرْشَادُ وَالدَّلَالَةُ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ — وَالْهُدَى: ضِدُّ الضَّلَالِ، وَهُوَ بَيَانُ طَرِيقِ الْحَقِّ وَالتَّوْفِيقُ لِسُلُوكِهِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Guidance — the divinely provided knowledge, inspiration, and enablement that leads to the straight path. Opposite of ḍalāl (misguidance). Hudā is both the map (revelation) and the ability to follow it (tawfīq).

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا التَّقَدُّمُ لِلْإِرْشَادِ، وَالْآخَرُ بَعْثُ الشَّيْءِ وَإِرْسَالُهُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) going ahead to guide; (2) sending something forth.

al_raghib.ar: الْهُدَى: الدَّلَالَةُ بِلُطْفٍ إِلَى مَا يُوصِلُ إِلَى الْمَطْلُوبِ. وَالْهِدَايَةُ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَوْجُهٍ: هِدَايَةُ الْإِلْهَامِ، وَهِدَايَةُ الْبَيَانِ، وَهِدَايَةُ التَّوْفِيقِ، وَهِدَايَةُ الْآخِرَةِ
al_raghib.en: Hudā: gently indicating what leads to the sought goal. Guidance is of four types: guidance of inspiration (innate), guidance of explanation (revelation), guidance of enablement (tawfīq), and guidance to the Hereafter.

quran_examples.ar: ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ
quran_examples.en: Guide us to the straight path
quran_examples.context: The central petition of every Muslim

quran_examples.ar: ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ
quran_examples.en: This is the Book — no doubt in it — a guidance for the God-conscious

quran_examples.ar: وَوَجَدَكَ ضَآلًّۭا فَهَدَىٰ
quran_examples.en: He found you lost and guided you

hadith.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى
hadith.en: O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency.

shades.name_en: Hudā — Divine Guidance through Revelation and Tawfīq
shades.explanation:
Hudā — guidance — is the Quran's most cherished concept and humanity's most urgent need. The opening surah's central petition — «ihdinā l-ṣirāṭa l-mustaqīm» (Guide us to the straight path — 1:6) — is recited by every Muslim at least seventeen times daily, making it the most frequent supplication in human history. The petition is not for knowledge alone (as if the ṣirāṭ were unknown) but for the comprehensive divine enablement (tawfīq) to know, love, and follow the straight path. Al-Rāghib's fourfold typology of hidāyah captures this comprehensiveness: Allah guides through innate inspiration (hidāyat al-ilhām — the fiṭrah), through revealed explanation (hidāyat al-bayān — the Quran), through enabling grace (hidāyat al-tawfīq — the actual ability to follow), and ultimately through admission to Paradise (hidāyat al-ākhirah — the final destination).

The Quran describes itself as «hudan li-l-nās» (guidance for mankind — 2:185) and «hudan li-l-muttaqīn» (guidance for the God-conscious — 2:2). The apparent tension — is the Quran guidance for all humanity or only for the pious? — is resolved by the exegetes: the Quran is objectively guidance for all (it contains the truth and the path), but subjectively it benefits only those who approach it with taqwā (reverence, openness, willingness to follow). Al-Ṭabarī explains: the Quran is guidance for all humanity in that it shows the right path; but it is specifically guidance for the muttaqīn in that they alone benefit from it. The same sun that illuminates the world can be blinding to one who refuses to open their eyes.

The verse 93:7 — «wa-wajadaka ḍāllan fa-hadā» (He found you lost and guided you) — describes the Prophet's ﷺ personal experience of hidāyah. The exegetes debate the meaning of «ḍāllan» (astray/lost): did it refer to the Prophet's pre-prophetic state of religious misguidance (as the majority hold, citing the surrounding context of Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā), or to his literal being lost in the valleys of Mecca as a child (as some early exegetes suggested)? Al-Ṭabarī reconciles both: the Prophet was «lost» in multiple senses — physically, intellectually, and spiritually — and Allah guided him in all dimensions. The guidance of the Prophet ﷺ from ḍalāl to hudā is the paradigm of divine hidāyah — complete, transformative, and unmerited.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَلَا مُضِلَّ لَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray

meaning.en: To be familiar, intimate, at ease; to perceive, to see; human beings (insān, nās, unās). The root bridges the concepts of social familiarity and humanity itself — humans are those who find comfort in each other's company.
meaning.ar: الْأُلْفَةُ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةُ — وَالْإِنْسَانُ: سُمِّيَ بِذَٰلِكَ لِأُنْسِهِ بِغَيْرِهِ، وَالْإِدْرَاكُ بِالْحَوَاسِّ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Familiarity and humanity — the root's two branches (social comfort and human identity) are etymologically linked: humans are beings who find solace in community.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْإِنْسَانُ — وَالْآخَرُ الْأُنْسُ وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الْوَحْشَةِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) human being (insān); (2) familiarity (uns), opposite of wildness/isolation.

quran_examples.ar: إِذْ رَءَا نَارًۭا فَقَالَ لِأَهْلِهِ ٱمْكُثُوٓا۟ إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًۭا
quran_examples.en: When he saw a fire and said to his family: Stay here; I have perceived a fire

hadith.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْلَفُ وَيُؤْلَفُ، وَلَا خَيْرَ فِيمَنْ لَا يَأْلَفُ وَلَا يُؤْلَفُ
hadith.en: The believer is sociable and is sociable with; there is no good in one who is not sociable and not sociable with.

shades.name_en: Insān — The Human Being as Social and Spiritual Creature
shades.explanation:
Al-insān — the human being — is described in the Quran with remarkable psychological depth. The human is created «fī aḥsani taqwīm» (in the best form — 95:4), honored above much of creation (17:70), and entrusted with the amānah that the heavens and earth refused (33:72). Yet the same human is «ẓalūman jahūlā» (unjust and ignorant — 33:72), «ḥalūʿā» (anxious/impatient — 70:19), «kafūr» (ungrateful — 22:66), «ya'isa kafūr» (despairing and ungrateful — 11:9), «kāna akthara shay'in jadalan» (the most argumentative of things — 18:54). The Quran's anthropology is brutally honest about human weakness while unwaveringly affirming human dignity and potential.

The Quran explicitly states that humanity was not created in vain (23:115) but for worship (51:56) and trial (67:2, 76:2). The human is a «khalīfah» (vicegerent — 2:30) — given authority over the earth as a trust, accountable for its use. This dual nature — honored yet weak, entrusted yet prone to betrayal — defines the Quranic view of insān. Al-Rāzī, in his tafsīr of 95:4, explains that «aḥsani taqwīm» refers to the human's creation with reason (ʿaql), upright posture (intiṣāb al-qāmah), comprehensive knowledge-capacity (qābil li-l-ʿulūm), and moral discernment (tamyīz al-khayr min al-sharr). The potential for the highest spiritual stations — above the angels — coexists with the potential for the lowest degradation — «asfala sāfilīn» (the lowest of the low — 95:5).

The word insān itself is etymologically connected by many exegetes to uns (familiarity, intimacy) — the human is a creature of relationships, finding meaning and identity through connection with Allah and with fellow humans. Others connect it to nisyān (forgetfulness) — the human forgets, errs, and needs constant reminding. Both etymologies capture complementary aspects of the human condition: we are social beings prone to forgetfulness, needing both divine guidance and human community to flourish.
shades.hadith_ar: كُلُّ مَوْلُودٍ يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ
shades.hadith_en: Every child is born upon the primordial nature (fiṭrah)

meaning.en: Mercy, compassion, loving tenderness. The root's core image is the womb (raḥim) — the place of nurturing, protection, and the strongest natural bonds of love. Divine mercy (raḥmah) encompasses all creation and is the dominant divine attribute in the Quran.
meaning.ar: الرِّقَّةُ وَالشَّفَقَةُ وَالْعَطْفُ — وَالرَّحِمُ: مَوْضِعُ تَكْوِينِ الْجَنِينِ، وَمِنْهُ اشْتُقَّتِ الرَّحْمَةُ لِأَنَّهَا أَبْلَغُ أَنْوَاعِ الْعِنَايَةِ

lexical_analysis.core_semantic_field: Compassionate care — mercy is not mere pity but active, nurturing love that protects, provides for, and brings to fulfillment. The womb (raḥim) is the physical symbol of the most unconditional love in human experience.

al_raghib.ar: الرَّحْمَةُ: رِقَّةٌ تَقْتَضِي الْإِحْسَانَ إِلَى الْمَرْحُومِ. وَقَدْ تُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي الرِّقَّةِ الْمُجَرَّدَةِ وَفِي الْإِحْسَانِ الْمُجَرَّدِ
al_raghib.en: Raḥmah: tenderness that requires goodness toward the one shown mercy. Used for pure tenderness and for pure beneficence.

quran_examples.ar: بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ
quran_examples.en: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful
quran_examples.context: The basmalah — every surah begins with divine mercy

hadith.ar: جَعَلَ اللَّهُ الرَّحْمَةَ مِائَةَ جُزْءٍ، فَأَمْسَكَ عِنْدَهُ تِسْعَةً وَتِسْعِينَ جُزْءًا، وَأَنْزَلَ فِي الْأَرْضِ جُزْءًا وَاحِدًا
hadith.en: Allah divided mercy into one hundred parts; He retained ninety-nine and sent one part to earth.

shades.name_en: al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm — The Divine Names of Mercy
shades.explanation:
The basmalah — «bismi Llāhi l-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm» — opens every surah (except one) with the twin names of divine mercy. The exegetical tradition has extensively analyzed the distinction between al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm. The majority view (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr): al-Raḥmān indicates the vastness of divine mercy — it encompasses all creation, believer and disbeliever, in this world (raḥmah ʿāmmah). Al-Raḥīm indicates the specificity of divine mercy — it is reserved for the believers in the Hereafter (raḥmah khāṣṣah). Al-Raḥmān is the intensive form (faʿlān) conveying abundance and expansiveness; al-Raḥīm is the attributive form (faʿīl) conveying constancy and permanence.

Al-Rāzī, in his detailed analysis, enumerates over a dozen exegetical opinions on the distinction. Some said al-Raḥmān is a proper name unique to Allah (never applied to creatures), while al-Raḥīm can be applied metaphorically to humans (as the Prophet ﷺ is described as «ra'ūfun raḥīm» — 9:128). Others said al-Raḥmān refers to the attribute of mercy in Allah's essence (ṣifah dhātiyyah), while al-Raḥīm refers to the effects of mercy on creation (ṣifah fiʿliyyah). Ibn ʿArabī (al-Futūḥāt) develops a mystical reading: al-Raḥmān is the mercy of existence itself — the divine effusion (fayḍ) that brings all things into being; al-Raḥīm is the mercy of perfection — the divine care that brings each thing to its full realization.

The Quran's preference for al-Raḥmān as the divine name summoned in prayer (17:110: «qul idʿū Llāha awi dʿū l-Raḥmān») indicates that mercy is the primary mode of divine-human relationship. When the believers call upon Allah, they call upon the Most Merciful — not the Avenger or the Judge. This theological emphasis on raḥmah over other attributes has profound implications for Islamic spirituality: fear of divine punishment is real, but hope in divine mercy is dominant.
shades.hadith_ar: لَمَّا قَضَى اللَّهُ الْخَلْقَ كَتَبَ فِي كِتَابٍ فَهُوَ عِنْدَهُ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ: إِنَّ رَحْمَتِي تَغْلِبُ عَلَى غَضَبِي
shades.hadith_en: When Allah completed creation, He wrote in a Book with Him above the Throne: My mercy prevails over My wrath.

meaning.en: To see, to look, to perceive visually; to hold an opinion, to think, to consider. The root bridges sensory perception and intellectual judgment — what one 'sees' shapes what one 'thinks.'

al_raghib.ar: الرُّؤْيَةُ: إِدْرَاكُ الْمَرْئِيِّ — وَذَٰلِكَ بِحَاسَّةِ الْبَصَرِ وَبِالْعَقْلِ أَيْضًا. وَمِنْهُ الرَّأْيُ: الِاعْتِقَادُ الْمُسْتَنْبَطُ
al_raghib.en: Ru'yah: perception of a visible object — through the sense of sight and also through the intellect. Hence ra'y: a deduced belief/judgment.

quran_examples.ar: مَا كَذَبَ ٱلْفُؤَادُ مَا رَأَىٰ
quran_examples.en: The heart did not lie about what it saw

quran_examples.ar: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلَّيْلُ رَءَا كَوْكَبًۭا
quran_examples.en: When the night covered him, he saw a star

hadith.ar: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ
hadith.en: To worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you.

shades.name_ar: رُؤْيَةُ اللَّهِ — النَّظَرُ إِلَى وَجْهِهِ الْكَرِيمِ
shades.explanation:
The Quran promises the believers the vision of Allah in the Hereafter: «wujūhun yawma'idhin nāḍirah, ilā rabbihā nāẓirah» (Faces that Day will be radiant — looking at their Lord — 75:22-23). The verb «nāẓirah» (looking) is from the root n-ẓ-r (to look), but the underlying concept is ru'yah (seeing, vision). This promised vision — al-ru'yā al-ʿuẓmā (the greatest vision) — is described as the supreme reward of Paradise, exceeding all other pleasures.

The theological debates about ru'yat Allāh (the vision of Allah) were among the most intense in early Islamic history. The Muʿtazilah denied the possibility of seeing Allah — in this world or the next — arguing that vision requires corporeality and spatial location, which are impossible for Allah. They interpreted «ilā rabbihā nāẓirah» as 'waiting for their Lord's reward' (from naẓara = to wait), not 'looking at their Lord.' The Ahl al-Sunnah, led by Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, al-Ashʿarī, and al-Māturīdī, affirmed the vision of Allah in the Hereafter as a reality — «bilā kayf» (without modality) — based on the apparent (ẓāhir) meaning of the Quranic text and the mutawātir ḥadīth: «innakum sa-tarawna rabbakum» (You will see your Lord — Bukhārī 554, Muslim 633).

The Ashʿarī argument for ru'yat Allāh was primarily textual: the Quran and Sunnah affirm it; reason does not deem it impossible (since vision does not require corporeality — we see our own souls in dreams without physical eyes). The Muʿtazilī denial was based on a rationalist epistemology that the Ashāʿirah rejected: reason cannot legislate what is possible or impossible for Allah; only revelation can. Al-Ashʿarī (al-Ibānah) argues that the believers' vision of Allah is the fulfillment of the divine promise and the ultimate expression of divine generosity — «li-lladhīna aḥsanū l-ḥusnā wa-ziyādah» (for those who do good is the best reward and more — 10:26). The «more» (ziyādah) is interpreted by the exegetes as the vision of Allah's Face.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّكُمْ سَتَرَوْنَ رَبَّكُمْ كَمَا تَرَوْنَ هَٰذَا الْقَمَرَ، لَا تُضَامُّونَ فِي رُؤْيَتِهِ
shades.hadith_en: You will see your Lord as you see this moon; you will not be crowded in seeing Him.

meaning.en: Wrongdoing, injustice, oppression, transgression; darkness. The root's physical sense (ẓulmah — darkness) provides the metaphor for moral wrongdoing: ẓulm is the darkness of the soul that puts things in the wrong place, violating rights and boundaries.
meaning.ar: وَضْعُ الشَّيْءِ فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضِعِهِ — وَالظُّلْمَةُ: ذَهَابُ النُّورِ

al_raghib.ar: الظُّلْمُ: وَضْعُ الشَّيْءِ فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضِعِهِ الْمُخْتَصِّ بِهِ. وَأَصْلُ الظُّلْمَةِ: عَدَمُ النُّورِ — وَمِنْهُ الظُّلْمُ لِأَنَّهُ يُظْلِمُ الْقَلْبَ
al_raghib.en: Ẓulm: putting something in other than its proper place. The origin of ẓulmah (darkness) is absence of light — hence ẓulm because it darkens the heart.

quran_examples.ar: وَقُلْنَا يَـٰٓـَٔادَمُ ٱسْكُنْ أَنتَ وَزَوْجُكَ ٱلْجَنَّةَ وَكُلَا مِنْهَا رَغَدًا حَيْثُ شِئْتُمَا وَلَا تَقْرَبَا هَـٰذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ فَتَكُونَا مِنَ ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ
quran_examples.en: We said: O Adam, dwell in the Garden, you and your wife... but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers

hadith.ar: يَا عِبَادِي، إِنِّي حَرَّمْتُ الظُّلْمَ عَلَى نَفْسِي وَجَعَلْتُهُ بَيْنَكُمْ مُحَرَّمًا فَلَا تَظَالَمُوا
hadith.en: O My servants, I have forbidden wrongdoing upon Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.

shades.name_en: Ẓulm as Violation of Rights — The Root of All Sin
shades.explanation:
Ẓulm — translated as wrongdoing, injustice, oppression, or transgression — is the Quran's most comprehensive term for sin. The root metaphor is spatial: ẓulm is putting something where it does not belong — violating the divinely established boundaries (ḥudūd Allāh). Al-Rāghib's definition «waḍʿu l-shay'i fī ghayri mawḍiʿih» (placing a thing in other than its proper place) captures the ethical geometry of ẓulm: rights, duties, and prohibitions are divinely placed; transgressing them is ẓulm.

The Quran classifies ẓulm into three ascending degrees. First: ẓulm al-nafs (wronging oneself) — the most common form, where the sinner harms primarily their own soul through disobedience (2:57, 3:117, 35:32). Second: ẓulm al-ghayr (wronging others) — violating the rights of fellow creatures (4:10 on devouring orphans' wealth, 49:11 on mockery and slander). Third: ẓulm against Allah — the gravest form, which is shirk (associating partners with Allah): «inna l-shirka la-ẓulmun ʿaẓīm» (indeed shirk is a tremendous wrongdoing — 31:13). Luqmān's counsel to his son places the warning against shirk at the apex of moral instruction, framing polytheism not merely as theological error but as the ultimate injustice — giving the Creator's exclusive right (worship) to creatures.

The ḥadīth qudsī in Muslim 2577 is the most powerful statement on ẓulm in the Islamic tradition: «yā ʿibādī, innī ḥarramtu l-ẓulma ʿalā nafsī wa-jaʿaltuhu baynakum muḥarraman fa-lā taẓālamū» (O My servants, I have forbidden wrongdoing upon Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another). The divine self-prohibition of ẓulm establishes justice as intrinsic to the divine nature — Allah does not wrong His servants not because He is constrained but because ẓulm is contrary to His perfection. This ḥadīth grounds the entire Islamic ethics of justice: if the All-Powerful refrains from ẓulm, how can weak, dependent creatures justify wronging one another?
shades.hadith_ar: اتَّقُوا الظُّلْمَ، فَإِنَّ الظُّلْمَ ظُلُمَاتٌ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
shades.hadith_en: Beware of wrongdoing, for wrongdoing will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection.

meaning.en: Truth, reality, right, justice, that which is established and binding. The root encompasses what is ontologically real (as opposed to bāṭil — falsehood), what is morally right (as opposed to ẓulm — injustice), and what is legally due (as opposed to mabkhūs — deprived).
meaning.ar: الثُّبُوتُ وَالْوُجُوبُ وَالصِّدْقُ — وَالْحَقُّ: ضِدُّ الْبَاطِلِ، وَهُوَ الْأَمْرُ الثَّابِتُ الَّذِي لَا يَسُوغُ إِنْكَارُهُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِحْكَامِ الشَّيْءِ وَصِحَّتِهِ. وَالْحَقُّ: ضِدُّ الْبَاطِلِ — سُمِّيَ لِأَنَّهُ يَثْبُتُ وَيُحِقُّ
ibn_faris.en: A single root indicating the firmness and correctness of something. Al-ḥaqq: opposite of falsehood — so named because it stands firm and is established.

quran_examples.ar: وَقُلْ جَآءَ ٱلْحَقُّ وَزَهَقَ ٱلْبَـٰطِلُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلْبَـٰطِلَ كَانَ زَهُوقًۭا
quran_examples.en: Say: The truth has come and falsehood has perished; indeed falsehood is ever perishing
quran_examples.context: The triumph of truth over falsehood

hadith.ar: الْحَلَالُ بَيِّنٌ وَالْحَرَامُ بَيِّنٌ، وَبَيْنَهُمَا أُمُورٌ مُشْتَبِهَاتٌ
hadith.en: The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters.

shades.name_en: al-Ḥaqq — Truth as Ontological and Moral Reality
shades.explanation:
Al-Ḥaqq is one of the most theologically dense terms in the Quran — simultaneously an attribute of Allah («dhālika bi-anna Llāha huwa l-Ḥaqq» — that is because Allah is the Truth — 22:6, 31:30), a description of the Quran («wa-inna l-lladhīna ūtū l-kitāba la-yaʿlamūna annahu l-Ḥaqqu min rabbihim» — those given the Book know it is the truth from their Lord — 2:144), and the foundation of moral order («wa-bi-l-ḥaqqi anzalnāhu wa-bi-l-ḥaqqi nazal» — with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended — 17:105). The convergence of ontological truth (what is real), revelatory truth (what is revealed), and moral truth (what is right) in a single term reflects the Quran's unified vision of reality: what truly exists (Allah) reveals what is truly the case (the Quran) and commands what is truly right (justice).

The Quranic dichotomy of ḥaqq and bāṭil — truth and falsehood — structures the entire moral and metaphysical landscape. 17:81, revealed as the Prophet ﷺ entered Mecca at the conquest, declares: «qul jā'a l-ḥaqqu wa-zahaqa l-bāṭilu, inna l-bāṭila kāna zahūqā» (Say: the truth has come and falsehood has perished — indeed falsehood is ever-perishing). Ibn Kathīr reports that the Prophet ﷺ entered the Kaʿbah and found it filled with 360 idols; he began striking them with his bow while reciting this verse, and the idols fell on their faces. The physical destruction of idols was the visible manifestation of the metaphysical triumph of ḥaqq over bāṭil.

In Islamic legal theory, ḥaqq (right) is a central category — distinguished between ḥaqq Allāh (the right of Allah — public rights, ritual obligations, penal sanctions) and ḥaqq al-ʿabd (the right of the individual — private claims, property, personal status). This distinction, developed by the fuqahāʾ, grounds the entire structure of Islamic law: some violations are against the divine order and require public sanction; others are against individual rights and require private remedy. The term ḥaqq thus bridges theology, ethics, and law — the truth of Allah, the rightness of action, and the rights of persons are all expressions of the same fundamental reality: the ḥaqq that is grounded in al-Ḥaqq.
shades.hadith_ar: اللَّهُمَّ أَرِنَا الْحَقَّ حَقًّا وَارْزُقْنَا اتِّبَاعَهُ، وَأَرِنَا الْبَاطِلَ بَاطِلًا وَارْزُقْنَا اجْتِنَابَهُ
shades.hadith_en: O Allah, show us the truth as truth and grant us its followership; show us falsehood as falsehood and grant us avoidance of it.

meaning.en: To write, record, prescribe, decree. The root encompasses the act of writing (kitābah), the written product (kitāb — book/scripture), and the divine act of prescribing obligations (kutiba — it is decreed/obligatory).
meaning.ar: الْجَمْعُ وَالضَّمُّ — الْكِتَابَةُ: ضَمُّ الْحُرُوفِ بَعْضِهَا إِلَى بَعْضٍ، وَالْكِتَابُ: مَا كُتِبَ وَجُمِعَ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ: الْجَمْعُ — يُقَالُ تَكَتَّبُوا: تَجَمَّعُوا، وَمِنْهُ الْكِتَابُ وَالْكِتَابَةُ لِأَنَّهُمَا يَجْمَعَانِ الْحُرُوفَ
ibn_faris.en: A single root: gathering. It's said takattabū — they gathered together. Hence kitāb and kitābah because they gather letters together.

quran_examples.ar: ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبُ لَا رَيْبَ ۛ فِيهِ ۛ هُدًۭى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ
quran_examples.en: This is the Book — no doubt in it — a guidance for the God-conscious

hadith.ar: إِنَّ أَوَّلَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ الْقَلَمَ، فَقَالَ لَهُ: اكْتُبْ. فَقَالَ: مَا أَكْتُبُ؟ قَالَ: اكْتُبِ الْقَدَرَ
hadith.en: The first thing Allah created was the Pen. He said: Write. It said: What shall I write? He said: Write the decree.

shades.name_en: al-Kitāb — The Book as Divine Revelation and Cosmic Decree
shades.explanation:
Al-Kitāb — the Book — is the Quran's self-designation, appearing from its second verse (2:2). The term encompasses multiple dimensions: (1) the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ — 85:22) on which all divine decrees are written before creation; (2) the revealed scriptures (Torah, Gospel, Quran) sent to prophets; (3) the record of deeds (kitāb al-aʿmāl — 18:49, 45:29) that each person will receive on the Day of Judgment; and (4) the divine decree (kitāb al-qadar) that governs all events. Al-Rāzī explains that the common thread is 'fixity and permanence' — what is written (maktūb) is fixed, established, and unalterable.

The concept of «al-Kitāb» is central to Islamic epistemology: knowledge is ultimately derived from the Book — whether the cosmic book of creation (al-kitāb al-takwīnī) or the revealed book of scripture (al-kitāb al-tadwīnī). Allah's first creative act in the ḥadīth tradition is the creation of the Pen (al-qalam) and the command «uktub» (Write! — Tirmidhī 2155). The entire cosmic order — past, present, and future — was inscribed in the Preserved Tablet before creation began. This theology of writing establishes a fixed moral order: right and wrong are not human conventions but divine inscriptions, written before human reason existed to debate them.

The Quran's frequent command «kutiba ʿalaykum» (it has been decreed/prescribed for you) — for fasting (2:183), for qisās (retaliation — 2:178), for bequests (2:180), for jihād (2:216) — uses the passive of kataba to express divine legislation. The obligations are «written» upon the believers — a metaphor that conveys both firmness (the obligation is fixed) and transcendence (the obligation originates from the Divine Author). Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that «kutiba» in legislative contexts carries the weight of divine authority: if Allah has «written» it, it is not subject to human revision or negotiation.
shades.hadith_ar: اكْتُبْ مَقَادِيرَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
shades.hadith_en: Write the decrees of everything until the Hour is established

meaning.en: To descend, come down, be sent down. The root expresses vertical movement from above to below — physically, spatially, and metaphysically. Most importantly, it describes the descent of divine revelation (tanzīl) from Allah to humanity.
meaning.ar: الْهُبُوطُ مِنْ عُلُوٍّ إِلَى سُفْلٍ — وَالتَّنْزِيلُ: إِنْزَالُ الْقُرْآنِ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَى النَّبِيِّ

al_raghib.ar: النُّزُولُ فِي الْأَصْلِ: انْحِطَاطٌ مِنْ عُلُوٍّ. وَالتَّنْزِيلُ: إِنْزَالُ الشَّيْءِ شَيْئًا بَعْدَ شَيْءٍ — وَمِنْهُ تَنْزِيلُ الْقُرْآنِ لِأَنَّهُ نَزَلَ مُتَفَرِّقًا
al_raghib.en: Nuzūl originally: descent from a height. Tanzīl: sending something down piece by piece — hence the tanzīl of the Quran because it descended gradually.

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَـٰهُ فِى لَيْلَةِ ٱلْقَدْرِ
quran_examples.en: Indeed We sent it down on the Night of Power

hadith.ar: يَنْزِلُ رَبُّنَا تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا
hadith.en: Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven.

shades.name_en: Tanzīl — The Gradual Descent of Divine Revelation
shades.name_ar: التَّنْزِيلُ — نُزُولُ الْوَحْيِ مُفَرَّقًا حَسَبَ الْحَاجَةِ
shades.explanation:
The Quran describes itself as «tanzīl» — that which has been sent down. The intensive Form II (tafʿīl) implies a gradual, piecemeal descent: the Quran was not revealed all at once but «nazzala» (sent down in portions) over twenty-three years in response to circumstances and needs. This gradualism (tadrīj) is itself a mercy — «wa-qur'ānan faraqnāhu li-taqra'ahu ʿalā l-nāsi ʿalā mukthin wa-nazzalnāhu tanzīlā» (a Quran which We divided so you might recite it to the people over time; We sent it down in stages — 17:106).

The theology of tanzīl distinguishes Islam from other religions' concepts of revelation. The Quran was not discovered (as buried tablets), not composed (as prophetic poetry), not incarnated (as divine person), but «sent down» (munazzal) from a transcendent source through the angel Jibrīl to the Prophet's heart. The vertical imagery of descent (nuzūl) emphasizes the absolute transcendence of the divine word: it originates «above» and comes «down» — the human recipient is passive, receiving what is given from on high. This vertical cosmology of revelation is reinforced by the descriptions of the Quran as existing in a «kitāb maknūn» (hidden book — 56:78) and «lawḥ maḥfūẓ» (preserved tablet — 85:22) before its earthly descent.

The theological debates about the Quran's createdness (khalq al-Qur'ān) in the early ʿAbbāsid period turned partly on the concept of nuzūl: if the Quran is Allah's speech (kalām Allāh) and divine speech is an eternal attribute, how can it «descend» in time? The Ḥanbalī response: the nuzūl of the Quran refers to the created expression (al-ʿibārah — the recited words and written text), not the uncreated meaning (al-maʿnā — the eternal divine speech). The Ashʿarī position: the Quran as recited and written is an expression (ʿibārah) of the eternal divine kalām, which «descends» in the sense of being made manifest, not in the sense of spatial movement.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ هَٰذَا الْقُرْآنَ أُنْزِلَ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ
shades.hadith_en: This Quran was revealed in seven aḥruf (modes/dialects)

meaning.en: To remember, to mention, to recall; remembrance, reminder, mention; male (dhakar). The root links the act of remembering (dhikr) with the spoken mention of what is remembered, and by extension the gender that is 'remembered' or 'mentioned' prominently in lineage.
meaning.ar: حِفْظُ الشَّيْءِ وَاسْتِحْضَارُهُ — وَالذِّكْرُ: ضِدُّ النِّسْيَانِ، وَالذَّكَرُ: ضِدُّ الْأُنْثَى

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الذِّكْرُ — حِفْظُ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْآخَرُ الذَّكَرُ — ضِدُّ الْأُنْثَى، وَسُمِّيَ الذَّكَرُ لِأَنَّهُ أَشْرَفُ وَأَنْبَهُ وَأَذْكَرُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) dhikr — preserving/remembering something; (2) dhakar — male, opposite of female, so named because he is more prominent and memorable.

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا ٱلذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَحَـٰفِظُونَ
quran_examples.en: Indeed We have sent down the Reminder, and We will surely preserve it

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُم بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ ۗ أَلَا بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ ٱلْقُلُوبُ
quran_examples.en: Those who believe and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah — indeed, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest

hadith.ar: مَثَلُ الَّذِي يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ وَالَّذِي لَا يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ مَثَلُ الْحَيِّ وَالْمَيِّتِ
hadith.en: The example of the one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not is like the living and the dead.

shades.name_en: Dhikr Allāh — Remembrance as the Heart's Life
shades.explanation:
Dhikr Allāh — the remembrance of Allah — is presented in the Quran as the fundamental spiritual practice that gives life to the heart. The verse 13:28 — «alā bi-dhikri Llāhi taṭma'innu l-qulūb» (indeed, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest) — is the charter of Islamic spirituality. The word «taṭma'innu» (find rest/tranquility) suggests that the heart in its natural state is restless, anxious, and agitated — and only dhikr can restore it to its fiṭrah of peace and contentment with its Creator.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Invocations) develops a comprehensive psychology of dhikr: the heart is like a mirror that tarnishes through negligence (ghaflah); dhikr polishes it until it reflects divine light. The more the heart is occupied with dhikr, the less room there is for waswās (satanic whisperings) and hawā (capricious desire). The ultimate aim of dhikr is not merely repetition of words but the state of ḥuḍūr (presence) — when the heart is so filled with awareness of Allah that it becomes a «bayt Allāh» (house of Allah) in which nothing else dwells.

The Quran commands dhikr in multiple forms: the ritual dhikr of prayer («aqimi l-ṣalāta li-dhikrī» — establish prayer for My remembrance — 20:14), the verbal dhikr of glorification and praise (33:41-42: «yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū dhkurū Llāha dhikran kathīrā, wa-sabbiḥūhu bukratan wa-aṣīlā»), the reflective dhikr of contemplating creation (3:191: «alladhīna yadhkurūna Llāha qiyāman wa-quʿūdan wa-ʿalā junūbihim wa-yatafakkarūna fī khalqi l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ»), and the ethical dhikr of acting upon what is remembered. The comprehensive nature of dhikr — ritual, verbal, contemplative, and ethical — makes it the central practice of the spiritual path (sulūk), the «key to the unseen» (miftāḥ al-ghayb) that opens the heart to divine presence.
shades.hadith_ar: مَثَلُ الَّذِي يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ وَالَّذِي لَا يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ مَثَلُ الْحَيِّ وَالْمَيِّتِ
shades.hadith_en: The one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead

meaning.en: To lie, to deny, to reject as false. The root encompasses both the active telling of falsehood (kadhib) and the rejection of truth (takdhīb — calling true things lies). Central to Quranic polemics as the primary response of disbelievers to prophetic messages.
meaning.ar: الْإِخْبَارُ بِخِلَافِ الْحَقِيقَةِ — وَالتَّكْذِيبُ: نِسْبَةُ الْغَيْرِ إِلَى الْكَذِبِ

al_raghib.ar: الْكَذِبُ: الْإِخْبَارُ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ بِخِلَافِ مَا هُوَ عَلَيْهِ. وَالتَّكْذِيبُ: نِسْبَةُ الْمُخْبِرِ إِلَى الْكَذِبِ
al_raghib.en: Kadhib: reporting something contrary to its reality. Takdhīb: attributing falsehood to the reporter.

quran_examples.ar: فَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّن كَذَبَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ وَكَذَّبَ بِٱلصِّدْقِ إِذْ جَآءَهُۥٓ
quran_examples.en: Who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him?
quran_examples.context: The double crime of lying about Allah and denying truth

hadith.ar: آيَةُ الْمُنَافِقِ ثَلَاثٌ: إِذَا حَدَّثَ كَذَبَ، وَإِذَا وَعَدَ أَخْلَفَ، وَإِذَا اؤْتُمِنَ خَانَ
hadith.en: The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, when entrusted he betrays.

shades.name_en: Takdhīb — Denial of Prophets as the Paradigm of Rejection
shades.explanation:
Takdhīb — calling the truth a lie — is the Quran's primary characterization of the disbelievers' response to prophetic messages. The pattern is repeated across dozens of surahs: a prophet comes to his people with clear proofs, and they respond with takdhīb — «kadhdhabat qawmu Nūḥin al-mursalīn» (the people of Noah denied the messengers — 26:105), «kadhdhabat Thamūdu al-mursalīn» (Thamūd denied — 26:141), «kadhdhabat qawmu Lūṭin al-mursalīn» (Lot's people denied — 26:160). The repetition of this pattern across the Quran's narrative cycle establishes takdhīb as the archetypal sin — not ignorance of the truth but willful rejection of it.

The Quran distinguishes between kādhib (one who lies — producing false speech) and mukadhdhib (one who calls truth a lie — rejecting true speech). The latter is more dangerous because it inverts the moral order: truth is labeled falsehood, the true prophet is called a liar, and the community is cut off from divine guidance. Al-Rāzī analyzes the psychology of takdhīb: it often stems not from intellectual doubt but from pride (istikbār), vested interests (manāfiʿ), and fear of social change — the disbelievers know the truth but reject it because accepting it would require moral, social, and economic transformation.

The Quran's most severe condemnations are reserved for those who both «kadhaba ʿalā Llāh» (lied about Allah — inventing false doctrines) and «kadhdhaba bi-l-ṣidqi» (denied the truth — rejecting authentic revelation — 39:32). This double offense — fabricating false religion while rejecting true religion — is the ultimate perversion of the human relationship with truth. The punishment for takdhīb in the Quran's narratives is consistent: the denying nations are destroyed by divine punishment after being warned, establishing the law (sunnah) that persistent denial of truth after clear proofs leads to collective ruin.
shades.hadith_ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ، فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ، وَإِنَّ الْفُجُورَ يَهْدِي إِلَى النَّارِ
shades.hadith_en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire.

meaning.en: To take, seize, grasp, receive, accept. A concrete verb of physical acquisition that extends to intellectual acceptance (taking knowledge), contractual obligation (taking a covenant), and divine punishment (seizing in retribution).
meaning.ar: التَّنَاوُلُ وَالْقَبْضُ وَالْحِيَازَةُ — وَالْأَخْذُ: تَنَاوُلُ الشَّيْءِ بِالْيَدِ أَوْ بِالْقُوَّةِ

al_raghib.ar: الْأَخْذُ: حَوْزُ الشَّيْءِ وَتَحْصِيلُهُ. وَيُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي الْأَشْيَاءِ الْمَادِّيَّةِ وَالْمَعْنَوِيَّةِ — كَأَخْذِ الْمِيثَاقِ وَأَخْذِ الْعِلْمِ
al_raghib.en: Akhdh: acquiring and obtaining something. Used for material and immaterial things — like taking a covenant or acquiring knowledge.

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذْ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِنۢ بَنِىٓ ءَادَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ
quran_examples.en: When your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants

hadith.ar: خُذُوا عَنِّي مَنَاسِكَكُمْ
hadith.en: Take from me your rites (of pilgrimage).

shades.name_en: Akhdh al-Mīthāq — The Divine Taking of the Covenant
shades.explanation:
The Quran presents divine-human relationship as fundamentally covenantal — Allah «takes» a mīthāq (covenant) from humanity at multiple levels: from the prophets (33:7), from the Children of Israel (2:63, 2:83, 2:93, 5:12, 5:70), from the People of the Book in general (3:187), and — in the most universal and mysterious passage — from all humanity in a primordial pre-existential state (7:172). The verb «akhadha» (He took) emphasizes divine initiative and human obligation: the covenant is not negotiated but divinely imposed; humanity's only choice is fulfillment or violation.

The primordial covenant of 7:172 — «wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min banī Ādama min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyatahum wa-ashhadahum ʿalā anfusihim: a-lastu bi-rabbikum? qālū: balā shahidnā» (When your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify about themselves: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify) — is one of the most theologically profound verses in the Quran. Al-Ṭabarī records extensive early interpretations: some took it literally (Allah extracted all human souls from Adam's back and made them testify), others metaphorically (the covenant is inscribed in the fiṭrah — every human intuitively knows their Lord), and yet others rationally (the verse describes the innate human capacity to recognize divine truth when presented with it).

Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim develop the covenant theology extensively: the primordial mīthāq explains why humans have an innate sense of right and wrong, an instinctive recognition of Allah, and a natural disposition (fiṭrah) toward Islam. The Prophet's ḥadīth «kullu mawlūdin yūladu ʿalā l-fiṭrah» (every child is born upon the primordial nature — Bukhārī 1359) is understood as referring to this primordial covenant — every human enters the world with the covenant imprinted on their soul, and their life is the process of either honoring or violating it.
shades.hadith_ar: أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ؟ قَالُوا: بَلَىٰ
shades.hadith_en: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify

meaning.en: To come, to arrive, to bring. A near-synonym of atā, with emphasis on arrival and bringing forth. Frequently used for eschatological coming — the Day of Judgment, the trumpet, divine decree.
meaning.ar: الْمَجِيءُ وَالْإِحْضَارُ — جَاءَ: أَتَى، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الذَّهَابِ

al_raghib.ar: الْمَجِيءُ: الْإِتْيَانُ مِنْ مَكَانٍ إِلَى آخَرَ. وَجَاءَ بِالشَّيْءِ: أَحْضَرَهُ. وَالْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ جَاءَ وَأَتَى: أَنَّ جَاءَ يَتَضَمَّنُ مَعْنَى الْوُصُولِ أَكْثَرَ
al_raghib.en: Maji': coming from one place to another. Jā'a bi-l-shay': brought it. The difference from atā: jā'a more strongly implies arrival/reaching.

quran_examples.ar: إِذَا جَآءَ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْفَتْحُ
quran_examples.en: When the help of Allah comes and the victory

quran_examples.ar: وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمْ كِتَـٰبٌۭ مِّنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ
quran_examples.en: When there came to them a Book from Allah

hadith.ar: إِذَا جَاءَ رَمَضَانُ فُتِّحَتْ أَبْوَابُ الْجَنَّةِ
hadith.en: When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened.

shades.name_en: Coming of Divine Decree and Eschatological Events
shades.explanation:
The verb «jā'a» (he came) is one of the most frequent in the Quran, appearing in contexts ranging from the arrival of prophets with clear proofs to the cataclysmic coming of the Day of Judgment. In 89:22 — «wa-jā'a rabbuka wa-l-malaku ṣaffan ṣaffā» (and your Lord comes, and the angels rank upon rank) — the verb frames the eschatological climax as a divine arrival. The exegetical treatment of this verse mirrors that of 6:158 (discussed under root Aty): the Salaf affirmed the text without asking 'how' (kayf), while the Khalaf interpreted it as the coming of divine command or punishment.

The Quran's rhetorical use of «jā'a» creates dramatic tension through its pairing with «lammā» (when): «wa-lammā jā'ahum kitābun min ʿindi Llāh» (and when a Book came to them from Allah — 2:89), «fa-lammā jā'ahum mā ʿarafū kafarū bihi» (but when what they recognized came to them, they disbelieved in it — 2:89). The pattern is: divine truth arrives (jā'a), is recognized (ʿarafū), yet is rejected (kafarū). The verb marks the moment of decision — the arrival of truth that demands response.

The distinction between jā'a and atā, while subtle, has been analyzed by Arabic linguists: jā'a more strongly emphasizes the completion of the journey and the arrival at the destination, while atā can refer to the process of coming. The Quran's choice between them is often rhetorically motivated — jā'a in eschatological contexts emphasizes the finality and inevitability of the arrival.
shades.hadith_ar: إِذَا جَاءَ رَمَضَانُ فُتِّحَتْ أَبْوَابُ الْجَنَّةِ
shades.hadith_en: When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened

meaning.en: To carry, bear, lift, transport; to be pregnant; to charge, burden, impose. The root's physical sense (carrying a load) extends to moral and spiritual bearing — carrying responsibility, bearing sin, carrying the divine trust.
meaning.ar: رَفْعُ الشَّيْءِ وَإِمْسَاكُهُ — وَالْحَمْلُ: مَا يُحْمَلُ عَلَى الظَّهْرِ أَوِ الرَّأْسِ أَوْ فِي الْبَطْنِ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْحَمْلُ — رَفْعُ الشَّيْءِ عَلَى الظَّهْرِ، وَالْآخَرُ الْحَمْلُ بِمَعْنَى الْحُبْلَى
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) carrying — lifting something onto the back; (2) pregnancy — the woman carrying a child.

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا ٱلْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱلْجِبَالِ فَأَبَيْنَ أَن يَحْمِلْنَهَا وَأَشْفَقْنَ مِنْهَا ۖ وَحَمَلَهَا ٱلْإِنسَـٰنُ
quran_examples.en: We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains — they refused to bear it and feared it. But man bore it.

hadith.ar: مَنْ حَمَلَ عَلَيْنَا السِّلَاحَ فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا
hadith.en: Whoever bears arms against us is not of us.

shades.name_en: Ḥaml al-Amānah — Bearing the Divine Trust
shades.explanation:
The concept of carrying (ḥaml) intersects with the most profound theological anthropology of the Quran. In 33:72, the amānah (divine trust) is something that must be «carried» (yaḥmilnahā) — a burden, a weight, a responsibility. The heavens, earth, and mountains — the greatest of created things — «refused to carry it» (fa-abayna an yaḥmilnahā). They were terrified of the weight. But «ḥamalahā l-insān» — the human being carried it. This primordial act of ḥaml defines the human condition: we are creatures who have volunteered, or been chosen, to carry a burden beyond our natural capacity.

The burden-bearing motif extends to the theme of sin and accountability. In 20:100-101, those who turn away from divine remembrance «yaḥmilu yawma l-qiyāmati wizrā» (will carry a burden on the Day of Resurrection). The burden (wizr) is the weight of sin — not transferable, not shareable. 35:18: «wa-lā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā» (no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another). This verse establishes individual moral accountability — each soul «carries» its own deeds, and none can «carry» for another. Al-Rāzī notes that this principle distinguishes the Quranic doctrine of accountability from the Christian concept of original sin and vicarious atonement: no one, not even a prophet, can «carry» the sins of another. Each soul bears its own ḥaml.

The theme of «carrying» is also central to the Quran's portrayal of the Prophet's ﷺ mission: «innā sanulqī ʿalayka qawlan thaqīlā» (Indeed We will cast upon you a heavy word — 73:5). The Quran is «thaqīl» — heavy, weighty — and the Prophet «carries» (yaḥmilu) it to humanity. The burden of prophethood — of receiving, preserving, conveying, and living the revelation — is a ḥaml that exhausted even the Prophet ﷺ, as evidenced by the revelations of comfort in Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā and al-Sharḥ.
shades.hadith_ar: أَثْقَلُ الصَّلَاةِ عَلَى الْمُنَافِقِينَ صَلَاةُ الْعِشَاءِ وَصَلَاةُ الْفَجْرِ
shades.hadith_en: The heaviest prayers for hypocrites are ʿIshāʾ and Fajr

meaning.en: To seal, stamp, close, conclude, finish. The root's physical sense (sealing a document or container) extends to the theological concept of hearts being sealed from guidance, and to the Prophet's role as the Seal of the Prophets.
meaning.ar: الطَّبْعُ وَالْخَتْمُ — مَنْعُ الْوُصُولِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ، وَالْفَرَاغُ مِنْهُ

al_raghib.ar: الْخَتْمُ: التَّغْطِيَةُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ وَالطَّبْعُ عَلَيْهِ لِئَلَّا يَصِلَ إِلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ أَوْ يَخْرُجَ مِنْهُ شَيْءٌ
al_raghib.en: Khatm: covering and stamping something so that nothing reaches it or exits from it.

quran_examples.ar: خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ
quran_examples.en: Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing
quran_examples.context: The seal on the disbelievers' hearts

quran_examples.ar: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍۢ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَـٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّـۧنَ
quran_examples.en: Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets

hadith.ar: إِنَّ الرَّسُولَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ آخِرَ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَمَسْجِدَهُ آخِرَ الْمَسَاجِدِ
hadith.en: The Messenger ﷺ was the last of the prophets, and his mosque is the last of the mosques.

shades.name_en: Khatm al-Nubuwwah — The Seal of Prophethood
shades.explanation:
The most theologically consequential usage of the root in the Quran is 33:40: «wa-khātama l-nabiyyīn» — and the Seal of the Prophets. The term «khātam» (seal) has been understood by the overwhelming consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Muslim ummah to mean that Muhammad ﷺ is the final prophet — there is no prophet after him, and his prophethood closes (yakhtimu) the institution of nubuwwah. The seal (khātam) on a document authenticates it and closes it — no further addition is possible after the seal is applied.

Ibn Kathīr, in his tafsīr of 33:40, collects the ḥadīth evidence for the finality of prophethood and declares that anyone claiming prophethood after Muhammad ﷺ is a «kadhdhāb dajjāl» (lying impostor). The Prophet's ﷺ own statements reinforce this: «lā nabiyya baʿdī» (there is no prophet after me — Bukhārī 3455, Muslim 1842), and the famous ḥadīth of the brick house in Bukhārī 3535, where the Prophet described himself as the final brick completing the edifice of prophethood.

The theological significance of khatm al-nubuwwah extends beyond merely stating that no future prophets will come. It establishes that the message brought by Muhammad ﷺ is complete, sufficient, and preserved — no further revelation is needed, and any claim to new revelation is necessarily false. The «seal» authenticates what has come before and prevents any addition or alteration. This principle is the foundation of Islamic orthodoxy's rejection of all post-Muhammadan claimants to prophethood — from Musaylimah al-Kadhdhāb in the Prophet's own lifetime to Bahā'ullāh and Mirzā Ghulām Aḥmad in the modern period.

The root also appears in the context of hearts being «sealed» (2:7, 6:46, 45:23) — a divine act of closing the heart to guidance as a consequence of persistent rejection. Al-Rāzī explains the relationship between the two usages: just as the seal (khātam) closes prophethood as a completed institution, the seal (khatm) on the heart closes it as a completed state of disbelief. In both cases, the seal marks finality — the end of a process, the impossibility of addition or reversal.
shades.hadith_ar: مَثَلِي وَمَثَلُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ كَمَثَلِ رَجُلٍ بَنَى دَارًا فَأَكْمَلَهَا وَأَحْسَنَهَا إِلَّا مَوْضِعَ لَبِنَةٍ، فَأَنَا تِلْكَ اللَّبِنَةُ، وَأَنَا خَاتَمُ النَّبِيِّينَ
shades.hadith_en: My example and that of the prophets is like a man who built a house, completing it — I am that final brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets.

meaning.en: To be safe, sound, at peace; to submit, surrender; peace, greeting. The root encompasses the concepts of safety (salāmah), submission to Allah (islām), and the greeting of peace (salām). It names the religion itself.
meaning.ar: السَّلَامَةُ وَالْبَرَاءَةُ مِنَ الْعُيُوبِ — وَالْإِسْلَامُ: الِاسْتِسْلَامُ لِلَّهِ، وَالسَّلَامُ: التَّحِيَّةُ وَالْأَمَانُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا السَّلَامَةُ — ضِدُّ الْعَطَبِ، وَالْآخَرُ التَّسْلِيمُ وَالِانْقِيَادُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) safety/soundness — opposite of destruction; (2) submission and compliance.

quran_examples.ar: ٱلْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِى وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلْإِسْلَـٰمَ دِينًۭا
quran_examples.en: Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favor, and chosen Islam as your religion

hadith.ar: الْمُسْلِمُ مَنْ سَلِمَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ وَيَدِهِ
hadith.en: The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.

hadith.ar: أَفْشُوا السَّلَامَ بَيْنَكُمْ
hadith.en: Spread the greeting of peace among yourselves.

shades.name_en: Islām — Submission to Allah as the Religion of All Prophets
shades.explanation:
Islām — submission to Allah — is simultaneously an act (the individual's surrender), a state (being muslim — one who submits), and a historical religion (the message brought by Muhammad ﷺ completing the messages of previous prophets). The root's dual meanings of 'safety' (salāmah) and 'submission' (istislām) converge in the word islām: true safety is found in submission to Allah. The one who submits (muslim) is the one who is safe (sālim) from divine punishment, from inner turmoil, and from the chaos of a life without divine guidance.

The Quran presents islām as the religion of all prophets — not a new religion beginning with Muhammad ﷺ but the primordial religion of humanity restored and completed. Abraham is described as «musliman ḥanīfan» (a submitter, inclining to truth — 3:67), and Jesus's disciples declare «āmannā bi-Llāh wa-shhad bi-annā muslimūn» (we believe in Allah; bear witness that we are submitters — 3:52, 5:111). The prophets are not Jews or Christians but muslimūn — those who submitted their will to Allah before the historical labels of Judaism and Christianity existed.

The verse 3:19 — «inna l-dīna ʿinda Llāhi l-islām» (indeed the religion with Allah is Islam) — establishes Islam as the only acceptable religion. Al-Ṭabarī explains: the dīn (religion/way of life) that Allah accepts is submission to Him through obedience — this is the core meaning of islām, present in every authentic prophetic message. The specific laws (sharā'iʿ) may differ between prophets, but the essential dīn — submission to the One God — is constant. The verse 3:85 — «wa-man yabtaghi ghayra l-islāmi dīnan fa-lan yuqbala minhu» (whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him) — universalizes this principle: no path to divine acceptance exists outside submission to Allah.
shades.hadith_ar: بُنِيَ الْإِسْلَامُ عَلَى خَمْسٍ
shades.hadith_en: Islam is built upon five (pillars)

meaning.en: To create, to bring into existence from nothing, to fashion, to form. The root designates the divine act of origination — bringing the universe, life, and all things into being without precedent or model. Also: character, disposition (khuluq).
meaning.ar: الْإِبْدَاعُ وَالْإِيجَادُ مِنَ الْعَدَمِ — وَالْخَلْقُ: تَقْدِيرُ الشَّيْءِ وَإِيجَادُهُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا تَقْدِيرُ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْآخَرُ مَلَاسَةُ الشَّيْءِ. فَالْخَلْقُ: الْإِيجَادُ عَلَى تَقْدِيرٍ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) measuring/estimating a thing; (2) smoothness. Khalaqa: bringing into existence according to a measure/design.

quran_examples.ar: ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ
quran_examples.en: Read in the name of your Lord who created
quran_examples.context: First revelation — creation as the foundation of knowledge

quran_examples.ar: وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا ٱلْإِنسَـٰنَ مِن سُلَـٰلَةٍۢ مِّن طِينٍۢ
quran_examples.en: We created man from an extract of clay

hadith.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَلَقَ آدَمَ عَلَى صُورَتِهِ
hadith.en: Allah created Adam in His form.

shades.name_ar: الْخَلْقُ — الْإِيجَادُ مِنَ الْعَدَمِ عَلَى غَيْرِ مِثَالٍ
shades.explanation:
Khalq — creation — is the divine act that constitutes the entire universe's existence and distinguishes the Creator from all else. The first revelation commands: «iqra' bi-smi rabbika lladhī khalaq» (Read in the name of your Lord who created — 96:1). Knowledge begins with recognition of creation — before revelation, before law, before worship, there is the fundamental fact that existence is created, not self-existent. The creator-creature distinction is the foundation of Islamic theology (tawḥīd al-rubūbiyyah): only Allah creates (khalq), and everything else is created (makhlūq).

The Quran distinguishes khalaqa from other verbs of making (jaʿala, ṣanaʿa, faṭara, bada'a, ansha'a) with theological precision. Khalaqa is creation ex nihilo — bringing into existence what did not exist before, without model or material. Jaʿala is making from existing material or appointing to function. Faṭara is primordial creation — the initial bringing into being. Bada'a is origination without precedent. Ansha'a is bringing forth in stages. The Quran's careful deployment of these overlapping terms reveals a sophisticated theology of creation that Islamic kalām later systematized.

The argument from creation (dalīl al-khalq) is the Quran's primary rational proof for Allah's existence and uniqueness: «am khuliqū min ghayri shay'in am humu l-khāliqūn? am khalaqū l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa? bal lā yūqinūn» (Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators? Did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather they are not certain — 52:35-36). The disjunctive syllogism is rhetorically powerful: either you were created from nothing (impossible — nothing cannot produce something), or you created yourselves (absurd — you would have to exist before existing to create yourselves), or you were created by a Creator. Al-Rāzī expands this into a full philosophical argument for the existence of a necessary, eternal Creator.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ خَلَقَ الْخَلْقَ حَتَّى إِذَا فَرَغَ مِنْهُمْ قَامَتِ الرَّحِمُ فَقَالَتْ: هَٰذَا مَقَامُ الْعَائِذِ بِكَ مِنَ الْقَطِيعَةِ
shades.hadith_en: When Allah finished creating creation, the womb (raḥim) stood up and said: This is the station of one who seeks refuge with You from being severed.

meaning.en: Before, in front of; to accept, receive, turn toward, face. The root bridges temporal anteriority (qabl — before), spatial confrontation (qibal — toward, facing), and interpersonal acceptance (qubūl — reception, approval).
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ بَعْدٍ — وَالْإِقْبَالُ: التَّوَجُّهُ، وَالْقَبُولُ: الرِّضَا وَالْأَخْذُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا ضِدُّ الدُّبُرِ — وَهُوَ الْقُدَّامُ وَمَا أَشْبَهَهُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْقَبُولُ وَهُوَ الْأَخْذُ بِرِضًا
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) opposite of behind — the front; (2) acceptance — taking with approval.

quran_examples.ar: وَبَشِّرِ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ جَنَّـٰتٍۢ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلْأَنْهَـٰرُ ۖ كُلَّمَا رُزِقُوا۟ مِنْهَا مِن ثَمَرَةٍۢ رِّزْقًۭا ۙ قَالُوا۟ هَـٰذَا ٱلَّذِى رُزِقْنَا مِن قَبْلُ
quran_examples.en: Whenever they are given fruit, they say: This is what we were given before

hadith.ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ
hadith.en: Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith — his past sins are forgiven.

shades.name_en: Qubūl — Divine Acceptance of Deeds and Repentance
shades.name_ar: الْقَبُولُ — رِضَا اللَّهِ وَقَبُولُهُ لِلْأَعْمَالِ وَالتَّوْبَةِ
shades.explanation:
The verb «qabila» (He accepted) applied to Allah expresses divine acceptance (qubūl) of human deeds, repentance, and worship. The Quran's first narrative of qubūl is Adam and Eve's repentance: «fa-talaqqā Ādamu min rabbihi kalimātin fa-tāba ʿalayhi, innahu huwa l-tawwābu l-raḥīm» (Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance — 2:37). Divine acceptance is not guaranteed but conditioned on sincerity: «innamā yataqabbalu Llāhu min al-muttaqīn» (Allah only accepts from the God-conscious — 5:27), spoken in the context of Abel's accepted sacrifice and Cain's rejected one.

Al-Qurṭubī, in his commentary on 5:27, elaborates the conditions of qubūl: the deed must be sincerely for Allah (ikhlāṣ), in accordance with divine law (sharīʿah), from lawful means (ḥalāl), and accompanied by taqwā (God-consciousness). The story of Hābīl and Qābīl (Abel and Cain) establishes that divine acceptance depends on the quality of the worshipper, not merely the quantity of the offering. Qābīl offered the worst of his crops, Hābīl the best of his flock — and Allah «accepted» only Hābīl's. The fire that descended from heaven to consume the accepted sacrifice was the visible sign of divine qubūl before prophets.

The Quran's emphasis on divine qubūl rather than mere divine knowledge of deeds has profound spiritual implications: the believer does not merely perform acts hoping they are recorded; they seek divine acceptance (qubūl), which is an additional act of divine generosity — Allah not only knows the deed but receives it, welcomes it, and rewards it. The fear that one's deeds may not be accepted (ʿadam al-qubūl) is a recurring theme in Islamic spirituality — the righteous are those who «give what they give while their hearts are fearful» (23:60) that their deeds may not be accepted.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَقْبَلُ صَلَاةَ أَحَدِكُمْ إِذَا أَحْدَثَ حَتَّى يَتَوَضَّأَ
shades.hadith_en: Allah does not accept the prayer of one who is in a state of impurity until he performs ablution

meaning.en: To know, recognize, acknowledge, be acquainted with; knowledge (maʿrifah) that comes through experience, familiarity, and discernment. Distinguished from ʿilm (knowledge through learning) — ʿirfān is intuitive, experiential recognition.
meaning.ar: الْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْعِلْمُ بِالشَّيْءِ مَعَ سُكُونِ النَّفْسِ إِلَيْهِ — وَالْعُرْفُ: الْمَعْرُوفُ مِنَ الْخَيْرِ

al_raghib.ar: الْمَعْرِفَةُ: إِدْرَاكُ الشَّيْءِ بِتَفَكُّرٍ وَتَدَبُّرٍ لِأَثَرِهِ، وَهِيَ أَخَصُّ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ. وَالْعُرْفُ: كُلُّ مَا تَعْرِفُهُ النَّفْسُ مِنَ الْخَيْرِ
al_raghib.en: Maʿrifah: perceiving something through reflection on its traces — more specific than ʿilm. ʿUrf: whatever the soul recognizes as good.

quran_examples.ar: وَبَيْنَهُمَا حِجَابٌۭ ۚ وَعَلَى ٱلْأَعْرَافِ رِجَالٌۭ يَعْرِفُونَ كُلًّۢا بِسِيمَىٰهُمْ
quran_examples.en: Between them is a barrier, and on the Heights are men who recognize all by their marks
quran_examples.context: The people of al-Aʿrāf recognizing others by their signs

hadith.ar: تَعَرَّفْ إِلَى اللَّهِ فِي الرَّخَاءِ يَعْرِفْكَ فِي الشِّدَّةِ
hadith.en: Know Allah in times of ease, and He will know you in times of hardship.

shades.explanation:
Maʿrifah — recognition/knowledge — is distinguished from ʿilm (knowledge) in classical Arabic and Islamic thought. While ʿilm is cognitive knowledge acquired through learning and reasoning, maʿrifah is experiential, intuitive recognition — knowing something because one has encountered it, lived with it, become familiar with its signs. The ahl al-maʿrifah in Islamic spirituality are those who know Allah not merely through doctrinal learning but through direct spiritual experience (dhawq — tasting).

The Quran's usage of ʿarafa reflects this experiential quality. In 7:46, the people of al-Aʿrāf «yaʿrifūna kullan bi-sīmāhum» — they recognize each person by their distinguishing marks (sīmā). This is recognition through visible signs, not abstract knowledge.
