In 2:146, the People of the Book «yaʿrifūnahu kamā yaʿrifūna abnā'ahum» — they recognize him (the Prophet) as they recognize their own sons. The recognition of the Prophet's truth is as intimate and unmistakable as recognizing one's own child — it is maʿrifah born of familiarity with the prophetic description in their scriptures.

The concept of al-maʿrūf (what is recognized as good) in the Quran (3:104, 3:110, 3:114, 7:157, 9:71, 9:112, 22:41, 31:17) is central to Islamic ethics. Al-maʿrūf is the moral common ground — what every sound soul (nafs salīmah) recognizes as good without elaborate argumentation: kindness, justice, generosity, honesty. The command to «command the maʿrūf and forbid the munkar» (al-amr bi-l-maʿrūf wa-l-nahy ʿan al-munkar) is the Quranic charter of social morality — the community's obligation to promote recognized good and prevent recognized evil. Ibn Taymiyyah (al-Ḥisbah) argues that al-maʿrūf and al-munkar are known through the combined testimony of fiṭrah, reason, and revelation — what all three recognize as good or evil is the universal moral standard.
shades.hadith_ar: تَعَرَّفْ إِلَى اللَّهِ فِي الرَّخَاءِ يَعْرِفْكَ فِي الشِّدَّةِ
shades.hadith_en: Know Allah in ease — He will know you in hardship

meaning.en: To fast, abstain, refrain. The root's physical sense (standing still, refraining from movement) extends to the ritual abstinence from food, drink, and desire during the prescribed period — and metaphorically to any form of restraint and self-discipline.
meaning.ar: الْإِمْسَاكُ وَالتَّرْكُ — وَالصَّوْمُ: الْإِمْسَاكُ عَنِ الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ وَسَائِرِ الْمُفْطِرَاتِ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِمْسَاكٍ وَرُكُودٍ فِي مَكَانٍ. وَالصَّوْمُ: الْإِمْسَاكُ عَنِ الطَّعَامِ
ibn_faris.en: A single root indicating restraint and stillness in place. Ṣawm: abstention from food.

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ
quran_examples.en: O believers, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become God-conscious
quran_examples.context: The obligation and purpose of fasting

hadith.ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ
hadith.en: Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith and seeking reward — his previous sins are forgiven.

hadith.ar: الصِّيَامُ جُنَّةٌ
hadith.en: Fasting is a shield.

shades.name_en: Ṣiyām — Fasting as Spiritual Training and Divine Prescription
shades.explanation:
Ṣiyām — fasting — is divinely prescribed «laʿallakum tattaqūn» (that you may become God-conscious — 2:183). The purpose of fasting is not deprivation but transformation — the cultivation of taqwā (God-consciousness, self-restraint, reverence). The etymology of ṣawm as 'restraint' (imsāk) reveals the spiritual logic: by restraining the body from lawful desires (food, drink, intimacy) during the day, the soul learns to restrain itself from unlawful desires at all times. Fasting is training in self-mastery.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Fasting) distinguishes three levels of ṣawm: ṣawm al-ʿumūm (the fast of the common people — abstaining from food, drink, and sexual activity), ṣawm al-khuṣūṣ (the fast of the elite — additionally restraining the eyes, tongue, ears, and limbs from sin), and ṣawm khuṣūṣ al-khuṣūṣ (the fast of the elite of the elite — the heart's fast from everything other than Allah, from every thought and concern that distracts from the Divine). The physical fast is the gateway; the spiritual fast is the destination.

The verse 2:183 establishes fasting as a universal religious practice — «kamā kutiba ʿalā lladhīna min qablikum» (as it was prescribed for those before you). Fasting is not a uniquely Islamic innovation but a primordial form of worship known to all prophetic communities. This universalizing of ṣawm connects the Muslim practice to the broader human tradition of ascetic discipline, while the specific regulations of Ramadan (2:185) give it Islamic particularity. Ibn Kathīr notes that the phrase «laʿallakum tattaqūn» is the wisdom (ḥikmah) behind the prescription — fasting is not an end in itself but a means to taqwā, which is the ultimate goal of all worship.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ لَمْ يَدَعْ قَوْلَ الزُّورِ وَالْعَمَلَ بِهِ فَلَيْسَ لِلَّهِ حَاجَةٌ فِي أَنْ يَدَعَ طَعَامَهُ وَشَرَابَهُ
shades.hadith_en: Whoever does not abandon false speech and acting upon it — Allah has no need for him to abandon his food and drink.

meaning.en: To be truthful, sincere, honest; to give charity (ṣadaqah). The root bridges the concepts of verbal truthfulness and material generosity — the ṣādiq (truthful one) is also the mutaṣaddiq (charitable giver), because true faith manifests in both word and deed.
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ الْكَذِبِ — وَالصَّدَقَةُ: مَا يُعْطَى لِلَّهِ، سُمِّيَتْ لِأَنَّهَا دَلِيلٌ عَلَى صِدْقِ الْإِيمَانِ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْقُوَّةُ وَالشِّدَّةُ، وَالْآخَرُ مُوَافَقَةُ الْقَوْلِ لِلْحَقِيقَةِ. وَالصَّدَقَةُ سُمِّيَتْ لِصِدْقِ صَاحِبِهَا فِي إِيمَانِهِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) strength and solidity; (2) correspondence of speech to reality. Ṣadaqah is so named because it proves the giver's sincerity in faith.

quran_examples.ar: لِّيَسْـَٔلَ ٱلصَّـٰدِقِينَ عَن صِدْقِهِمْ
quran_examples.en: That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلصَّدَقَـٰتُ لِلْفُقَرَآءِ وَٱلْمَسَـٰكِينِ
quran_examples.en: Charities are only for the poor and the needy

hadith.ar: عَلَيْكُمْ بِالصِّدْقِ، فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْبِرِّ، وَإِنَّ الْبِرَّ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
hadith.en: Adhere to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise.

shades.name_en: Ṣidq — Truthfulness as the Foundation of Faith
shades.explanation:
Ṣidq — truthfulness — is the soul of īmān. The Quran commands: «yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū ttaqū Llāha wa-kūnū maʿa l-ṣādiqīn» (O believers, fear Allah and be with the truthful — 9:119). The ṣādiqūn (truthful ones) are those whose outward speech matches inward reality, whose promises are kept, whose testimony is honest, and whose entire being is aligned with the truth. The Prophet's ﷺ pre-prophetic title «al-Amīn al-Ṣādiq» (the Trustworthy, the Truthful) combined the trustworthiness of his character with the veracity of his speech — he was known never to have lied even before receiving revelation.

The ḥadīth in Bukhārī 6094 presents ṣidq as the gateway to all virtue: «inna l-ṣidqa yahdī ilā l-birri, wa-inna l-birra yahdī ilā l-jannah» (truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise). The chain of causation — ṣidq → birr → jannah — establishes truthfulness as the foundational moral quality from which all other virtues flow. Conversely, «wa-inna l-kadhiba yahdī ilā l-fujūri, wa-inna l-fujūra yahdī ilā l-nār» (lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire). The moral universe is structured around the truth/lie axis.

The concept of ṣadaqah (charity) derives from this root because giving wealth for Allah's sake is the material proof of the giver's ṣidq — their claim to faith is verified by their willingness to part with what they love for Allah. The ṣadaqah is not merely a transfer of wealth but an act of taṣdīq (verification) — it proves that the giver's īmān is genuine, not merely verbal. Al-Rāghib explains: charity is called ṣadaqah because it testifies to (yuṣaddiqu) the sincerity of the giver's faith — it is the visible evidence of an invisible conviction.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْبِرِّ، وَإِنَّ الْبِرَّ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
shades.hadith_en: Truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise

meaning.en: To judge, rule, govern, decide; to be wise, to perfect. The root encompasses divine judgment (ḥukm), human governance, juridical decision-making, and wisdom (ḥikmah) — the ability to put things in their proper place.
meaning.ar: الْمَنْعُ وَالْإِحْكَامُ — وَالْحُكْمُ: الْقَضَاءُ بِالْعَدْلِ، وَالْحِكْمَةُ: مَعْرِفَةُ حَقَائِقِ الْأَشْيَاءِ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ: الْمَنْعُ. وَالْحُكْمُ سُمِّيَ حُكْمًا لِأَنَّهُ يَمْنَعُ مِنَ الظُّلْمِ. وَالْحِكْمَةُ: الْعِلْمُ الَّذِي يَمْنَعُ صَاحِبَهُ مِنَ الْجَهْلِ
ibn_faris.en: A single root: prevention. Ḥukm (judgment) prevents injustice. Ḥikmah (wisdom) prevents its possessor from ignorance.

quran_examples.ar: يُؤْتِى ٱلْحِكْمَةَ مَن يَشَآءُ ۚ وَمَن يُؤْتَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِىَ خَيْرًۭا كَثِيرًۭا
quran_examples.en: He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good
quran_examples.context: Ḥikmah as the supreme divine gift

hadith.ar: لَا حَسَدَ إِلَّا فِي اثْنَتَيْنِ: رَجُلٌ آتَاهُ اللَّهُ مَالًا فَسُلِّطَ عَلَى هَلَكَتِهِ فِي الْحَقِّ، وَرَجُلٌ آتَاهُ اللَّهُ الْحِكْمَةَ فَهُوَ يَقْضِي بِهَا وَيُعَلِّمُهَا
hadith.en: There is no envy except in two: a man given wealth by Allah and he spends it in truth, and a man given wisdom by Allah and he judges by it and teaches it.

shades.name_en: Ḥikmah — Divine Wisdom as Integrated Knowledge and Action
shades.explanation:
Ḥikmah — wisdom — is one of the most profound Quranic concepts, defined classically as «waḍʿu l-shay'i fī mawḍiʿih» (placing each thing in its proper place). This definition, attributed to numerous scholars from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī to Ibn al-Qayyim, captures the essence of ḥikmah: it is not merely knowledge but the practical wisdom that enables one to act correctly at the right time, in the right way, for the right reason. The ḥakīm (wise one) knows not just what is true but what is appropriate — in speech, in judgment, in governance, in personal conduct.

The Quran presents ḥikmah as a divine gift granted to prophets and the righteous: «wa-ātaynāhu l-ḥikmata wa-faṣla l-khiṭāb» (We gave him wisdom and decisive speech — 38:20, describing David). Luqmān's counsel to his son in Sūrat Luqmān (31:12-19) is the Quran's paradigm of ḥikmah — practical moral wisdom combining theology (do not associate partners with Allah), ethics (be dutiful to parents), spirituality (establish prayer), and social conduct (do not turn your cheek in contempt, lower your voice). The ḥakīm integrates knowledge, action, and character.

The relationship between ḥikmah and the Quran is intimate: «wa-anzala Llāhu ʿalayka l-kitāba wa-l-ḥikmah» (Allah has sent down upon you the Book and the Wisdom — 4:113). The exegetes debate whether «al-ḥikmah» here refers to the Sunnah of the Prophet (as al-Shāfiʿī argued — the wisdom is the prophetic explanation of the Book), or to the understanding of the Quran (as others held), or to the legal rulings contained in the Quran. Al-Ṭabarī synthesizes: al-ḥikmah is the knowledge of the religion, its laws, and the wisdom of its prescriptions — encompassing both the revealed text and its correct understanding and application. The pairing of kitāb (Book) and ḥikmah (Wisdom) in multiple verses (2:129, 2:151, 2:231, 3:164, 4:113, 62:2) establishes that divine guidance includes both the text and its wise interpretation — the letter and the spirit, the law and the wisdom behind it.
shades.hadith_ar: الْحِكْمَةُ ضَالَّةُ الْمُؤْمِنِ، حَيْثُمَا وَجَدَهَا فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهَا
shades.hadith_en: Wisdom is the lost property of the believer — wherever he finds it, he is most entitled to it.

meaning.en: To go, depart, leave, pass away; gold (dhahab). The root's primary sense (movement, departure) contrasts with its nominal meaning (gold — the permanent, incorruptible metal), creating a semantic tension between transience and permanence.

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الذَّهَابُ — الْمُرُورُ، وَالْآخَرُ الذَّهَبُ — الْمَعْدِنُ الثَّمِينُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) going — passing; (2) gold — the precious metal.

quran_examples.ar: مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِى ٱسْتَوْقَدَ نَارًۭا فَلَمَّآ أَضَآءَتْ مَا حَوْلَهُۥ ذَهَبَ ٱللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ
quran_examples.en: Their example is like one who kindled a fire — when it illuminated, Allah took away their light
quran_examples.context: Allah removing the light of the hypocrites

hadith.ar: يَذْهَبُ الصَّالِحُونَ الْأَوَّلُ فَالْأَوَّلُ، وَيَبْقَى حُثَالَةٌ كَحُثَالَةِ الشَّعِيرِ
hadith.en: The righteous will depart one after another, until only the dregs remain.

shades.name_en: Dhahāb — Departure, Passing, and Divine Removal
shades.explanation:
The verb «dhahaba» (he went/departed) carries the sense of passing away, vanishing, being removed. In 2:17, Allah «dhahaba bi-nūrihim» — He took away their light — the verb expresses divine removal of something previously granted. The hypocrites had temporary illumination, but Allah caused it to depart. The transience conveyed by dhahaba contrasts with the permanence suggested by the noun dhahab (gold) — a semantic tension that the Quran exploits: gold appears permanent to worldly eyes, but in eschatological perspective, even gold «passes away» (57:20).

The Quran's description of worldly life consistently uses verbs of departure and transience: «iʿlamū annamā l-ḥayātu l-dunyā laʿibun wa-lahwun wa-zīnatun wa-tafākhurun baynakum wa-takāthurun fī l-amwāli wa-l-awlād» (Know that the life of this world is play, diversion, adornment, boasting among you, and competition in wealth and children — 57:20). The dunyā is characterized not by permanence but by departure — everything in it «yadhhabu» (goes away). The gold (dhahab) that seems so solid and permanent is, in truth, as transient as everything else the root describes.

The root also appears in descriptions of divine punishment: in 20:97, Moses tells the Samaritan who made the golden calf: «fa-inna laka mawʿidan lan tukhlafahu, wa-nẓur ilā ilāhika lladhī ẓalta ʿalayhi ʿākifan, la-nuḥarriqannahu thumma la-nansifannahu fī l-yammi nasfā» — the false god will be burned and scattered. The gold that was worshipped will «go away» — destroyed and dispersed. The contrast between human attachment to gold (dhahab) and its ultimate departure (dhahāb) is one of the Quran's methods for relativizing worldly attachments.
shades.hadith_ar: لَوْ كَانَ لِابْنِ آدَمَ وَادِيَانِ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ لَابْتَغَى إِلَيْهِمَا ثَالِثًا
shades.hadith_en: If the son of Adam had two valleys of gold, he would desire a third

meaning.en: To own, possess, rule, have dominion over; king, ruler, owner; kingdom, sovereignty. The root expresses comprehensive authority — legal ownership (milk), political rule (mulk), and divine sovereignty (malakūt).
meaning.ar: الْقُدْرَةُ وَالشِّدَّةُ — وَالْمُلْكُ: سَعَةُ التَّصَرُّفِ وَالْقُدْرَةُ الْمُطْلَقَةُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْقُوَّةُ وَالشِّدَّةُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْحُكْمُ وَالصَّلَاحِيَةُ. فَالْمَلِكُ: ذُو الْمُلْكِ — أَيِ الْقُدْرَةِ وَالسُّلْطَانِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) strength and intensity; (2) authority and competence. Al-malik: possessor of mulk — power and sovereignty.

quran_examples.ar: مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ
quran_examples.en: Master of the Day of Judgment
quran_examples.context: Divine sovereignty on the Last Day

hadith.ar: يَقْبِضُ اللَّهُ الْأَرْضَ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَيَطْوِي السَّمَاءَ بِيَمِينِهِ ثُمَّ يَقُولُ: أَنَا الْمَلِكُ، أَيْنَ مُلُوكُ الْأَرْضِ؟
hadith.en: Allah will grasp the earth and fold the heaven in His Right Hand, then say: I am the King — where are the kings of the earth?

shades.name_en: Mulk — Divine Sovereignty and the Kingdom of Allah
shades.explanation:
Al-Mulk — sovereignty, dominion, kingdom — is one of the most frequently affirmed attributes of Allah in the Quran. The basmalah's description of Allah as «Māliki yawmi l-dīn» (Master of the Day of Judgment — 1:4, in one canonical reading) or «Maliki yawmi l-dīn» (King of the Day of Judgment — in another) establishes divine sovereignty as the interpretive key to history: whatever powers appear to rule in this world, the ultimate mulk belongs to Allah alone. The shift from Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn (Lord of the Worlds — 1:2) to Mālik/Malik Yawm al-Dīn (Master/King of the Day of Judgment — 1:4) in al-Fātiḥah maps the movement from this world (where Allah's mulk is real but often contested by human claims to sovereignty) to the Hereafter (where Allah's mulk is manifest and unchallenged).

The Quran's frequent phrase «lahu mulku l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ» (to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth) appears over twenty times, establishing the comprehensive scope of divine mulk. Nothing in the cosmos — from the smallest particle to the largest galaxy, from the hidden thought to the public act — falls outside Allah's ownership and authority. Al-Rāzī's commentary on 3:26 — «quli llāhumma mālika l-mulki tu'tī l-mulka man tashā'u wa-tanziʿu l-mulka mimman tashā'u» (Say: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and take it from whom You will) — develops a political theology: all human political authority is a temporary, contingent gift (iʿṭāʾ) from the true Mālik, and He can withdraw it at any moment. No human king, president, or emperor truly «owns» power — they merely hold it on loan from the Owner of Sovereignty.

The divine name al-Malik (the King) and al-Mālik (the Owner/Master) express different aspects of divine sovereignty. Al-Malik emphasizes authority and command; al-Mālik emphasizes ownership and possession. Together, they establish that Allah's mulk is both de jure (by right — He is the legitimate Sovereign) and de facto (by power — He is the actual Owner of everything that exists). The ḥadīth qudsī in Bukhārī 7382 — Allah grasping the earth and folding the heavens, then declaring «anā l-Malik» (I am the King) — dramatizes the ultimate revelation of divine mulk on the Day when all pretenders to sovereignty are silenced.
shades.hadith_ar: أَنَا الْمَلِكُ، أَيْنَ مُلُوكُ الْأَرْضِ؟
shades.hadith_en: I am the King — where are the kings of the earth?

meaning.en: Evil, harm, bad, worse. The root denotes what is objectively harmful and morally wrong — the opposite of khayr (good). Used in comparative contexts (worse) and to describe the innate human tendency toward harm.
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ الْخَيْرِ — الشَّرُّ: مَا يَضُرُّ وَيُؤْذِي، وَهُوَ ضَرْبَانِ: شَرٌّ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ وَشَرٌّ فِي الْأَعْيَانِ

al_raghib.ar: الشَّرُّ: ضِدُّ الْخَيْرِ. وَهُوَ ضَرْبَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا شَرٌّ بِالذَّاتِ — وَهُوَ قَلِيلٌ، وَالْآخَرُ شَرٌّ بِالْإِضَافَةِ
al_raghib.en: Evil is the opposite of good. Two types: (1) intrinsically evil — rare; (2) relatively evil — by comparison.

quran_examples.ar: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ
quran_examples.en: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the dawn

quran_examples.ar: وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تَكْرَهُوا۟ شَيْـًۭٔا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ ۖ وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تُحِبُّوا۟ شَيْـًۭٔا وَهُوَ شَرٌّۭ لَّكُمْ
quran_examples.en: Perhaps you hate something and it is good for you, and perhaps you love something and it is evil for you
quran_examples.context: The relativity of perceived good and evil

hadith.ar: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ
hadith.en: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the dawn from the evil of what He created.

shades.name_en: Sharr — The Nature of Evil and Seeking Refuge
shades.explanation:
The Quran's treatment of sharr (evil) is comprehensive and nuanced. Evil is real — not an illusion or merely the absence of good — but its reality is temporary and ultimately subordinated to divine wisdom. The verse 2:216 — «wa-ʿasā an takrahū shay'an wa-huwa khayrun lakum, wa-ʿasā an tuḥibbū shay'an wa-huwa sharrun lakum» (perhaps you hate something and it is good for you, perhaps you love something and it is evil for you) — relativizes human perception of good and evil. What appears evil to limited human perspective may be, in the divine plan, a vehicle for greater good.

The two muʿawwidhatān (Sūrat al-Falaq and Sūrat al-Nās — 113-114) are the Quran's primary liturgies of protection from sharr. Al-Falaq enumerates five sources of evil: the evil of creation generally, the evil of darkness when it settles, the evil of sorceresses blowing on knots, and the evil of the envier when he envies. Al-Nās identifies the ultimate source of evil: the whisperer (al-waswās al-khannās) who whispers into human hearts — from among jinn and humanity. The combined message: evil has multiple manifestations in the created world, but its root is the satanic whisper that exploits human weakness.

The Ashʿarī theological tradition, articulated most systematically by al-Rāzī, developed a sophisticated theodicy from the Quran's treatment of sharr. Allah is the Creator of all things, including what humans perceive as evil, but Allah does not create pure evil — He creates things and events that may be evil from one perspective but serve a greater good in His comprehensive wisdom. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Trust) argues that the true believer sees the hand of divine wisdom even in what appears harmful — «laysa fī l-imkāni abdaʿu mimmā kān» (there is nothing in the realm of possibility more excellent than what exists). The proper response to sharr is not to question divine justice but to seek refuge (istiʿādhah) in Allah from it — acknowledging our vulnerability and His protective power.
shades.hadith_ar: مَا مِنْ شَيْءٍ أَثْقَلُ فِي مِيزَانِ الْمُؤْمِنِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ مِنْ حُسْنِ الْخُلُقِ
shades.hadith_en: Nothing is heavier in the believer's scale on the Day of Resurrection than good character

meaning.en: To measure, determine, decree, have power over. The root encompasses divine predestination (qadar), human capability (qudrah), and the measured, precise nature of creation. Everything is created «bi-qadar» — with exact measure and purpose.
meaning.ar: التَّقْدِيرُ وَالْقَضَاءُ — وَالْقُدْرَةُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ: التَّمَكُّنُ مِنْهُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا غَايَةُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَنِهَايَتُهُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْمُلْكُ وَالْقُوَّةُ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) the measure and limit of everything; (2) possession and power.

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَـٰهُ فِى لَيْلَةِ ٱلْقَدْرِ
quran_examples.en: Indeed We sent it down on the Night of Power/Decree

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَـٰهُ بِقَدَرٍۢ
quran_examples.en: Indeed We created everything with measure (qadar)
quran_examples.context: The measured, purposeful nature of creation

hadith.ar: الْإِيمَانُ أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاللَّهِ وَمَلَائِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَتُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ
hadith.en: Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in divine decree (qadar) — its good and its evil.

shades.name_en: Qadar — Divine Decree and the Measured Order of Creation
shades.name_ar: الْقَدَرُ — التَّقْدِيرُ الْإِلٰهِيُّ وَنِظَامُ الْخَلْقِ الْمَوْزُونُ
shades.explanation:
The doctrine of qadar — divine decree and predestination — is one of the six articles of faith (arkān al-īmān) in Islam, as articulated in the Ḥadīth Jibrīl: «wa-tu'mina bi-l-qadari khayrihi wa-sharrihi» (and you believe in divine decree — its good and its evil — Muslim 8). The root q-d-r provides the language for this doctrine: taqdīr is Allah's eternal determination of all things; qadar is the actualized decree in time; qudrah is Allah's absolute power to execute His decree; and taqdīr also means 'measuring' — creation is not random but precisely measured.

The theological debates about qadar were the first major doctrinal controversies in Islamic history. The Qadariyyah (early advocates of free will, later absorbed into the Muʿtazilah) emphasized human moral responsibility and argued that Allah's justice requires that humans be the creators of their own acts — otherwise punishment for divinely created acts would be unjust. The Jabriyyah (determinists) emphasized divine omnipotence and argued that Allah is the Creator of all acts, including human acts — otherwise Allah's power would be limited. The mainstream Ahl al-Sunnah position, articulated by al-Ashʿarī and al-Māturīdī, sought a middle path: Allah is the Creator of all acts (including human acts), but humans have genuine acquisition (kasb) of their acts, which grounds moral responsibility. This position was further refined by later Ashʿarī theologians (al-Bāqillānī, al-Juwaynī, al-Ghazālī) into the theory of kasb (acquisition) — Allah creates the act, the human acquires it through their intention and will.

The verse 54:49 — «innā kulla shay'in khalaqnāhu bi-qadar» (We created everything with measure) — establishes that creation is not random but precisely measured and purposeful. The cosmos is a mawzūn (balanced) system, and every event has its appointed measure (miqdār). The Night of Qadr (Laylat al-Qadr — 97:1-5) is the night when the measured decree (qadar) for the coming year is sent down — connecting the concept of divine decree with the revelation of the Quran and the annual determination of events. Ibn Kathīr, in his tafsīr of Sūrat al-Qadr, reports that on this night, the precise details of life, death, provision, and all events for the coming year are decreed by divine wisdom — demonstrating that qadar is not merely abstract predestination but a living, annually renewed divine governance of the world.
shades.hadith_ar: تُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ
shades.hadith_en: To believe in divine decree — its good and its evil

meaning.en: To count, calculate, reckon, take account; to consider, think, deem; sufficiency. The root encompasses divine reckoning (ḥisāb) on the Day of Judgment, human accounting and calculation, and the assessment of what is sufficient (ḥasb).
meaning.ar: الْعَدُّ وَالْإِحْصَاءُ — وَالْحِسَابُ: مُحَاسَبَةُ اللَّهِ لِعِبَادِهِ، وَالْحَسْبُ: الْكِفَايَةُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْعَدُّ، وَالْآخَرُ الْكِفَايَةُ. تَقُولُ: حَسَبْتُ الشَّيْءَ — أَيْ عَدَدْتُهُ، وَأَحْسَبَنِي الشَّيْءُ — أَيْ كَفَانِي
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) counting/numbering; (2) sufficiency. You say: I counted something, and: something sufficed me.

quran_examples.ar: أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌۭ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ سَرِيعُ ٱلْحِسَابِ
quran_examples.en: Those have a share of what they earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning

quran_examples.ar: وَنَضَعُ ٱلْمَوَٰزِينَ ٱلْقِسْطَ لِيَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَـٰمَةِ فَلَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌۭ شَيْـًۭٔا ۖ وَإِن كَانَ مِثْقَالَ حَبَّةٍۢ مِّنْ خَرْدَلٍ أَتَيْنَا بِهَا ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِنَا حَـٰسِبِينَ
quran_examples.en: We set the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection — no soul will be wronged at all. Even if a mustard seed's weight, We will bring it. Sufficient are We as Reckoners.

hadith.ar: حَاسِبُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُحَاسَبُوا
hadith.en: Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account.

shades.name_en: Ḥisāb — Divine Reckoning and the Ethics of Accountability
shades.explanation:
Ḥisāb — reckoning, accounting — is central to the Quran's theology of moral responsibility. Every soul will be «called to account» (yuḥāsabu) for its deeds on the Day of Judgment. The metaphor is financial: life is a transaction, deeds are credits and debits, and the Final Day is the settlement of accounts. The precision of divine ḥisāb is absolute: «wa-in kāna mithqāla ḥabbatin min khardalin ataynā bihā, wa-kafā binā ḥāsibīn» (even if it is a mustard seed's weight, We will bring it — sufficient are We as Reckoners — 21:47). No deed, however small, escapes the divine ledger.

The Quran's emphasis on ḥisāb generates a distinctive moral psychology: the believer lives with the constant awareness of being «accountable» (mas'ūl). Every word (50:18 — «mā yalfiẓu min qawlin illā ladayhi raqībun ʿatīd» — no word is uttered without a watcher ready), every deed, every intention is being recorded and will be weighed. This awareness (murāqabah) is the spiritual fruit of belief in ḥisāb: the believer engages in self-reckoning (muḥāsabat al-nafs) before the ultimate reckoning. The ḥadīth «ḥāsibū anfusakum qabla an tuḥāsabū» (take account of yourselves before you are taken to account — Tirmidhī 2459) establishes the practice of nightly self-examination as a core spiritual discipline.

The swiftness of divine ḥisāb — «wa-Llāhu sarīʿu l-ḥisāb» (Allah is swift in reckoning — 2:202, 3:19, 3:199, 5:4, 14:51, 24:39, 40:17) — is both a promise and a warning. It promises that the accounting will not be interminably delayed — the divine Judge does not need time to deliberate, evidence to be gathered, or arguments to be heard. He already knows all. But the swiftness is also a warning: none will escape the accounting, and it will come upon all creation as quickly as the blinking of an eye. Ibn Kathīr explains that «sarīʿ al-ḥisāb» means Allah will judge all of creation — from Adam to the last human — in the time it takes to slaughter a camel and distribute its meat, or even less, according to some narrations.
shades.hadith_ar: حَاسِبُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُحَاسَبُوا، وَزِنُوا أَعْمَالَكُمْ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُوزَنُوا
shades.hadith_en: Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account; weigh your deeds before they are weighed

meaning.en: To fulfill, pay in full, complete; to die (wafā — the soul being received in full). The root bridges commercial fulfillment (paying debts completely) and eschatological completion (death as the soul's full reception by Allah).
meaning.ar: إِتْمَامُ الشَّيْءِ وَإِكْمَالُهُ — وَالْوَفَاءُ: الْإِتْيَانُ بِالْكَامِلِ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْوَفَاةُ: الْمَوْتُ

al_raghib.ar: الْوَفَاءُ: إِتْمَامُ الشَّيْءِ عَلَى وُجُوهِهِ. وَالْوَفَاةُ: الْمَوْتُ — مِنْ إِتْمَامِ الْأَجَلِ
al_raghib.en: Wafāʾ: completing a thing in all its aspects. Wafāt: death — from the completion of one's appointed term.

quran_examples.ar: فَكَيْفَ إِذَا جَمَعْنَـٰهُمْ لِيَوْمٍۢ لَّا رَيْبَ فِيهِ ۖ وَوُفِّيَتْ كُلُّ نَفْسٍۢ مَّا كَسَبَتْ
quran_examples.en: How will it be when We gather them on a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul will be paid in full what it earned?
quran_examples.context: Full recompense on the Last Day

hadith.ar: مَنْ أَخْلَصَ أَرْبَعِينَ يَوْمًا لِلَّهِ فَتَفَجَّرَتْ يَنَابِيعُ الْحِكْمَةِ مِنْ قَلْبِهِ عَلَى لِسَانِهِ
hadith.en: Whoever sincerely devotes forty days to Allah — the springs of wisdom will gush from his heart onto his tongue.

shades.name_en: Wafāʾ and Wafāt — Fulfillment of Covenants and of Life
shades.name_ar: الْوَفَاءُ وَالْوَفَاةُ — إِتْمَامُ الْعَهْدِ وَإِكْمَالُ الْأَجَلِ
shades.explanation:
The root's semantic range — fulfillment of covenants, full payment, and death — is united by the core concept of completion. To fulfill (wafā) a covenant is to bring it to its complete end without deficiency. To die (wafāt) is for the soul's appointed time to reach its complete end. The verb nawaffā (We cause to die) describes the moment of full completion: the body completes its function, the soul completes its earthly journey, and the entire person returns to Allah with their complete record.

The Quran's ethical teaching on fulfilling covenants (al-wafāʾ bi-l-ʿahd) is among its most emphatic moral instructions. 9:4 — «illā lladhīna ʿāhadtum mina l-mushrikīna thumma lam yanqusūkum shay'an wa-lam yuẓāhirū ʿalaykum aḥadan fa-atimū ilayhim ʿahdahum ilā muddatihim» — instructs Muslims to fulfill their treaties with the polytheists who have kept their terms. The principle: treaty obligations are binding regardless of the other party's religion; breaking a covenant is among the most serious moral violations. The hadīth in Musnad Aḥmad 1441 — «al-wafāʾ bi-l-ʿahd» (fulfill the covenant) is one of the four most beloved deeds to Allah.

The double meaning of w-y-f (fulfillment and death) is leveraged rhetorically in verses like 3:144 — «wa-mā Muhammadun illā rasūlun qad khalat min qablihi l-rusulu, afa-in māta aw qutila inqalabtum ʿalā aʿqābikum» (Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?). The w-f-y root connects the death of the Prophet (wafāt) with the death of all prophets (māta) and the apostasy-fear that death may cause. The believer's response: «wa-man yanqalib ʿalā ʿaqibayhi fa-lan yaḍurra Llāha shay'an» (whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all) — the covenant with Allah is the only death that matters, not the death of the covenant-bearer.
shades.hadith_ar: أَحَبُّ الْأَعْمَالِ إِلَى اللَّهِ أَرْبَعٌ: الْوَفَاءُ بِالْعَهْدِ، وَالصَّدْقُ فِي الْحَدِيثِ، وَحُسْنُ الْخُلُقِ، وَكَثْرَةُ الْجِمَاعِ مِنْ غَيْرِ مَعْصِيَةٍ
shades.hadith_en: The most beloved deeds to Allah are four: fulfilling covenants, truthful speech, good character, and intimate relations without sin.

meaning.en: To return, turn back, repeat, revert. The root encompasses the act of return (ʿawda), the habit (ʿādah), and the eschatological return to Allah (maʿād). Also: firewood (ʿūd) — a wood that has been dried/seasoned through repeated cycles.
meaning.ar: الرُّجُوعُ — وَالْمَعَادُ: الْمَصِيرُ، وَالْعَادَةُ: الْفِعْلُ الْمُكَرَّرُ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الرُّجُوعُ، وَالْآخَرُ الزَّمَانُ. وَالْعَادَةُ: كُلُّ فِعْلٍ يُعَادُ تَكْرَارًا
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) return; (2) time. ʿĀdah: every act that is repeatedly returned to.

quran_examples.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَـٰهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ
quran_examples.en: Those who believe, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them

hadith.ar: مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ
hadith.en: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day — let him speak good or remain silent.

shades.name_en: al-Maʿād — The Return to Allah and the Eschatological Journey
shades.name_ar: الْمَعَادُ — الرُّجُوعُ إِلَى اللَّهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
shades.explanation:
The concept of al-maʿād (the return) is the Quran's name for the entire eschatological journey — the soul's departure from the body, the barzakh, the resurrection, the reckoning, and the final return to Allah. The word maʿād is itself from this root (ʿ-w-d), but with the form ma-ʿād (place/time of return). The Quran presents life as a journey whose only destination is the return to Allah: «wa-anna ilā rabbika l-muntahā» (and that to your Lord is the final return — 53:42). The whole of human existence is, in this sense, a «going out» from Allah and an inevitable «coming back» to Him.

The ʿādah (habit, custom) — that which is repeated — reflects the root's sense of cyclical return. Islamic worship is built on ʿādah: daily prayers repeated five times, the annual ṣawm of Ramadan, the weekly Jumuʿah, the lifetime hajj. The ʿawāʾid are the cycles of devotion that mark the Muslim's life, each return being both a repetition and a renewal. The ḥadīth «niyyat al-mu'min khayrun min ʿamalihi» (the intention of the believer is better than his action) highlights the inner dimension of repeated acts: the same ʿādah performed with renewed sincerity each time is greater than the same act performed mechanically.

The literary and rhetorical power of ʿ-w-d is exploited in verses that pair return with progression: «innā lillāh wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn» (we belong to Allah, and to Him we return — 2:156) — the verbal noun rājiʿūn (returning) frames death and suffering as ʿawda (return) to Allah, transforming grief into acceptance. The verse was revealed when the Muslim family of Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib was struck with tragedy, and it became the Islamic prayer at every loss. The root ʿ-w-d thus provides the linguistic foundation for the most profound Islamic response to loss: not denial, not despair, but ʿawda — the conscious return to the One who gave.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ
shades.hadith_en: Actions are by intentions

meaning.en: To seek, request, demand, ask for. The root denotes active pursuit of something — knowledge, refuge, help, or any object of desire. Differs from suʾāl (asking) in its emphasis on effort and seeking.

al_raghib.ar: الطَّلَبُ: الْبُحْثُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ لِأَخْذِهِ — وَهُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنَ السُّؤَالِ
al_raghib.en: Ṭalab: seeking after something to take it — broader than suʾāl (asking).

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذْ قُلْتُمْ يَـٰمُوسَىٰ لَن نَّصْبِرَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامٍۢ وَٰحِدٍۢ فَٱدْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُخْرِجْ لَنَا مِمَّا تُنۢبِتُ ٱلْأَرْضُ
quran_examples.en: When you said: O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food — pray to your Lord for us that He may bring forth for us from the earth

hadith.ar: طَلَبُ الْعِلْمِ فَرِيضَةٌ عَلَى كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ
hadith.en: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.

shades.name_en: Ṭalab al-ʿIlm — The Pursuit of Knowledge as Sacred Seeking
shades.explanation:
The root ṭ-l-b provides the lexical foundation for the Islamic ethos of seeking. The ḥadīth «ṭalab al-ʿilmi farīḍatun ʿalā kulli muslim» (seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim) makes ṭalab a religious obligation. The verb frames the pursuit of knowledge as an active quest — not passive reception but diligent seeking. The muṭṭalib (seeker) walks to the teacher, travels for the sake of one ḥadīth, devotes years to mastering the sciences. The act of seeking is itself a form of worship.

In the Quran, the verb ṭalaba (he sought) describes the relentless pursuit of the disbelievers: «inni Uthāma bāna l-mujrimūn fī ḍalālihim yaʿūḍūn» (the criminals are indeed in error — they used to be called to prostration — 83:4, using the related root ʿ-w-d). The believers, by contrast, are those who «yūfūn» (fulfill) and «yuʾtūn» (give), persistently and faithfully. The verb ṭ-l-b can also describe the human pursuit of power: Pharaoh «iṣtaghā» (he behaved arrogantly) and demanded absolute loyalty, while the believers «ṭalabū» (sought) Allah's pleasure.

The noun ṭālib (seeker) became a key term in Ṣūfī spirituality: the sālik (wayfarer) is also a ṭālib (seeker) of Allah, engaged in the lifelong quest for the Face of the Beloved. The famous ḥadīth of the dervish — «lammā khalaqahu l-ḥubb kāna l-khalqu ʿadan ʿanhu» (when love created creation, creation was hidden from it) — describes the original ṭ-l-b of the human soul for its Origin, which only ends in the maʿrifa of divine encounter. The ṭālib's journey is the longest — but it is the one the soul was created for.
shades.hadith_ar: طَلَبُ الْعِلْمِ فَرِيضَةٌ عَلَى كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ
shades.hadith_en: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim

meaning.en: To corrupt, ruin, spoil, be in disarray. The root denotes any state in which something is taken out of its proper, sound condition — physical corruption, moral decay, social disorder. The opposite of ʿaṣāḥ (soundness, reform).
meaning.ar: الْخُرُوجُ مِنَ الْحَقِّ إِلَى الْبَاطِلِ — وَالْفَسَادُ: إِخْلَالُ النِّظَامِ وَإِبْطَالُ الْمَقْصُودِ

al_raghib.ar: الْفَسَادُ: خُرُوجُ الشَّيْءِ عَنِ الِاعْتِدَالِ — سَوَاءٌ فِي الْأَجْسَادِ أَوِ الْأَخْلَاقِ أَوِ الْأَحْوَالِ
al_raghib.en: Fasād: a thing's departure from equilibrium — in bodies, in character, in conditions.

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذَا تَوَلَّىٰ سَعَىٰ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لِيُفْسِدَ فِيهَا وَيُهْلِكَ ٱلْحَرْثَ وَٱلنَّسْلَ
quran_examples.en: When he turns away, he seeks to spread corruption on the earth and destroy crops and offspring

hadith.ar: مَنْ دَعَا إِلَى هُدًى كَانَ لَهُ مِنَ الْأَجْرِ مِثْلُ أُجُورِ مَنْ تَبِعَهُ
hadith.en: Whoever calls to guidance has the reward of all who follow him.

shades.name_en: Fasād — Corruption as Cosmic and Moral Disorder
shades.explanation:
Fasād — corruption — is the disruption of the divinely established order (ʿaṣāḥ). The Quran presents the cosmos as originally in a state of balance and order — «ṣāwāʾ kullun» (all things are balanced — 21:30 in one reading) — and human action can either preserve or disrupt this balance. Corruption is not merely a moral category but a cosmic one: «alā yaqūlūna bi-l-arḍi yufsidūnaha» — they say: Why is he (the Prophet) not given a kingdom? They have made a great corruption in the land (the broader context of al-Qalam 68:1-8).

The Quran's most famous usage of f-s-d in the phrase «kullun ṭālibun» (every seeker) frames the universal human condition: every person seeks something. But not all seeking is sound. The mufsid (corruptor) seeks power through destruction; the muṣliḥ (reformer) seeks order through justice. The Prophet's ﷺ hijra (emigration) is the paradigm of leaving fasād for ʿaṣāḥ, fleeing the corruptor (Fasād) for the just community (Madīnat al-Rasūl). The Quran's vocabulary of fasād vs. is-ḥ (reform, soundness) structures the entire moral universe: every human action is on a continuum between ḥayr (good) and sharr (evil), between ʿaṣāḥ (sound) and fasād (corrupt).

The Quran's prescription for combating fasād is comprehensive: amr bi-l-maʿrūf wa-l-nahy ʿan al-munkar (commanding good and forbidding evil — 3:104, 9:71, 9:112) is the communal response, while taubah (repentance) and is-ḥ (reform) are the individual responses. The political theology of fasād is explicit: «wa-Llāhu lā yuḥibbu l-fāsidin» (Allah does not love the corruptors — 5:64) — He opposes and resists them. The Quran's most powerful affirmation of ʿaṣāḥ is in 11:85: «inn ʿādat al-miṣṭūn haqqa ʿalayka lamā taḥummīn» — the people of Shuʿayb's madīnah are warned that they have been causing fasād in the land by cheating in trade, and the divine response is the advent of a just ruler who will reform them. The implication: political order is the necessary counterpart to moral soundness.
shades.hadith_ar: مَنْ أَحْيَا أَرْضًا مَيْتَةً فَهِيَ لَهُ
shades.en: Whoever revives a dead land, it is his.

meaning.en: To break, shatter, defeat, suffer loss. The root encompasses physical breaking of objects, the breaking of a journey, and the spiritual defeat of tyrants. Also: losses (k-s-r) in trade — opposite of profit.
meaning.ar: إِزَالَةُ الْوَصْلِ بَيْنَ جُزْأَيِ الشَّيْءِ — وَالْكَسْرُ: إِخْرَاجُ الشَّيْءِ مِنَ الِاسْتِقَامَةِ

al_raghib.ar: الْكَسْرُ: فَصْلُ الشَّيْءِ بَعْضِهِ عَنْ بَعْضٍ. وَالْكَسْرُ: الْخَسَارُ — لِأَنَّ التَّاجِرَ يَنْقُصُ مَالُهُ. وَالتَّكْسِيرُ: الْقَهْرُ وَالْغَلَبَةُ
al_raghib.en: Kusr: separating parts of a thing. Khusrān (loss) — because the trader's wealth is reduced. Taksīr: overwhelming and defeating.

quran_examples.ar: وَنُنَزِّلُ مِنَ ٱلْقُرْءَانِ مَا هُوَ شِفَآءٌۭ وَرَحْمَةٌۭ لِّلْمُؤْمِنِينَ ۙ وَلَا يَزِيدُ ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ إِلَّا خَسَارًۭا
quran_examples.en: We send down of the Quran what is healing and mercy to the believers, but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss
quran_examples.context: Quran as cure for the faithful, loss for the wrongdoers

hadith.ar: الْخَاسِرُونَ هُمُ الَّذِينَ خَسِرُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَأَهْلِيهِمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
hadith.en: The losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Judgment.

shades.name_en: Khusrān — Loss, Deficit, and the Final Reckoning
shades.explanation:
Khusrān — loss, deficit — is the opposite of ribḥ (profit) and forms one of the central categories of Quranic moral assessment. The verb khasiya (to lose) and its intensive participle khāsirūn (losers) appear throughout the Quran's eschatological passages, where the question of «who loses?» is the ultimate spiritual concern. The verdict is sobering: «wa-man yakfur bi-l-īmāni fa-qad ḥaṣala ʿamaluhu» — whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have indeed been in vain (5:5). Faith is the prerequisite for eternal profit; rejection of it is the precondition for loss.

The Quran's theology of khusrān is presented in four dimensions: (1) the loss of faith (2:108) — the person who exchanges belief for disbelief has lost the way; (2) the loss of righteous deeds (5:5) — the disbelief negates the work; (3) the loss of self (39:15) — «wa-man yakfur fa-iyyāka ʿalā nafsih» (whoever disbelieves — against himself is his denial — 39:15, using root k-f-r's negation); and (4) the loss of the family and community (39:65) — those who came with evil deeds will find their deeds rejected, and they will lose the bonds of kinship that they thought would save them.

The most profound use of khusrān is in 6:20 — «wa-idh ʿagḥā lladhīna kafarū ʿalayhi dhārun» (those who disbelieved were given to understand a great loss — the actual verse is 2:102). The word dhārun (lit. 'great loss') is a noun of magnitude — not just any loss, but a vast, comprehensive, eternal loss. Those who disbelieve and die in disbelief are the khusrān of ultimate proportions. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ) develops a powerful meditation on khusrān: the believer should periodically «visit» the thought of the Day of Reckoning, asking: «what have I gained and what have I lost?» The ʿuqbā (end) is what determines the nature of the khusrān — a life of worship ending in Paradise is ultimate profit; a life of sin ending in Hell is ultimate loss.
shades.hadith_ar: الْخَاسِرُونَ مَنْ خَسِرُوا أَهْلِيهِمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ
shades.hadith_en: The losers are those who lost their families and wealth

meaning.en: To live, be alive; life. The root designates biological, spiritual, and eternal life. Allah is al-Ḥayy (the Ever-Living); humans and other creatures are subject to alternating states of life and death.
meaning.ar: الْحَيَاةُ ضِدُّ الْمَوْتِ — وَالْحَيُّ: مَنْ كَانَ ذَا حَيَاةٍ، وَالْحَيُّ مِنَ اللَّهِ: صِفَةُ الذَّاتِ الْأَزَلِيَّةِ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ: الْحَيَاةُ. وَالْحَيُّ فِي صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ: صِفَةٌ أَزَلِيَّةٌ لَمْ تَزَلْ وَلَا تَزَالُ
ibn_faris.en: A single root: life. Al-Ḥayy in Allah's attributes: an eternal attribute — was, and shall ever be.

quran_examples.ar: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَـٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ
quran_examples.en: Allah — there is no god but He — the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all

hadith.ar: إِنَّ لِلَّهِ تِسْعَةً وَتِسْعِينَ اسْمًا، مِائَةً إِلَّا وَاحِدًا، مَنْ أَحْصَاهَا دَخَلَ الْجَنَّةَ
hadith.en: Allah has ninety-nine names — one hundred minus one — whoever enumerates them enters Paradise.

shades.name_en: al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm — Divine Life as the Foundation of All Existence
shades.name_ar: الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ — صِفَةُ الذَّاتِ الْإِلٰهِيَّةِ الْأَزَلِيَّةُ
shades.explanation:
Al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm — the Ever-Living, the Sustainer — are the paired divine attributes that introduce Āyat al-Kursī (2:255), the Quran's most powerful verse. The two names complement each other: al-Ḥayy (the Living) affirms that Allah has true, perfect, eternal life — not biological life (which requires sustenance and is vulnerable to death) but the life of pure actuality, the life that is its own source. Al-Qayyūm (the Sustainer) affirms that Allah stands by Himself (qā'im bi-nafsihi) and upon Him all creation stands (muqīm li-ghayrihi). Together: the One who lives by His own essence sustains all that lives by His power.

The divine attribute al-Ḥayy is the foundation of all other divine attributes. Al-ʿAlīm (All-Knowing) is alive with knowledge; al-Qadīr (All-Powerful) is alive with power; al-Murīd (Willing) is alive with will. All divine attributes are attributes of a living subject. Without life, the attributes would be impotent. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī develops this point: «al-ḥayāt al-muṭlaqah allatī hiya maẓhar al-aʿlām al-ilāhiyyah kullahā» — the absolute life that is the locus of all divine attributes. The essence of Allah's life is unknowable; what we know is its manifestations in creation and the names that reveal aspects of it.

The contrast between al-Ḥayy and al-Mayyit (the Dead) is repeatedly deployed in the Quran to dramatize the difference between faith and disbelief: «a-fa-mayyitun ahya'a Llāhu, wa-jaʿalakum khilāfata l-arḍ» (He gave life to the dead and made you successors on earth — 27:62). The believer is alive (ḥayy) by virtue of īmān; the disbeliever is spiritually dead — his limbs move, but his soul is in a state of death. The famous ḥadīth — the Prophet walking through a market striking the shoulders of people and saying «ji'ū lil-khalāṣ» (come to salvation, for you are dead) — illustrates this spiritual pathology: outwardly living but inwardly dead. The Quran's call to faith is a call to life (al-ḥayawān), for whoever truly lives, lives by faith.
shades.hadith_ar: الْحَيُّ الَّذِي لَا يَمُوتُ، وَالْكَافُّ الَّذِي لَا يَضُمُّ، وَالسُّكَّتُ الَّذِي لَا تَعْجَلُ
shades.hadith_en: The Ever-Living who does not die, the sufficient who does not need, the eternal who does not hurry

meaning.en: To turn, circle, revolve, alternate. The root encompasses rotation in space, succession in time (dawr — era), and alternation between states. Also: a generation or age.
meaning.ar: الطَّوْفَانُ حَوْلَ الشَّيْءِ — وَالدَّوْرُ: طَلَبُ الشَّيْءِ مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ

al_raghib.ar: الدَّوْرَانُ: الطَّوْفُ حَوْلَ الشَّيْءِ. وَالدَّوْرُ: الْوَقْتُ الْمُسْتَأْنَفُ الَّذِي يَجِيءُ بَعْدَ غَيْرِهِ
al_raghib.en: Dawrān: orbiting around something. Dawr: a renewed period that comes after another.

quran_examples.ar: فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضَىٰهَا ۚ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ
quran_examples.en: We will surely turn you to a direction that will please you; turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque
quran_examples.context: The change of qibla — a turning in direction

hadith.ar: الْأَعْمَالُ بِالْخَوَاتِيمِ، وَخَاتِمَةُ عَمَلِكَ يَوْمَ لِقَاءِ اللَّهِ
hadith.en: Actions are judged by their endings — the end of your deeds is what matters when you meet Allah.

shades.name_en: Dawr — Cycles of Time and the Return of Creation to Allah
shades.explanation:
The verb dāra (he turned) and its derivatives in the Quran primarily describe spatial turning — turning one's face toward a direction (the qibla, the heavens), turning away from another. The most famous example is the divine command to «fa-walli wajhaka» — turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque (2:144). The change of qibla from Jerusalem to Mecca is the paradigmatic dawr — a turning that involves both spatial orientation (which direction to face) and historical orientation (which community is now central to the divine plan). The verb captures the deliberate act of reorientation that Islam demands.

Beyond spatial dawr, the Quran uses the root for time cycles and epochs: «wa-in yahūdūka fa-in Allāha huwa waliyyuhu wa-rūḥuhu wa-jarīluh» — using related terms for divine support in times of changing fate. The historical dawr of nations — rise and fall, rise and fall — is described using verbs of turning: Pharaoh's turn to tyranny, Moses's turn to leadership, the Quraysh's turn to opulence, the Muslims' turn to empire. The Quran's narrative cycle traces the dawr of divine plan through historical turning points.

In Islamic eschatology, the concept of al-dawr — the great cycle of creation, dissolution, and renewal — emerges from related roots. The metaphysical thinkers (philosophers and some Ṣūfīs) developed elaborate theories of cosmic dawr — the periodic renewal (tajdīd) of creation, the cycles of existence that move from emanation through return. Ibn ʿArabī's theory of the «dawr awwal» and «dawr thānī» (first and second cycles) — of emanation from Allah and return to Him — provides the philosophical framework. The Quranic basis for this is the affirmation that all creation turns (yaqūmu, qāma) — established by Allah and returned to Him: «wa-li-Llāhi l-amru min qablu wa-min baʿd» (Allah's is the command before and after — 30:4), and «yauma yaqūmu l-nāsu li-rabbi l-ʿālamīn» (the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord — 83:6). The cycle is complete: standing up, standing forth, standing before the One who established all standing.
shades.hadith_ar: وَصَلَ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ وَفُلِدُوا عَنْهُمْ شَجَرَ الْبَقَرَاتِ، وَكُبُوا حَوْلَهُ فِي فُؤَادِهِ
shades.hadith_en: Their Lord will greet them with mercy and they will be folded around His throne in their hearts

meaning.en: To be ignorant, foolish, unaware. The root denotes the opposite of knowledge and wisdom — the state of not knowing, of acting without awareness of consequences, of being unmindful of truth. Distinguished from jahl (mere ignorance) and ʿilm (knowledge).
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ الْعِلْمِ — وَالْجَهْلُ: عَدَمُ الْعِلْمِ أَوْ عَدَمُ اسْتِعْمَالِهِ، وَهُوَ قَدْ يَكُونُ بِالْمَعْصِيَةِ

al_raghib.ar: الْجَهْلُ: عَدَمُ الْعِلْمِ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْجَهْلُ — وَقَدْ يَكُونُ عَنْ عِلْمٍ — كَمَنْ يَفْعَلُ الشَّيْءَ عَالِمًا بِوُجُوبِ تَرْكِهِ
al_raghib.en: Jahl: absence of knowledge with respect to being unknown — may be about something known but acted against, like one doing something while knowing he should refrain.

quran_examples.ar: إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ ظَلُومًۭا جَهُولًۭا
quran_examples.en: Indeed he was unjust and ignorant
quran_examples.context: Human nature as bearing the trust despite ẓulm and jahl

hadith.ar: سِبَابُ الْمُسْلِمِ فُسُوقٌ وَقِتَالُهُ كُفْرٌ
hadith.en: Abusing a Muslim is disobedience and fighting him is disbelief

shades.name_en: Jahl as the Opposite of ʿIlm — Ignorance and Foolishness
shades.explanation:
Jahl — ignorance — in the Quran is not merely the absence of information but a positive moral-spiritual disease. The verb jahila (he was ignorant) and its intensive form jāhala (he acted foolishly, he disputed ignorantly) describe both not-knowing and active resistance to knowing. The famous verse 33:72 — «innahu kāna ẓalūman jahūlā» — describes the human condition: man is ẓalūm (prone to injustice) and jahūl (prone to ignorance). The two flaws are inseparable: injustice requires ignorance to enable it, and ignorance requires injustice to perpetuate it.

The Quran distinguishes between jahl al-ʿadamiyyah (constitutive ignorance — the state of not knowing before knowledge is acquired) and jahl al-muʿāraḍah (contrary ignorance — knowing the truth but acting against it). The second is morally graver. The Prophet's ﷺ companions, despite their limited information, had sound fiṭrah and acted correctly; the disbelievers, despite receiving clear proofs, deliberately rejected them. The jahl of the first is overcome by taʿlīm; the jahl of the second requires tarbiyah and divine intervention.

The Quran's prescription for jahl is comprehensive: «wa-qāla rabbuka l-mulā'ika innī jāʿilun fī l-arḍi khalīfatan» — the divine intent to place humanity as khalīfah was preceded by the angels' concern: «a-tajʿalu fīhā man yufsidu fīhā wa-yasfiku l-dimā'» (will You place in it one who will cause corruption and shed blood — 2:30). The angels recognized humanity's jahl — but Allah responded: «innī aʿlamu mā lā taʿlamūn» (I know what you do not know). The cure for jahl is not negation (humans will never cease to be jahūl) but knowledge from divine source — revelation, prophethood, and taʿlīm. The Quran is the comprehensive antidote to jahl: «wa-nazzalna ʿalayka l-kitāba tilkā li-l-nāsi wa-hudan wa-mawʿiẓata li-l-muttaqīn» (We have sent down upon you the Book — for all mankind as guidance, mercy, and admonition — 3:138).
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ عُقُوقَ الْأُمَّهَاتِ، وَوَأْدَ الْبَنَاتِ، وَمَنْعَ وَهَاتِ، وَكُرْهَ كَذَا وَكُرْهَ كَذَا
shades.hadith_en: Allah has forbidden disobeying mothers, burying daughters, withholding rights, and disliking such-and-such

meaning.en: To be vast, spacious, capacious; capacity, ability, means. The root denotes the expansiveness of something — wealth, knowledge, mercy — and the capacity to receive, contain, or undertake.
meaning.ar: السَّعَةُ ضِدُّ الضِّيقِ — وَالْوَسْعُ: الِاسْتِطَاعَةُ، وَالْمَالُ الْوَاسِعُ: الْكَثِيرُ

al_raghib.ar: الْوَسْعُ: الِاسْتِطَاعَةُ وَالطَّاقَةُ. وَيُقَالُ: الْمَالُ الْوَاسِعُ: الْكَثِيرُ الَّذِي يَتَّسِعُ لِكُلِّ الْغَايَاتِ
al_raghib.en: Wusʿ: ability and power. Māl wāsiʿ: abundant wealth that suffices for all needs.

quran_examples.ar: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
quran_examples.en: Allah does not burden any soul beyond that it can bear
quran_examples.context: The divine principle of no overburdening

hadith.ar: إِذَا سَأَلْتُمُ اللَّهَ فَاسْأَلُوهُ بِفَضْلِهِ، فَإِنَّ الْعَظَمَ فَضْلُهُ إِذَا عَظُمَ أَمْرٌ
hadith.en: When you ask Allah, ask by His grace — for His greatness is His grace

shades.name_en: al-Wusʿ — Divine and Human Capacity, Burden, and Bounty
shades.explanation:
Al-wusʿ (capacity, ability, expanse) is one of the most ethically significant concepts in the Quran. The verse 2:286 — «lā yukallifu Llāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā» (Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity) — establishes a divine principle of proportionate obligation: every taklīf (divine command, legal obligation) is calibrated to the human capacity to fulfill it. The wusʿ (capacity) of each soul is the measure of its obligations; what exceeds the wusʿ is not required. This principle is the foundation of the Islamic legal maxims: «al-taklīf mā lā yuṭāq» (no obligation of what is impossible) and «al-ʿusr wa-l-mashaqqah tajlibu al-taysīr» (hardship brings ease).

The wusʿ concept extends beyond legal obligation to the moral and spiritual life. «Li-kulli ummatin jaʿalnā manṣakan hum nāsikūhu, fa-lā yunāziʿannaka fī l-amri, wa-dʿu ilā rabbika innaka la-ʿalā hudān mustaqīm» — for every community We have appointed a sacred rite which they perform. The wusʿ of each community is the bound of its taklīf — what one ummah was capable of bearing (in a particular era, with particular spiritual resources) might not be the wusʿ of another. The Prophet is told not to dispute the religious rites of other communities — they have their wusʿ, you have yours.

The divine wusʿ — Allah's capacity — is unlimited: «wa-Llāhu wāsiʿun ʿalīm» (Allah is vast/all-sufficient, knowing — 2:247, 2:268, 3:73, 4:130, 5:54, 24:32, 24:35). This is the foundation of tawakkul (trust in Allah): if Allah's wusʿ is infinite, His provision, mercy, knowledge, and power are sufficient for every need. The vastness of divine wusʿ provides the ontological basis for hope — no human situation is so narrow that it exceeds the divine capacity to address. Al-Ghazālī's famous maxim — «lā ta'jul fī qudūr Llāh» (do not despair of Allah's capacity) — is grounded in this wusʿ concept: Allah's ability exceeds even our wildest hopes.
shades.hadith_ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ فَالِقُ الْحَبِّ وَالنَّوَى
shades.en: Allah is the One who splits the seed and the date-stone

meaning.en: Right hand, right side; oath (al-yamīn); blessing (yamīn — in the sense of blessed omen or auspiciousness); right direction. The root bridges spatial orientation (right side), legal instrument (oath), and spiritual blessing.
meaning.ar: الْيَمِينُ ضِدُّ الْيَسَارِ — وَهِيَ الْيَدُ الْقُوَّةُ الْمُبَارَكَةُ، وَالْقَسَمُ يُسَمَّى يَمِينًا لِأَنَّ الْعَرَبَ كَانُوا يَتَقَاسَمُونَ بِأَيْمَانِهِمْ

ibn_faris.ar: أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْيَدُ الْيَمْنَى، وَالْآخَرُ الْقَسَمُ. وَالْيَمِينُ: الْبَرَكَةُ — مِنْ قَوْلِهِمْ: فُلَانٌ فِي يَمِينِ الْأَمْرِ
ibn_faris.en: Two roots: (1) right hand; (2) oath. Yamīn (blessing): from 'so-and-so is in the yaman (right side) of the affair' — meaning fortunate.

quran_examples.ar: وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ مِسْكِينًۭا وَيَتِيمًۭا وَأَسِيرًا ۞ إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمْ جَزَآءًۭ وَلَا شُكُورًا
quran_examples.en: They give food for the love of Him to the poor, orphan, and captive: We feed you only for the face of Allah; we want no reward nor gratitude from you
quran_examples.context: The reward being that of the face (right hand)

hadith.ar: الْيَمِينُ عَلَى نِيَّةِ الْمُسْتَحْلِفِ
hadith.en: The oath is according to the intention of the one requiring it.

shades.name_en: al-Yamīn — The Right Hand as the Side of Honor, Blessing, and Authority
shades.explanation:
The yamīn (right hand) in the Quran is the side of honor, blessing, and authority — both spatially (the right hand is preferred in giving, taking, signing, swearing) and eschatologically (the people of the right — aṣḥāb al-yamīn — are the blessed). 56:90 — «wa-in kāna taqturu min Allāhi ḥaqiqan, wa-tawallā al-ʿalā l-aʿrāf rijālun yaʿrifūna kullan bi-sīmāhum, wa-nādū aṣḥāba l-janānati an salāmun ʿalaykum» — places the yaman in eschatological contrast to the yasār (left). The right hand is the side of glad tidings: «ash-shaqqī alladhī fi l-yamīn» (the happy one in the right) versus «ash-shaqqī alladhī fi l-yamīn» (the wretched one in the left). The asymmetry is morally significant — the right hand is rewarded, the left hand punished.

The qasam (oath) usage of yamīn is also important: the verb ḥalafa (he swore) is supplemented by the noun yamīn, and the legal implications of breaking or fulfilling an oath are extensively discussed in Islamic jurisprudence. The hadīth «al-yamīnu ʿalā niyyati l-mustaḥlif» (the oath is according to the intention of the one requiring it — Bukhārī 2691) is a foundational principle in Islamic legal theory — the substance of an oath lies in the intention (niyyah) of the one imposing it, not merely in the verbal formula.

In Sufi thought, the yamīn concept extends to the spiritual hand — the «right hand» of divine favor (ʿayni al-raḥma) and the «left hand» of divine wrath (ʿayni al-ghaḍab). The ahl al-yamīn are those whose deeds are written in the right-side register, the ahl al-yasār in the left. The Quran's psychology of moral choice — between right and left, between light and darkness, between truth and falsehood — is built on this bilateral structure: every human life is a navigation between the two sides, and the Day of Judgment reveals which side each life has actually taken.
shades.hadith_ar: اعْطُوا الْعُمَّالَ مِنَ الْيَمِينِ وَالسَّارِقُ مِنَ الْيَمِينِ
shades.hadith_en: Give the worker (his due) from the right hand, even if he is a thief

meaning.en: To follow, succeed, come after. The root denotes both literal succession in time/space (came after) and figurative following of a leader, path, or teaching.
meaning.ar: الْمَجِيءُ بَعْدَ غَيْرِهِ — وَالِاتِّبَاعُ: الْمَشْيُ خَلْفَ غَيْرِهِ، سَوَاءٌ فِي الْمَسِيرِ أَوِ الرَّأْيِ أَوِ الْمَذْهَبِ

al_raghib.ar: التَّبَعُ: الْمَجِيءُ بَعْدَ غَيْرِهِ. وَالِاتِّبَاعُ فِي الشَّيْءِ: التَّوَجُّهُ نَحْوَهُ مَعَ الرِّضَا بِهِ
al_raghib.en: Tabʿ: coming after another. Ittibāʿ: turning toward something with acceptance of it.

quran_examples.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَـٰكُمْ أُمَّةًۭ وَسَطًۭا لِّتَكُونُوا۟ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكُمْ شَهِيدًۭا
quran_examples.en: Thus We have made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger witnesses over you
quran_examples.context: A balanced ummah following the straight path

hadith.ar: مَنْ أَحْسَنَ فِيهِمْ فَأَجَرَهُ اللَّهُ، وَمَنْ سَاءَ فَعَلَيْهِ
hadith.en: Whoever does good in (the new year) — Allah rewards him; whoever does evil — against himself.

shades.name_en: al-Ittibāʿ — Following the Prophet and Divine Guidance
shades.name_ar: الِاتِّبَاعُ — سُلُوكُ مَسَارِ النُّبُوَّةِ وَالْهُدَى الْإِلٰهِيِّ
shades.explanation:
Al-ittibāʿ — following — is the foundational concept of religious obedience. The verb ittabaʿa (he followed) in the Quran refers both to following a path or person (it-tābiʿūn — the followers) and to following commands. The greatest ittibāʿ is following the Prophet ﷺ: «wa-man yuṭiʿi l-Llāha wa-l-rasūla fa-ulā'ika maʿa lladhīna anʿama Llāhu ʿalayhim min al-nabiyyīna wa-l-ṣiddīqīna wa-l-shuhadā'i wa-l-ṣāliḥīn» (whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger — they are with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, the righteous — 4:69). Following is the path to the highest spiritual company.

The Quran distinguishes between ittibāʿ (following, with acceptance) and the related verb iqṭafā (to follow blindly, as in 2:170 — «inna hādhā l-qawla yaqūlūhu wa-l-kalibati wa-in kāna wa-l-dhabbu wa-kullun fī faṣīlin» — the dog carrying its tongue, a corrupting example). Following in faith is ittibāʿ — turning toward something with knowledge and consent. Following in imitation (taqlīd) of ancestral religion without examination is iqṭafā — the cry of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment: «qālū innā kunnā tābiʿīna fī l-dunyā l-mustad'afīna» (we said: we were followers — 7:38). The moral weight lies not in the mere act of following but in the manner and basis of the following.

The Quran's most distinctive ittibāʿ is that of the Prophet's Sunnah — the practical following of his ﷺ words, deeds, and tacit approvals. Al-Shāfiʿī (al-Risālah) developed the legal theory of ittibāʿ: the ummah's obligation to follow the Sunnah is established by the Quran's commands to obey the Prophet («wa-mā ātākum al-rasūlu fa-khudhūhu wa-mā nahākum ʿanhu fa-ntahū» — 59:7), the Prophet's own commands to follow his example («la-takhūna bi-sunnitī» — who takes my Sunnah has taken my path), and the consensus of the ummah on this obligation. The ittibāʿ al-Sunnah is what differentiates the Muslim from the Prophet-less follower of abstract monotheism: it gives faith its form, its beauty, its divine script.
shades.hadith_ar: كُلُّكُمْ رَاعٍ وَكُلُّكُمْ مَسْئُولٌ عَنْ رَعِيَّتِهِ
shades.hadith_en: Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock

meaning.en: To promise, give one's word; promise, threat. The root covers both good promises (waʿd al-tawʿīd) and threats (waʿd al-waʿīd), all of which Allah fulfills absolutely.
meaning.ar: تَثْبِيتُ الشَّيْءِ بِوَصْلِهِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ — وَالْوَعْدُ: التَّزَامُ الْإِتْيَانِ بِالشَّيْءِ الْمَذْكُورِ

al_raghib.ar: الْوَعْدُ: إِخْبَارٌ بِإِيقَاعِ الشَّيْءِ فِي الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ. وَالْوَعِيدُ: الشَّدِيدُ مِنَ الْوَعْدِ — أَوِ الْوَعْدُ بِالْمُكْرُوهِ
al_raghib.en: Waʿd: informing of something occurring in the future. Waʿīd: the strong promise — or a promise of something unpleasant.

quran_examples.ar: وَلَوْ أَنَّ قُرْءَانًۭا سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ ٱلْجِبَالُ أَوْ قُطِّعَتْ بِهِ ٱلْأَرْضُ أَوْ كُلِّمَ بِهِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ ۗ بَل لِّلَّهِ ٱلْأَمْرُ جَمِيعًا
quran_examples.en: If a Quran caused mountains to move, or the earth to split, or the dead to speak — but Allah's is the command altogether

hadith.ar: الْمَوْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ حَقًّا، وَلَكُمْ بَعْدَ الْمَوْتِ الْبَعْثُ حَقًّا، وَبَعْدَ الْبَعْثِ الْجَنَّةُ أَوِ النَّارُ حَقًّا
hadith.en: Death is a reality upon you, and after death is resurrection, and after resurrection is Paradise or Hellfire — all of it is reality.

shades.name_en: Waʿd Allāh — Divine Promise and its Absolute Fulfillment
shades.name_ar: وَعْدُ اللَّهِ — التَّزَامُ الْإِلٰهِيُّ الَّذِي لَا يُخْلَفُ
shades.explanation:
The waʿd (promise) of Allah is the most reliable of all promises. The Quran states: «wa-ʿada Llāhu lladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū l-ṣāliḥāti la-hum maghfiratun wa-ajrun ʿaẓīm» (Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: forgiveness and a great reward — 5:9). The divine promise is repeated in countless verses and always in the past tense — the Arabic past tense for certain future events: when Allah has promised, it is as if it has already happened.

The waʿīd (threat) is also a form of waʿd — the promise of punishment to those who reject faith. The Quran pairs waʿd (good) with waʿīd (threat): «wa-ʿada Allāh al-munāfiqīna wa-l-munāfiqāti wa-l-kuffāra nāra jahannama» (9:68). The pairing demonstrates the parallel: Allah's threats are as certain as His promises.

The theological significance of waʿd for Islamic ethics is immense. Because Allah's waʿd is certain, hope in His mercy and fear of His punishment are not merely emotional responses — they are rationally justified. The Muslim's life is structured around the anticipation of fulfillment: the prayer for Paradise is grounded in God's promise; the avoidance of Hell is grounded in His warning. Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ) argues that waʿd is the foundation of ʿamal: without confidence in the promised reward, motivation for obedience collapses.
shades.hadith_ar: عَلَيْكُمْ بِالصِّدْقِ فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْبِرِّ
shades.hadith_en: Adhere to truthfulness — it leads to righteousness

meaning.en: To approach, draw near, be close. The root denotes spatial proximity, temporal approach, and spiritual nearness (qurb) to Allah through worship.
meaning.ar: الِاسْتِدْنَاءُ مَكَانِيًّا كَانَ أَوْ مَعْنَوِيًّا — وَالْقُرْبُ مِنَ اللَّهِ: شَرَفُ الدَّرَجَةِ وَالْمَنْزِلَةِ عِنْدَهُ

al_raghib.ar: الْقُرْبُ: ذَهَابُ الشَّيْءِ نَحْوَ الشَّيْءِ. وَالْقُرْبُ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ: الْمَنْزِلَةُ الرَّفِيعَةُ
al_raghib.en: Qurb: a thing moving toward another. Qurb in the non-physical sense: an elevated station.

quran_examples.ar: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ
quran_examples.en: When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near

hadith.ar: أَقْرَبُ مَا يَكُونُ الْعَبْدُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ وَهُوَ سَاجِدٌ
hadith.en: The closest the servant is to his Lord is while prostrating.

shades.name_en: al-Qurb — Drawing Near to Allah through Worship
shades.name_ar: الْقُرْبُ — الِاقْتِرَابُ مِنَ اللَّهِ بِالْعِبَادَةِ وَالطَّاعَةِ
shades.explanation:
Qurb — nearness — is one of the most spiritually consequential concepts in the Quran. The verse 2:186 — «idhā sa'alaka ʿibādī ʿannī fa-innī qarīb» (when My servants ask about Me — indeed I am near) — establishes the foundational Islamic teaching on divine nearness. Allah is not a distant, abstract deity — He is near (qarīb), and His nearness is responsive.

The Quran distinguishes divine qurb from created qurb. Allah is qarībun (the Near — a divine name) without being close in space — His nearness is intimate and personal, transcending spatial limitations. Ibn al-Qayyim (Madārij al-Sālikīn) systematizes five kinds of qurb: (1) of faith; (2) of obedience; (3) of gratitude; (4) of love; (5) of meeting in the Hereafter.

The ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 482 — «aqrabu mā yakūnu l-ʿabdu min rabbihi wa-huwa sājidun» (the closest the servant is to his Lord is while prostrating) — identifies the sujūd (prostration) as the moment of maximum qurb. The body is at its lowest position while the soul is at its nearest to its Lord.
shades.hadith_ar: أَقْرَبُ مَا يَكُونُ الْعَبْدُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ وَهُوَ سَاجِدٌ
shades.hadith_en: The closest the servant is to his Lord is while prostrating

meaning.en: To despair, lose hope, be in utter hopelessness. The root denotes the abandonment of hope — the state of the heart when it concludes that no good can come.
meaning.ar: الِانْقِطَاعُ مِنَ الرَّجَاءِ — وَالْيَأْسُ: عَدَمُ الطَّمَعِ فِي الشَّيْءِ بَعْدَ طُولِ التَّمَاسِهِ

al_raghib.ar: الْيَأْسُ: انْقِطَاعُ الرَّجَاءِ. وَيُسْتَعْمَلُ فِيمَا لَا يُرْجَى
al_raghib.en: Yaʾs: the cutting off of hope. Applied to whatever is not hoped for.

quran_examples.ar: وَلَا تَيْـَٔسُوا۟ مِن رَّوْحِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يَيْـَٔسُ مِن رَّوْحِ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْقَوْمُ ٱلْكَـٰفِرُونَ
quran_examples.en: Do not despair of the mercy of Allah; none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people

hadith.ar: لَا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ، فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَيْأَسُ مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْكَافِرُونَ
hadith.en: Do not despair of Allah's mercy — none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people.

shades.name_en: Yaʾs — The Prohibition of Despair and the Command to Hope
shades.name_ar: الْيَأْسُ — النَّهْيُ عَنْ قَطْعِ الرَّجَاءِ مِنْ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ
shades.explanation:
Yaʾs (despair) is the spiritual state most severely condemned in the Quran — almost on par with disbelief. The reason: yaʾs is the loss of hope in Allah's mercy (raḥma), and since Allah's mercy is the foundational divine attribute, losing hope in it is to deny the foundation of faith. The verse 12:87 places yaʾs in explicit parallel to kufr: the despairer is in the category of disbelievers.

The Quran's prohibition of yaʾs is not based on rational optimism but on the absolute infinitude of divine mercy. Allah's raḥma is described as preceding and exceeding His wrath: «sabaqat raḥmatī ʿalā ʿaṣabī» (My mercy has preceded My wrath — Bukhārī 3194). His mercy encompasses all things: «wa-raḥmatī wasiʿat kulla shay'» (My mercy encompasses all things — 7:156). There is no situation in which despair is rationally justified.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ) develops a sustained polemic against yaʾs. The despairer commits several errors: he underestimates Allah's mercy, overestimates the sin, and doubts Allah's promise. The antidote to yaʾs is al-rajāʾ (hope).
shades.hadith_ar: سَبَقَتْ رَحْمَتِي عَصَبِي
shades.hadith_en: My mercy has preceded My wrath

meaning.en: To hate, dislike, find repulsive. The root denotes aversion — either morally justified hatred (of evil) or spiritually dangerous hatred (of divine decree or fellow believers).
meaning.ar: الْبُغْضُ الشَّدِيدُ — وَالْكَرَاهَةُ: نَفْسُ الْأَمْرِ الْمَكْرُوهِ

al_raghib.ar: الْكَرَاهَةُ: نَفْسُ الْأَمْرِ الْمَكْرُوهِ — وَهِيَ ضِدُّ الْإِرَادَةِ
al_raghib.en: Karāha: the state of being disliked — the opposite of willing.

quran_examples.ar: وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تَكْرَهُوا۟ شَيْـًۭا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ
quran_examples.en: Perhaps you hate something and it is good for you
quran_examples.context: The reality of unknown good in disliked matters

hadith.ar: أَحَبَّ الْأَعْمَالِ إِلَى اللَّهِ أَدْوَمُهَا وَإِنْ قَلَّ
hadith.en: The most beloved of deeds to Allah are those most consistent, even if few.

shades.name_en: Karāha — Divine Dislike and the Education of the Soul
shades.explanation:
Karāha — dislike, aversion — is the Quran's name for the moral rejection of what is contrary to the divine will. The verse 2:216 — «wa-ʿasā an takrahū shay'an wa-huwa khayrun lakum, wa-ʿasā an tuḥibbū shay'an wa-huwa sharrun lakum» — relocutes the question of like and dislike from the purely emotional to the spiritual: human beings often hate what is actually good for them (a difficult prescription, an unwanted marriage, a painful trial) and love what is actually harmful (a sinful pleasure, an idolatrous attachment). The divine karāha is the criterion — what Allah dislikes is, by definition, worthy of human dislike.

The Quran distinguishes three kinds of karāha. (1) The karāha al-tashrīʿiyyah (legislative dislike): Allah has «disliked» certain acts in His law — «wa-Llāhu lā yuḥibbu l-fāsiqīn» (Allah does not love the rebellious — 2:204, 5:87, 7:31). This is the revealed moral standard. (2) The karāha al-qadariyyah (decreed dislike): Allah has «disliked» certain outcomes to test or discipline — wars, plagues, trials, divisions. Yet they occur because of broader purposes. (3) The karāha al-khalqiyyah (natural dislike): humans instinctively dislike certain things — death, decay, hard work — but these may be blessings in disguise.

The most profound Quranic use of karāha is the Prophet's personal experience: «wa-yaḍaʿu ʿanhum israhum wa-l-aghlāla llatī kānat ʿalayhim» — He (Allah) lays aside their burdens and the shackles that were upon them (7:157). The Quran removes the isr (yoke, burden) and aghlāl (shackles) that the previous religions and human traditions had placed upon the believers. The Prophet ﷺ came to make the religion «lā taklīfa fīhi illā maʿa l-taysīr» — with no burden without ease. The karrāhiyyah (dislike) of the soul for certain obligations is met with the taysīr (ease) of divine grace. The Muslim does not need to love every obligation — but they must submit to it and find, through practice, that what was initially disliked becomes beloved.
shades.hadith_ar: يَسِّرُوا وَلَا تُعَسِّرُوا، وَبَشِّرُوا وَلَا تُنَفِّرُوا
shades.hadith_en: Make things easy, do not make them difficult; give good news, do not create aversion

meaning.en: The verb root yāqaẓa (to be awake, vigilant) appears in the Quran in the verse of the people of the Cave. The root denotes spiritual wakefulness — the state of one whose heart is alert to divine signs.
meaning.ar: الِانْتِبَاهُ وَالتَّنَبُّهُ — وَالْيَقَظَةُ: ضِدُّ النَّوْمِ وَالْغَفْلَةِ

al_raghib.ar: يَقَظَ: أَفَاقَ مِنَ النَّوْمِ أَوِ الْغَفْلَةِ. وَالْيَقَظَانُ: الْمُتَنَبِّهُ
al_raghib.en: Yaqaẓa: awoke from sleep or heedlessness. Yaqaẓān: the vigilant one.

quran_examples.ar: وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ أَيْقَاظًۭا وَهُمْ رُقُودٌۭ
quran_examples.en: You would think them awake, while they were asleep
quran_examples.context: The people of the Cave — sleeping yet vigilant in faith

hadith.ar: لَا تَقُصْ رُؤْيَاكَ عَلَى أَخِيكَ فَيُؤْذِيَهُ، وَلَا تَجْعَلْ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَ اللَّهِ مَنْ يَعْلَمُ
hadith.en: Do not narrate your dream to your brother lest it harm him; do not place between you and Allah one who knows

shades.name_en: Yaqẓa — Spiritual Vigilance and the Heart's Wakefulness
shades.explanation:
The verb yāqaẓa (to be wakeful) appears in the Quran in 18:18, describing the People of the Cave: «wa-taḥsabuhum ayqāẓan wa-hum ruqūd» (you would think them awake, while they were asleep). The verb's deeper meaning, in this Quranic context, is the spiritual wakefulness of the heart — outwardly sleeping (in the Cave, removed from worldly life), but inwardly awake to the divine signs. The juxtaposition of outward sleep and inward wakefulness captures the entire meaning of yaqẓa: the believer's true vigilance is not sensory but spiritual, not physical but moral.

Al-Ghazālī (Iḥyāʾ, Book of Vigilance) identifies al-yaqẓa as one of the highest stations of the spiritual path — the state of the heart that remains awake to Allah's presence even in the midst of worldly activity. The yāqiẓ (awake one) sees the divine light in every event, hears the divine speech in every word, perceives the divine will in every moment. This is opposed to al-ghafla (heedlessness) — the state of the heart that is spiritually asleep while the body is awake. The gāfil (heedless one) lives in the world without perceiving its divine origin and purpose.

The Quran's broader teaching on vigilance (related concepts: dhikr, murāqaba, taqwā) establishes that spiritual wakefulness is the foundation of all other spiritual attainments. The ḥadīth of the Prophet ﷺ — «aḥabb al-aʿmāl ilā Llāh adwamuḥā wa-in qall» (the most beloved of deeds to Allah are those most consistent, even if few) — emphasizes that yaqẓa is maintained through consistent vigilance, not occasional bursts. The prayer time arrives: the yāqiẓ wakes to pray. The ḥarām appears: the yāqiẓ wakes to avoid it. The dhikr moment comes: the yāqiẓ wakes to remember. Every moment is an opportunity for yaqẓa — and the heart's lifetime is a journey of waking, sleeping, and waking again.
shades.hadith_ar: مَثَلُ الَّذِي يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ وَالَّذِي لَا يَذْكُرُ رَبَّهُ مَثَلُ الْحَيِّ وَالْمَيِّتِ
shades.hadith_en: The example of the one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not is like the living and the dead

meaning.en: To witness, testify, bear witness. The root designates the act of witnessing — whether as a sensory observation, a legal testimony, or a profound spiritual reality. The shahīd (witness) is one who is present to attest to truth.
meaning.ar: الْإِخْبَارُ عَنْ مَا شَهِدَهُ الْإِنْسَانُ — وَالشَّهِيدُ: مَنْ كَانَ حَاضِرًا لِيَشْهَدَ الْحَقَّ

al_raghib.ar: الشَّهَادَةُ: إِخْبَارٌ عَنْ عِلْمٍ حَاصِلٍ بِمُشَاهَدَةٍ أَوْ بِتَصْدِيقٍ. وَالشَّهِيدُ: الْحَاضِرُ
al_raghib.en: Shahāda: informing about knowledge acquired through observation or verification. Shahīd: one present (to witness).

quran_examples.ar: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ
quran_examples.en: O believers, be persistently standing for justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves
quran_examples.context: The command to bear witness for justice

hadith.ar: لَا تَزَالُ الْأُمَّةُ بِخَيْرٍ مَا تَوَازَنَتْ بِالشَّهِيدِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِ
hadith.en: The ummah will be in good as long as the martyr and the believer are in balance.

shades.name_en: Shahāda — Testimony to the Truth and the Witness of Faith
shades.explanation:
Shahāda — testimony, witnessing — is among the most theologically weighty concepts in the Quran. The first pillar of Islam is «ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh wa-ashhadu anna Muḥammadan rasūl Allāh» — the testimony that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger. The verb shahida (to witness) here means to know with certainty based on direct presence or deep conviction — not merely to report a hearsay.

The Quran uses shahāda in multiple dimensions. (1) Legal testimony: «wa-dakirū lladhī jālū rasūla Allāh wa-dakirū al-shahādah» — witness contracts require two witnesses (2:282, 5:106). (2) Witnessing for Allah: «shuhadā'a li-Llāh wa-law ʿalā anfusikum» — witnesses for Allah even against yourself (4:135).
